Trusting stdin there would turn every write into an _empty file_, so `ShellFs::connect` proves it
instead of assuming it: it runs `cat` with stdin `stdin-probe`, and the capability holds only if
`stdin-probe` comes back. `CommandRunner::run_with_stdin` defaults to `ErrorKind::Unsupported`, so a
runner without stdin support probes as absent too. Because a probe is only one sample (a
load-balanced endpoint mid-rollout can pass it on one replica and take the write on another), both
write scripts also check that the temp holds exactly `bytes.len()` bytes before the `mv`. A lost
stdin is then a `short write` error, and the old file is left intact.

stdin exists for `ShellFs`'s writes and nothing else. `bash` still runs every model command with
stdin closed (`Stdio::null()`).

**The response is capped.** `HttpExecRunner` reads the body incrementally, up to
`DEFAULT_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` (16 MiB; `--exec-max-response-bytes` on `run` and `serve`, where it
also applies to every per-session `set_exec_endpoint`). It stops reading at the cap, and a declared
`Content-Length` over the cap fails before any of the body is read. **An oversized response is an
error, not a truncated result.** The body is one JSON object, so a prefix cannot be parsed. There is
no honest partial `ExecResult` to hand back (the exit code may come after the output), and passing
off whatever fit as the command's output would be a confident wrong answer. The error says the
command _ran_, so the model narrows its output (`| head`) rather than blindly re-running something
that may not be idempotent. The cap bounds memory in a process that may serve many tenants, and it
sits far above anything a tool consumes (`bash` keeps ~30 KB), so legitimate output never meets it. It
applies to v1.1 objects only: a v1.2 stream is read a frame at a time, so a streaming `bash` with
huge output behaves as it does locally — a bounded tail and a truncation marker, not an error.

The endpoint must accept request bodies as large as the files the agent writes (≈4/3 of the file
size with `stdin_base64`).

`tests/exec_endpoint_writes.rs` covers 200 KiB writes through both a v1.1 and a v1 mock (the v1 one
must fall back to chunks, and never produce an empty file), the size check under a probe that lied,
every chunk boundary, and templates that forward stdin and ones that swallow it.
`tests/exec_endpoint_response_cap.rs` streams an endless body and a lying `Content-Length` at the
runner. `fs_backend_parity.rs` diffs both write paths against `LocalFs`: the ripgrep rung probes
stdin as present, and the POSIX rung pins it absent. The CI `exec-live` shard runs the chunked path
for real on busybox, since its `docker exec` has no `-i`.

#### What the remote world changes, tool by tool

Service mode (the agent running outside the sandbox, one replica serving many tenants; see "Service
mode — one replica, many tenants") is what makes this load-bearing.

`PathWorld` is not only about where the _bytes_ are. Once a backend is `Remote`, **no tool may
consult this host to decide anything** — not because a host syscall fails, but because it succeeds.
`is_dir` on a sandbox path, `$HOME`, `/bin/bash`, `canonicalize`, a `.git` in an ancestor: each
returns a confident, plausible answer about the wrong machine, and the mistake is invisible in the
output. On a replica serving many tenants it is worse than invisible — it is the host leaking into a
tenant's session.

Every tool takes its world from the backend (`FsBackend::world()`), asked **per call** rather than
captured, because `ExecCell` can be re-pointed by `set_exec_endpoint` with no registry rebuild.

| Decision                                                                       | Local                                            | Remote                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `~` in a path (`read`/`write`/`edit`/`ls`/`grep`/`find`) and in `bash`'s `cwd` | this process's `$HOME`                           | the target's home, or left as `~` when it isn't known                                       |
| a relative path with no tool root (`write_key`)                                | joined onto the process cwd                      | left relative — the replica's cwd is not the target's                                       |
| `write`/`edit`'s same-file key                                                 | `canonicalize` (unifies symlink aliases)         | lexical only                                                                                |
| `bash`'s `cwd` pre-check                                                       | `is_dir`, with pi's two messages                 | none; the remote shell reports a bad `cwd`                                                  |
| `bash`'s shell                                                                 | `/bin/bash`, else `bash` on `$PATH`, else `sh`   | `ToolConfig::remote_shell`, else `sh`                                                       |
| `bash`'s oversized output                                                      | spilled to a temp file, `Full output: <path>`    | no file; the marker says to redirect into the sandbox and read that                         |
| `bash`'s idle yield, progress and jobs                                         | always                                           | when the runner's output is live (v1.2 stream, template); over v1.1 the call waits for exit |
| `rg --no-require-git` (`ShellFs`)                                              | `.git` in an ancestor, host `stat`s              | the same walk run **on the target**, cached per root                                        |
| `grep`/`find` result paths with no tool root (`output::display_base`)          | relative to the process cwd, absolute outside it | as the search produced them — relative if typed relative                                    |

Two of those deserve their reasoning spelled out.

**`sh`, not `bash`, is the remote default.** Guessing `bash` would be the same mistake in a different
spelling: a busybox sandbox (Alpine — a large share of real ones) has no `bash` at all, so every
command would die on the shell rather than on its own merits. Losing `[[` and `pipefail` degrades a
command; losing the shell fails all of them. Whoever stands the sandbox up is the one who can ask it
(`command -v bash`) and pass the answer in.

**The spill file is conditional, and `bash`'s description says so** rather than promising one. The
world is asked per call, and `Tool::description` returns a `&str` — so a flag resolved in `new()`
would be a stale snapshot for exactly the session that attaches a sandbox mid-life, which is the
session that most needs the right answer. The description therefore states the condition ("whether
the complete output was saved to a temp file, or has to be re-run redirected to a file") and the
runtime marker (`output.rs`'s `full_output_segment`) says which case actually happened, with the
action to take when there is no file.

The git-repo probe is the one place the remote world _adds_ a round trip: one `sh` script per distinct search
root, memoized on the backend, walking ancestors for a `.git` with `dirname` and `[ -e ]` (not `git
rev-parse` — a sandbox with no git installed is ordinary, while a missing `.git` genuinely means "not
a repository"). It runs only on the ripgrep rung, since `--no-require-git` is a ripgrep flag and the
POSIX rungs honor no `.gitignore` at all.

`tests/fs_backend_remote_world.rs` and `tests/bash_remote_world.rs` make the host and the target
_disagree_ — a `$HOME` that isn't the sandbox's, a root inside a git repo here and not there, a
directory that exists there and not here — and assert the target's answer won, with the local half of
each behavior asserted alongside it.

### Run lifecycle

A run's plan, current tool, closing prose and outcome are otherwise only visible on a session
connection that a consumer has to hold for the whole duration. [`lifecycle`](src/lifecycle.rs) makes
that record a structured output of the host, independent of any client.

**This is telemetry, not a tool.** The runtime emits it. The model is never asked and cannot
influence it. Facts come from the loop (tool start/end, step counter, todo list, last visible
assistant text) and from the host (retry, persist, the response the client was told). It lives in
this crate, not `agent-core`: `AgentEnd` cannot see retry, persist, or the client response, and
deliberately does not fire on abort.

Unconfigured ([`NoLifecycle`](src/lifecycle.rs)): zero I/O, zero behavioural difference. A slow or
unreachable consumer is logged and dropped; `emit` never awaits the network.

A **run** is one accepted `serve` `prompt` (including whole-run retries) or one CLI `run` invocation.
Busy rejection is not a run. Subagent children are not first-class runs. Identity is host-minted
(`session_store::new_id()`). An optional client prompt `id` is echoed as `command_id`; `session_id`
is carried. Prompt `id` is optional and missing on CLI `run`, so it cannot be the primary key.

Spine: `started → progress* → succeeded | failed | aborted`. Exactly one `started` and one terminal
per `run_id`. Progress after terminal is dropped. `started` without a later terminal (SIGKILL) is
**unknown**, not failed.

`session_named` sits outside that spine. It carries the title a session generated for itself from its
opening exchange (see **Session titles** below) and is emitted at most once per session, between the
run finishing and its terminal event — so it is deliberately _not_ gated on the run-state machine
`started`/terminal share, and a consumer must not expect it in any particular position. Durable like
`started` and the terminal events rather than latest-wins progress: a consumer that misses it never
learns the title, because nothing regenerates one. It is a **session** fact rather than a run one,
which is why it is its own event instead of a field smeared across every terminal event — it becomes
true exactly once, and the consumer's job is a single upsert.

Terminal kind matches that host's client contract:

- `serve` natural end / `stop_after_turn`: `Succeeded`
- `serve` refusal: `Succeeded` + `refused: true` (client gets `success: true`)
- `serve` persist fail: `Failed`
- `serve` abort: `Aborted`
- CLI text-mode refusal: `Failed` + `refused: true` (`exit(1)`)
- CLI JSON-mode refusal: `Succeeded` + `refused: true` (exit 0)

#### Session titles

A session names itself once, from its first successful run, via one extra model call
(`agent_core::session_title`, `Agent::title_for`). It is the highest-priority field
`session_store::search_rank` checks and was `None` for every session nobody had explicitly named, so
the field ranked first was empty almost always.

Four properties, each of which is a cost decision rather than a quality one:

- **After the client has its answer.** The call runs after the `prompt` response is emitted, so its
  latency is never charged to the turn the user is waiting on.
- **At most once per session**, tracked by session id, not by `title.is_none()` — a failed attempt
  leaves the title `None`, so without the guard a model that reliably declines would charge an extra
  call on every turn, forever.
- **Never when there is no store.** `set_title` is a no-op without persistence, so the call could
  only be waste.
- **Never fatal.** A model error, a refusal, or an unusable reply all leave the session untitled and
  working. `session_title::clean_title` rejects rather than repairs: a wrong title is worse than
  none, because it is what a person scans for and what ranking weighs most heavily.

It is generated once and never regenerated — a session is about what it was opened for, and
re-titling it later would make it change names underneath whoever was looking for it.

**Why the agent and not the control plane.** A title is derived from conversation content, and in a
fleet the replica is the only component holding both the transcript and the tenant's key. Everything
else a session catalog wants — filtering, sorting, paging, facets — is derivable from the lifecycle
events a consumer already receives, and belongs there. See [FLEET.md](FLEET.md).

Progress is a latest-wins sample: tool **names** (never arguments), `steps`, optional
`attempt`/`todos`/`depth`. Todos ride on progress (full-replace). Emit on `ToolStart`/`ToolEnd`,
todo updates, and `TurnEnd`. An optional **heartbeat** timer (default 10s,
`--lifecycle-heartbeat-secs` / `AI_AGENT_LIFECYCLE_HEARTBEAT_SECS`; `0` disables it) re-POSTs only
if the sample has changed since the last POST — a long `bash` is one progress event, not one per
tick. Silence means unchanged, not dead. Heartbeat names the timer; the wire event is `progress`.
The closing summary is visible `Text` only (`agents::last_assistant_text`), capped
at 4000 Unicode scalars, attached on the terminal event.

Transport: one outbound worker, HTTP POST JSON. Durable queue for started/terminal (retry, then
log+drop). Per-`run_id` slot for progress (overwrite, no retry). A run id is forgotten once its
terminal POST has flushed or been dropped, so a long-lived `serve` does not retain one String per
run. Config:
`--lifecycle-url` / `AI_AGENT_LIFECYCLE_URL`, `--lifecycle-header` / `AI_AGENT_LIFECYCLE_HEADER`,
`--lifecycle-heartbeat-secs` / `AI_AGENT_LIFECYCLE_HEARTBEAT_SECS`.
The URL is validated at startup (`http`/`https`, or `unix:///path/to.sock` when the consumer shares
this machine — no host to name, no TLS to terminate); a typo fails before any session runs. Daemon
sessions share one `Arc<dyn RunLifecycle>` worker.

`tests/serve_lifecycle.rs` drives this against a real `serve`/`run` binary and a ~30-line mock
collector — the same shape as `tests/exec_endpoint.rs`.

### Shell tools — a shared `CommandRunner` seam

`bash` doesn't spawn processes directly; it goes through `tools::exec::CommandRunner` (as does
`ShellFs`), implemented for production by `RealRunner`
(`tokio::process::Command` with `kill_on_drop(true)`, a process-group leader — via a `GroupKillGuard`
RAII drop guard so a backgrounded grandchild is killed on _either_ a timeout _or_ the caller dropping
the future (cancellation) — **stdin closed** (`Stdio::null()`, matching pi's
`stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "pipe"]`) so a model-run command can never block reading the agent process's
real stdin (a shared terminal in `run`, or `serve`'s NDJSON control pipe), and **bounded streaming
capture** for the non-`bash` runner path). The
actual kill (`kill_process_group`) shells out to `kill -KILL -<pgid>` first and, if that doesn't
succeed, falls back to `kill -KILL <pgid>` (no leading `-`, targeting just the original process rather
than its whole group) — matching pi's own `killProcessTree`'s group-then-direct fallback — so a
sandboxing/permission quirk that rejects the group-scoped signal doesn't leave even the original
process behind with nothing else to reap it. This is
the same seam pattern as `agent_core`'s `Tool`/`ModelTransport` traits — it's what lets tests inject
a recording runner and assert the exact argv, and what lets `HttpExecRunner`/`TemplateRunner` run the
same tools remotely. `serve`'s own `bash`/`abort_bash` RPC commands run outside the model loop on a
separate host `bash` instance (`build_tools` with `bash_waits_for_exit`) over the same runner.

- **`bash`**: runs through a **resolved real `bash`** (`/bin/bash`, else `bash` on `$PATH`, else `sh` —
  `resolve_shell()`, cached), not a hardcoded `sh -c`, since a model-generated command routinely uses
  associative arrays/`[[`/`pipefail`/process substitution that a POSIX `sh` (often `dash`) rejects.
  `--bash-shell-path`/`AI_AGENT_BASH_SHELL_PATH` overrides auto-resolution outright (`Bash::with_shell_path`,
  matching pi's `shellPath` setting) — for an environment where the auto-detected binary is wrong.
  Existence is checked once, at CLI-argument time in `main.rs`, so a bad override fails the process
  immediately rather than surfacing as a confusing spawn error on the first `bash` call, and so the
  check doesn't have to be threaded through every `build_tools` rebuild (`set_model`/`set_thinking`
  each rebuild the registry from `ServeConfig`). `--bash-command-prefix`/`AI_AGENT_BASH_COMMAND_PREFIX`
  (matching pi's own `shellCommandPrefix` setting) prepends a line to every command in the same shell
  invocation (`Bash::with_command_prefix`) — the tool-level method existed, fully tested, well before
  either binary had a way to actually set it; both `run_task` and `serve`'s `build_tools` now reach it
  through `ToolConfig::bash_command_prefix`, read by `default_registry_with_config`.
  `timeout_ms` decides when the call returns, never when the command dies (see "`bash` timeouts"
  below); it is validated as a positive integer capped at `MAX_TIMEOUT_MS` (`i32::MAX` ms, pi's own
  `resolveTimeoutMs` bound). The tool's model-facing `description` (`describe()`) states the truncation
  budget and the windows after which a call returns, rendered at construction from the instance's own
  idle window, so a `bash` that waits for exit (`serve`'s host command) does not promise a job.
  Output streams through one `OutputAccumulator` (`tools/output.rs`): a rolling byte tail
  (`DEFAULT_MAX_BYTES`, 50 KiB) is kept for display while the _complete_ stream spills to a temp file
  once it outgrows that window (`"Full output: <path>"` marker), so the model can go read the whole
  thing if the tail isn't enough; while the command runs, `ToolProgress` streams an initial empty
  update then throttled snapshots (`UPDATE_THROTTLE`, 100 ms) of the output so far, plus truncation
  details, ahead of the final result. A **live** (not-yet-finished) snapshot holds back any trailing
  bytes that look like an incomplete multi-byte UTF-8 sequence (`incomplete_utf8_suffix_len`, keyed off
  `str::from_utf8`'s own `error_len() == None` — "ran out of input mid-sequence" — case) rather than
  lossily decoding them to `U+FFFD` right away, matching pi's stateful `TextDecoder({stream: true})`,
  which withholds an incomplete trailing sequence until the rest of it arrives in a later chunk; a chunk
  boundary landing mid-character (e.g. splitting a 4-byte emoji across two `append` calls) used to show
  a transient replacement character in the interim progress update even though the full character was
  never actually lost, just not fully buffered yet. Once `finish()` has run there's no more data coming,
  so the same held-back bytes (if still incomplete) fall through to the ordinary lossy decode — a
  genuine truncation, not an in-flight boundary. The combined text is run through output hygiene — ANSI/OSC escape
  stripping and C0 control-char sanitizing so terminal/binary noise can't corrupt the model's context —
  before either an `(no output)` placeholder (success, genuinely silent) or an appended status line
  (`"Command exited with code N"` / `"Command was killed by SIGKILL (9) …"` / `"Command timed out after N
  seconds: the sandbox's exec endpoint stopped it."` (only a runner's deadline; `bash` sets none) /
  `"Command cancelled"`, all but the success case with no placeholder glued in front). Only an exit code of
  literally `0` is success: `ExitStatus::code()` is `None` for a signal-terminated process, so `ExecResult`
  carries the signal alongside the code (`exec::exit_signal`, Unix-only) and `bash` reports it as a failure
  naming the signal. Previously that `None` shared an arm with `Some(0)` and an OOM-killed build, a SIGSEGV,
  or a SIGTERM'd server all reported **success** to the model — silently, with `(no output)` standing in for
  the output the command never got to produce. A cancellation kills the call's own fresh command like
  a `bash_job` kill (dropping the `Job`), so a backgrounded grandchild process can't outlive it. A job
  that already has a number is different: cancelling a `bash_job` wait on it (an `abort`, or a
  command that ends the run) parks it again and returns "Wait cancelled; job N is still running.",
  because the model was told how long that job lives and a cancelled wait must not end it. Cancellation is
  cooperative, not just an external `Drop`: `attach` races the running job against the call's own
  `ToolProgress::cancelled()` (the same `CancellationToken` a caller like `serve`'s `abort_bash` trips),
  and on a trip flushes whatever the always-current `OutputAccumulator` already captured before
  returning — matching pi's `bash-executor.ts`, whose own accumulator is independent of its throttled
  progress callback and so is never stale at cancellation time. Without this, a command that produced
  output early and then went quiet (e.g. `printf …; sleep 30`) could lose that output entirely on
  cancellation: the throttled `ToolProgress` snapshot the caller would otherwise have to rely on may
  never have fired for it (a burst arriving within one `UPDATE_THROTTLE` window of the previous emit is
  suppressed until the _next_ chunk, which here never comes).
- **`bash` and hung commands (`IDLE_YIELD`, `bash_job`)**: a command that prints nothing for
  `IDLE_YIELD` (60 s) returns its output so far plus "still running as job K"; the command is **not**
  stopped. In the longctx eval, 12 calls over 100 s were 65% of
  all `bash` wall time, and every 30-minute timeout was an infinite loop in freshly written code: the
  output stops (or, through `| tail`/`> log`, never starts) and the command never exits. The eval's
  legitimate full suites finish in under 17 s with gaps of at most 4 s between outputs, but a clean
  release build of this repo goes **204 s without output**. So silence is grounds to _ask_ the model,
  never to kill.
  - Every call runs as a `Job` on its own task (`exec_detachable`); `attach` waits on the job's
    shared state (output, its shell leaving processes behind, its end — one `Notify` for all three),
    its yield deadline and the call's own cancellation. New output gets its live update even when the
    command ended right behind it.
  - **A call always returns.** Besides the silence window, the call that starts a command returns by
    `OUTPUT_CEILING` (10 min) however much it prints — a server logging requests used to hold its call
    until the 30-minute timeout — and a `bash_job` wait returns by `WAIT_CEILING` (5 min). Both sit
    above the 3 min 44 s release build of this repo, so a build that prints as it goes still finishes
    in the call that started it, or in one wait.
    The yield text names the reason: "No output for N s", "Still printing after N s", or "Returned
    after your timeout_ms of N ms" (nothing, for a `bash_job` peek).
  - **`bash_job`** (`{job, kill?, timeout_ms?}`, `JOB_TOOL`) is registered over the same `Bash`
    instance and its job table, and follows `bash` through every tool filter (`filter_allows`). A call
    reports the output since the last report: the final result (at once, for a job that already
    ended), or "Job N is still running (…)" — short, since the start told the model how to use the
    job. `timeout_ms` means what it means on `bash` (how long this call waits; the job keeps running
    and its exit is noticed), in the same words in both schemas, and is validated the same way before
    the job leaves the table — except that 0 is allowed: a **peek**, returning at once with what the
    job printed since. On `bash` 0 would return before the command printed anything; on a running
    job it is the cheap way to see a server's or watcher's latest output. `kill` stops every process
    the job started and waits for them (a `timeout_ms` sent with it is ignored). These are not
    optional fields on `bash` because gpt-6-luna fills every property of a schema (`"job": 0` on
    every call in a live probe; `"kill": false` on every `bash_job` wait).
  - **One silence window for every attach** (`idle_window`): 60 s for the call that started the
    command and for each `bash_job` wait. It used to grow ×4 per report (60 s, 240 s, 960 s), so a
    legitimately silent build was reported once instead of every minute; that was designed before
    finish notices. Now an early return costs one model turn (Luna's median turn in the background
    A/B: 2.5 s, p90 4.8 s) and the model hears the exit regardless, while a grown window costs its
    whole length on a job that never exits. In that A/B (8 background tasks × 3, Luna) all 8 waits
    that ended on silence were on servers or watchers that never exit, each returned exactly at its
    window with no new output (so the report was all there when the wait began), and the one grown
    window was a 240 s wait on a watcher; the 4 legitimate waits were on a build printing every
    2.5 s, which no window touches. Without growth a 240 s silent build costs two more turns (~5 s);
    one grown wait on a watcher cost 180 s more.
  - **Remote worlds yield when their output is live.** A runner promises live output by reporting a
    `Kill` through `run_streaming_tracked` (see "Streaming (v1.2) and killing remote commands"):
    `RealRunner`, `HttpExecRunner` once its endpoint has passed the v1.2 probe, and `TemplateRunner`
    all do, and from then on a remote job yields, streams progress, is noticed when it ends, is evicted
    and is carried through compaction exactly as a local one. A v1.1 endpoint streams nothing, so its
    silence says nothing about the command; there the call still waits for exit (`idle_window` is
    `None` while `remote && !live`), and `bash`'s description names that exception rather than
    promising a job that never comes. `track` wakes the waiting call, which computed its idle deadline
    before the output was known to be live. Adoption (below) is this host's alone: on a remote stream
    the endpoint owns the process group and ends the stream when the shell exits.
  - **`serve`'s host `bash` command waits for exit** (`ToolConfig::bash_waits_for_exit`,
    `Bash::with_idle_yield(None)`): it has no `bash_job` to come back with. What its command leaves
    running is still adopted into the session's table, so the model sees it. Its wire `timeout_ms` is
    the client's own deadline: the `serve` handler cancels the call at it (the same cancel as
    `abort_bash`) and reports "Command timed out after N seconds"; it is never handed to the tool.
  - A `Job` owns its task and its processes. Dropping it kills the command: a call whose future is
    dropped, a cancelled call, or a dropped table leaves nothing behind. `kill_live_jobs` runs in
    `finish_process_cleanup` before every `process::exit`, which runs no destructors. How to stop the
    command reaches `bash` through `CommandRunner::run_streaming_tracked` as a `tools::exec::Kill`:
    this host's job processes (`Kill::Procs`, below), or a runner's blocking hook (close a v1.2
    stream, or kill through a template's transport). `bash_job` kill, `Job`'s `Drop` and
    `kill_live_jobs` all call `Kill::kill`, so local and remote jobs die by the same three paths.
  - Evidence (seeded-hang sqlparse, an injected infinite loop; Haiku and Luna): hang wall time
    fell from a median 2,096 s to 480 s on Haiku (−77%, 6/6 fixed in both arms) and from 1,952 s to
    396 s on Luna (−80%; 11/12 fixed against 6/6, the miss a run that killed the hang and then spent
    its 30-step cap exploring). On a legitimately silent build of 100 s and of 240 s (2 Haiku + 1 Luna each) every
    run was reported once and finished in the wait that followed (under the ×4 window growth, since
    removed: see "One silence window for every attach"): one extra turn per long command, none for the
    control. The first, fixed-window version cut hang time 87%, but a wait also yielded
    after 60 s of silence. A `sleep 100` that took ~130 s inside `bash` in that run took 130 s in the
    control arm too, and 100.0 s on a quiet host, bare, in the eval's PID namespace and through
    `bash`: it was host load, not output polling or the process-group wait.
  - Deleted arms: `--bash-yield-secs` (a wall-clock schedule, Codex's `yield_time_ms` shape; untested
    and superseded) and `--bash-timeout-guidance` (advise sizing `timeout_ms`; a "probably stuck"
    hint), which left hang wall time unchanged (Haiku 2,416 → 1,946 s median, Luna 1,952 → 1,907 s,
    within noise) and lost a Luna pass.
- **`bash` jobs: the model is told, never made to poll (`tools/bash_jobs.rs`)**. In 10,779 eval
  `bash` calls models never backgrounded anything themselves, every yield on a code task was a real
  hang, and in 27 of 85 yields the model kept working while the job ran — two parked infinite loops
  were never waited on or killed. The field's recurring failures (Claude Code, Codex, opencode,
  Gemini CLI, OpenHands, read from source) are making the model poll, `cmd &` leaving an invisible
  orphan, relaunching a job compaction made it forget, and servers outliving the session. So the job
  table (`BashJobs`) is an `agent_core::Background` (see "Background work" under Core Mechanism):
  - **Finish notice.** A parked job that ends becomes, at the loop's next tool-results turn (or at a
    would-stop, before the run may end), one text: `[job N exited with code C after S s:`cmd`]` (or
    "was killed by SIGx", "timed out after S s (the sandbox's exec endpoint stopped it)", or "ended … (the processes its
    command left running have exited)"), the last `NOTICE_TAIL_LINES` (20) lines since the last
    report, and `bash_job {"job": N} returns the full output.` A job whose shell exits while parked
    but leaves processes running gets one notice saying so, and becomes adopted. A job reported by an
    attached `bash_job` wait is never parked when it ends, so it gets no notice. An ended job stays in
    the table, output unread, until `bash_job` reads it — at most `MAX_ENDED_JOBS` (8), the oldest
    dropped first, and the next notice says which were dropped. The yield text says "You will be told
    when it exits, so do not poll it or sleep".
  - **Kinds decide lifetime and caps (`JobKind`).** `Yielded` (its call returned early — silence,
    the ceiling, or the model's `timeout_ms`: foreground work the model expected to finish) never
    outlives the turn —
    `BashJobs::end_turn` stops it when the run ends, however it ends, in `run` and `serve` alike, so
    an idle session never accumulates hung loops — and is evicted, oldest first, past
    `MAX_YIELDED_JOBS` (4). `Background` (`run_in_background`) and `Adopted` (the command left
    processes running) are intended — the model asked for them: each lives until it exits, is killed,
    or its owner ends; neither is ever evicted, and together they are capped at `MAX_INTENDED_JOBS`
    (8): a background start past it is refused before the command runs, an adoption past it is
    stopped at once, and either result lists the running jobs to stop first. A yielded job whose
    shell exits leaving processes running becomes adopted; a background job stays background. Every
    result that parks a job says its lifetime ("it is stopped when you end your turn", "it is stopped
    for you when the run ends", "it keeps running after your turn ends").
  - **The end of a run.** At a would-stop with jobs running that no earlier reminder listed, the model
    gets one `[background jobs]` reminder (id, command, age, why it is a job) — at most one per run
    (the loop's gate), and each job is listed once (`Job::reminded`, kept on the job so a `bash_job`
    wait that takes it out and parks it again does not make it news), so ending again ends. The
    reminder says what ending does, per kind, then "If you still need a job's result, wait for it
    with bash_job {"job": N}; otherwise just end your turn." (`REMINDER_ASK`). It used to offer "Wait
    for one (bash_job {"job": N}), stop it (…), or end your turn": in the background A/B 3 of the 8
    waits on never-exiting servers came right after it, and in 2 of 24 runs it fired again after the
    model waited or started a job (one run 3 times). A stopped job is said to be "stopped for you (no
    need to kill it)" — most of that A/B's 44 kills were cleanup the end did anyway — and in `serve` a
    kept job's line says how to stop one no longer needed. Yielded jobs are stopped; intended ones
    follow the host's `EndPolicy` — `run` stops them
    with the process (`BashJobs::stop_all` after the last turn), `serve` leaves them running and wakes
    the idle session when one ends (see the `serve` data flow). Every stopped job is reported with its
    `kind`: in `run` as one `bash_jobs_stopped` line in `--json` (before any structured output) and on
    stderr; in `serve` as a `bash_jobs_stopped` frame before the prompt's terminal response. Every
    stop (`end_turn`, `stop_all`, in `run` and `serve` alike) runs on the blocking pool, never the
    runtime thread: a v1.2 job's kill waits for its stream's future (on that runtime) to let the
    connection go, so a stop run inline starved it — each remote job cost the kill's full 2 s bound,
    and its stream closed only at the process exit (`tests/bash_jobs_stop_remote.rs`). A
    subagent's jobs end with its registry. These ends, a `bash_job` kill, and the caps are the only
    things that stop a job: there is no per-command kill deadline (see "`bash` timeouts").
  - **One table per owner.** `ToolConfig::bash_jobs` hands `bash` the host's table: `run`'s, or the
    `serve` session's (kept on its `ExecCell`, so a `set_model` rebuild keeps the jobs). `None` (a
    subagent) is a table of the registry's own. `serve`'s host `bash` command (the client's, not the
    model's) gets a third: `host_bash_jobs`, a table of the session's that nothing takes notices from.
    What a client's `cmd &` leaves running is parked there, so it never wakes the model (a paid turn
    nobody asked for, quoting output the client may have excluded from context), never appears in a
    notice, reminder or carry, and the result says "it runs until the session ends" instead of
    `bash_job` instructions (an instance that never detaches has no `bash_job`). It survives a
    transcript switch (the processes are the client's, not a history's) and is stopped, unreported,
    when the session ends; ended entries are dropped at the next host command (`forget_ended`).
  - **Compaction carries the table** (`Background::carry`): running and ended-unread jobs (id,
    command, state, age) as a `<background-jobs>` block beside every summary, so a compacted model
    does not start a job again. Rendered from the live table and attached as a request-only block on
    the summary message: never in the persisted summary, `CompactionProvenance` or the MCP App
    context sidecar, because after a restart the jobs are gone and a persisted copy would describe
    them as running. A reopened summarized session's first request instead says no jobs are running,
    which also corrects a summary whose prose claims one is (`tests/bash_jobs_serve_carry.rs`).
  - **Reopen (`Background::resume`).** A table reads the transcript of the first run it serves —
    once, and again after `stop_all` (a `serve` transcript switch) resets it — because a reopened
    session's jobs are gone: `serve`'s session end (service-mode reap after detach, every deploy,
    the daemon's idle reaper, a restart) and `run`'s exit stop them. It used to restart ids at 1 and
    tell the model nothing, so a reopened model took a dead dev server for live, and a new job got
    id 1 again — `bash_job {"job": 1, "kill": true}` killed the wrong process. Now the counter is
    seeded past the highest id the transcript mentions (`bash`/`bash_job` calls and results, notices,
    a summary's prose, assistant text — an over-count only skips numbers; other tools' results are
    not read), and the jobs it shows still running at its end (a `bash` result that parked one,
    minus finish notices, `bash_job` results that are not "still running", evictions, and yielded
    jobs a later prompt's turn-end stopped) are listed in one `[background jobs]` note (`reopen_note`,
    the one place it is written) — "no longer running … New jobs are numbered from N" — attached
    as a request-only block to the run's prompt: in every request of the process (a stable cached
    prefix), never persisted, never saved by the MCP App context sidecar
    (`background::is_process_state`), so each later reopen re-reads the transcript and says it
    again. Summarized or not; a summarized session also still gets its `<background-jobs>` block. A
    kill result names the command it killed (``Job 3 (`npm run dev`) killed after 4 s.``). Tests:
    `tools/bash_jobs_reopen_tests.rs` (the reader, seeding, a kill), `tests/bash_jobs_reopen.rs`
    (a `serve` restart and `run --continue`). A remote job the sandbox kept (next item) is not
    gone: it is in the table again by the first run, and the note lists it as "(still running)"
    under its old number, separately from the ones that were stopped; one that ended meanwhile is
    left to its finish notice. While the read-back is still deferred (a reopened service session
    that has not used its sandbox, next item but one), the note does not guess: an intended job
    the transcript left running is listed "(not yet checked)", with how to check one now. The
    read-back reports each of them later — one it found is in the table (running, or ended with its
    notice due), one it did not gets a `[job N is no longer running: …]` notice, once
    (`BashJobs::set_pending_reattach`).
  - **A killed process's survivors (`BashJobs::stop_survivors`).** A SIGKILL or an OOM kill runs no
    exit path, so the local jobs that process ran — background, and a foreground command still
    attached — outlive it. Each local job's processes are journaled in the session as they spawn:
    a sealed `bash_job_procs` custom entry (`PROCS_ENTRY_KIND`, one of `HOST_CUSTOM_KINDS`, so a
    client cannot plant one) holding its process group, the leader's start time and its tag, and
    again with its job number once parked (`BashJobs::set_recorder`: `run` appends through its
    `RunJournal`; `serve` sends through its journal channel, stamped with the session). The next
    process to open the session (`run` before its first turn; `serve` at start and on every
    transcript change) reads them back and stops the survivors before the first run: a record counts
    only if a live process carries its tag (a group number alone proves nothing), and is then
    stopped as any job is — tag and group, the group only while the recorded leader still holds
    the number (`exec::GroupId`'s recycled-pgid guard), SIGTERM, the grace, then SIGKILL
    (`exec::kill_all`). Never a tag the reopening process itself carries. The reopen note then says
    what is true per job: "stopped now", "could not be stopped" (naming what is left, processes of
    another uid), or "not running" (stopped when the session closed, or exited); a foreground
    command is named by its command. Sandbox jobs are never journaled here: the sandbox owns them
    and they are reattached (next item). Tests: `tools/bash_jobs_reopen_tests.rs`,
    `tests/bash_jobs_reopen_after_kill.rs` (SIGKILL a `run` and a `serve` with a background and a
    foreground `sleep`, reopen, both are stopped and the note says so).
  - **Remote jobs belong to the sandbox (`tools::bash_sandbox`).** A session's table has a job
    scope (`BashJobs::set_scope`: `serve` and `run` set `JobScope::for_session(tenant, session)`;
    a subagent's table and `serve`'s host table have none and keep the stream-owned lifetime). With
    one, and a sandbox that passes the job probe, every remote command runs as a sandbox job
    (`exec_endpoint::jobs`, see "Sandbox jobs"): held, so a foreground command still dies with its
    call, its turn or its replica — the endpoint kills the held start's stream on disconnect and the
    keeper kills the job within half a second. When the command becomes an intended job — parked by
    a background start's settle, or adopted at its shell's exit, including a parked yielded job
    whose shell exits (`notices` keeps it from there) — the table **keeps** it under its job number
    and kind with the offset of the output already shown (`bash_sandbox::keep`); under
    `EndPolicy::KeepRunning` the job is then **released**: dropping it (a reap, a deploy, a crash,
    the session's end) only lets go of its stream, and the exit path's `kill_live_jobs` skips it.
    Only a kill (`bash_job`, the `Kill` hook running the sandbox's `kill`, which also deletes the
    directory), an explicit end, or the sandbox's own end stops it. Each later report of its output
    records `seen` in the sandbox. Ends: `serve`'s session end calls `BashJobs::release` (stop
    what this process owns, let go of what the sandbox owns); a transcript switch (`new_session`,
    `switch_session`, a switching fork) and `delete_session` are explicit ends — `stop_all`, then
    `bash_sandbox::wipe` of the old (or deleted) session's scope, so nothing of it outlives the
    switch even if the table had lost track; `run` (`StopAtEnd`) kills kept jobs at its end as
    before. The lifetime text says so: "it keeps running in the sandbox until it exits, you stop it,
    or the session ends". Over v1.1 nothing can be held, so a background job starts kept and is
    followed by polling: `run_in_background` now works there, and a foreground command still waits
    for its exit. A kept job whose held stream breaks (a network blip) is followed by polling from
    where the stream left off instead of being reported failed.
  - **Reattach (`bash_sandbox::reattach`).** Where a session opens (`serve_session` after its exec
    target is set, again after a transcript switch; `run` before its first turn) the table lists the
    scope — unless its sandbox is attached lazily and not built yet (`ExecCell::pending`: a
    reopened service session, see "Sandbox snapshot"), which listing it would wake. Then
    `bash_sandbox::reattach_later` defers it, and `bash_sandbox::reconcile` runs it, once (single
    flight), the first time it is needed: at the top of a `bash` call that runs in the sandbox (after
    `CommandRunner::ready`, before anything new is numbered), at a `bash_job` call (a job asked
    about is checked first; a probe that fails then is that call's error), or at the top of
    `serve`'s loop once anything else has woken the sandbox. Because it answers a caller asking right
    now, it reads each running job's new output in before handing it to its follow (`read_in`, a few
    `read`s from the `seen` offset) and waits, bounded, for the ends of the jobs it found already
    ended — so a peek straight after shows what a job printed while nobody was attached, and a job
    that ended as ended. A read-back that fails stays pending for the next use. Test:
    `tests/bash_sandbox_jobs.rs`'s deferred reattach, over every transport. A kept job with a number is the session's: under `KeepRunning` it is parked again under
    that number (the id counter is raised past it), released, followed from its `seen` offset — so
    a peek or its notice shows only what is new — with its shell's exit already reported; one that
    ended meanwhile gets an ordinary finish notice timed by the sandbox's `end` epoch (which, in
    `serve`, wakes the idle session like any other end). Under `StopAtEnd` it is killed, as the run
    that started it would have. Everything else — a held job whose replica died, a kept start whose
    number was never recorded because the call that started it was lost — belongs to a turn that is
    over and is killed. **Delivered once:** a reported end (a notice, or a `bash_job` result) queues
    the job's directory for deletion, and the host deletes them where the reports are known to be
    persisted (`BashJobs::collect_garbage`: the top of `serve`'s loop, the end of `run`), so a replica
    that dies after noticing but before persisting leaves the job for the next replica to notice
    again, and one that persisted never repeats it. Tests: `tests/bash_sandbox_jobs.rs` (a background
    job, an adoption and a yielded command across a dropped table and a reattach, over the v1.2 mock,
    the v1.1 mock and a template transport; the ended-while-detached notice exactly once; a replica
    that dies before persisting; `StopAtEnd`; `release`; the reopen note) and
    `tests/bash_jobs_serve_sandbox.rs` (a real `serve` process ends, the job runs on, the next one
    reports it still running, peeks its new output, and kills it; a job that ended between processes
    is noticed once). Across real replicas, `crates/fleet-sim` grades it on the local-directory and
    NFS substrates, over a v1.3 sandbox and a v1.2-only one: `sandbox-job-survives-its-replica` (a
    dev server started on one replica, that replica killed outright, the session reopened on the
    other: listed "not yet checked" until the model's first look, then still running, its output
    read on from the seen offset, killed from there) and `sandbox-job-exit-noticed-once` (a build
    that finishes while its replica drains away is noticed exactly once on the next, at its first
    `bash`).
- **`run_in_background` (`Start::Background`, `JobKind::Background`)**. A boolean on `bash`, not a
  tool of its own: in the background-shell probe (1,500 trials on Luna, Sol, Kimi K2.7 Code and Qwen
  3.8 Flash with the real system prompt and tools) it beat a separate start tool on every model, was
  never set wrongly on 400+ short commands (Luna and Sol send `false` on every call), and backgrounded
  server starts 88% (Luna, Sol), 73% (Kimi, plus 13% its own `docker -d`) and 50% (Qwen) of the time.
  The description sentence and the field text are the measured wording. A background call is refused
  before anything runs when it could not outlive its call — the runner cannot track a job
  (`CommandRunner::tracks_jobs`: false for a v1.1 endpoint, which can neither stream nor stop a
  command) and there is no sandbox to own it (a v1.1 sandbox with a job scope runs it as a kept
  sandbox job) — or when `MAX_INTENDED_JOBS` are already running. Otherwise the command starts as a job and the call waits `BACKGROUND_SETTLE` (1.5 s), or
  less if it exits: a command that dies at once reports its exit in this result, not as a notice a
  turn later. Measured time-to-exit of failed starts on the dev box (three runs each): a bad flag or
  missing command 1–3 ms, Python and Node servers on a port in use 24–90 ms, `npm run`/`npm start` with
  a missing script 76–112 ms, `npx` of a missing package 330–587 ms, `docker run` of a missing image
  907–979 ms; 1.5 s covers the slowest with half again in hand, and a good start pays it once. Still
  running at the settle, it is parked as an intended job and the result is its first output (or "(no
  output yet)") plus "Running in the background as job N (its lifetime). You will be told when it
  exits, so do not poll it or sleep." and the three uses spelled out: a peek (`timeout_ms: 0`) to see
  what it printed since, a wait only "to wait for it to finish (a build or a test run, not a
  server)", and a kill. The A/B's waits on servers and watchers wanted their latest output — after an
  edit, or to check readiness — not an exit. A `bash_job` wait on it that yields re-parks it as
  background.
- **`bash` timeouts: none kills a command.** The probe showed models read `timeout_ms` as "hand back
  control after this long" (Codex's `yield_time_ms`; Claude Code also backgrounds at its timeout):
  with a killing `timeout_ms`, Luna started servers with `timeout_ms: 1000` in 12 of 23 tries, Sol gave
  long builds and suites 10 s in 12 of 30, and in the 701-run eval 30 of the 37 timeouts were short
  model-chosen ones that killed real work. So `timeout_ms` is exactly that now: the call returns at
  it (`Yield::Timeout`, "Returned after your timeout_ms of N ms") and the command keeps running as a
  yielded job. It only ever makes a call return sooner: the idle window still catches a hang. The
  30-minute default kill, `--bash-timeout-ms` and its env var are gone, and
  `CommandRunner::run_streaming_tracked` takes no timeout: a job lives until it exits, its kind's
  owner ends it (turn, run, session), a `bash_job` kill, or a cap. Two places still need a deadline,
  both internal and never model-facing:
  - **A runner that cannot track a job** (the trait's default `run_streaming_tracked`; an exec
    endpoint on v1.1) gets `exec::UNTRACKED_DEADLINE` (30 minutes): it streams nothing and reports no
    `Kill`, so without a deadline a hung command would hold its call forever. There `timeout_ms`
    cannot hand control back either (the call waits for exit, as P0 already did), and a call that
    outlived its `timeout_ms` says so: "This sandbox's exec endpoint cannot return before a command
    exits, so `timeout_ms` had no effect."
  - **The v1.2 wire** requires a `timeout_ms`. A streamed job sends `exec_endpoint::STREAM_DEADLINE`
    (`i32::MAX` ms, ~24.8 days — the longest a Node endpoint's `setTimeout` holds): the connection is
    the job's lifetime, and the deadline only bounds one that outlives every session.

  A runner's own deadline still surfaces honestly ("Command timed out after N seconds: the sandbox's
  exec endpoint stopped it.", with N measured). `serve`'s host `bash` command keeps its wire
  `timeout_ms` as the client's deadline, enforced by the handler as a cancel (see above). Tests:
  `tools/bash_background_tests.rs` (settle, immediate failure, eviction, the shared cap, timeout
  returns and keeps running, lifetimes and reminders per host, `bash_job`'s peek and `timeout_ms`),
  `tests/bash_background_run.rs` and `tests/bash_background_serve.rs` (one reminder per run, then
  each kind's end), `tests/bash_background_remote.rs`.
- **What a command leaves running is adopted, never leaked (`tools/bash_proc.rs`)**. `cmd &`, a
  daemon, `nohup`: when the shell exits with processes it started still alive, the call returns its
  output plus "The command exited but left a process (`…`) running; it is tracked as job N:
  bash_job {"job": N, "kill": true} stops it", and the job keeps streaming their output (if they hold
  the pipe) until they exit. Previously `GroupKillGuard` was disarmed when the shell exited, so such a
  process was untracked and outlived the agent. The requirement is that nothing a command starts
  outlives the agent untracked, including `setsid`, `nohup … &`, `timeout` (its own process group)
  and double forks; the mechanism was picked on what each candidate does in the places the agent runs:
  - **Process-group liveness** (`kill(-pgid, 0)`) misses exactly the processes most likely to outlive
    the agent: `setsid`, a daemon's double fork and `timeout` all leave the group.
  - **A cgroup v2 per job** (`cgroup.kill`, `cgroup.events`) is the strongest, but needs a delegated,
    writable cgroup. Measured on the dev box (Debian 13, kernel 6.12): the agent runs in
    `/user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-c12.scope`, owned by root and mode 755 — no subgroup can be
    made. GitHub-hosted runners put the job in a root-owned system service's cgroup, and the agent's
    container image (`Dockerfile.agent`, ECS) mounts `/sys/fs/cgroup` read-only by default. It would be
    a mechanism that works almost nowhere the agent runs.
  - **`PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER` plus descendant tracking** keeps orphans in the agent's tree, but on
    its own cannot say which job an orphan came from. (The agent is now a subreaper anyway, see "The
    agent as its descendants' subreaper" below, which also answers how it reaps without taking
    tokio's exit statuses; a job's processes are still found by the tag.)
  - **Chosen: an environment tag** (`TAG_ENV` = `AI_AGENT_JOB_TAG`). Every job's shell starts with a
    unique tag (agent pid, start time, sequence; appended to any inherited tag, so an agent run inside
    another agent's job is still stopped by the outer one). An environment survives `fork`/`exec`,
    `setsid`, `nohup`, `timeout` and double forks, and `/proc/<pid>/environ` (the environment a process
    started with) is readable for our own uid without privilege — on a dev box, in CI, in a container
    and in a Firecracker guest alike. A job's processes are the live (non-zombie) ones that carry the
    tag **or** are still in its process group (which also covers one that cleared its environment),
    **or** descend from one of those, **or** were found by an earlier scan: membership is keyed by
    pid and start time and lasts the process's life, so a descendant found through its parent stays
    the job's after that parent exits. Descent is what reaches a process that both cleared its
    environment and left the group while its parent chain is intact (`setsid env -i …`). One scan
    reads every `/proc/<pid>/stat` once, resolves descent in memory, and is taken **before** any
    signal is sent, so a process that exits on the TERM cannot re-parent a descendant out of reach.
    **The group number is ours only while the group lives**: once the shell is reaped and the group
    empty (a `setsid` leftover has left it), the kernel may hand the number to an unrelated process,
    which can lead a group with it — and a job that matched or signalled "group `pgid`" would claim and
    SIGKILL a stranger (reproduced by recycling the pid inside `unshare -Urpf --mount-proc`). So the
    shell's start time is recorded at spawn (`exec::GroupId`): the group is signalled as a unit only
    while the shell itself holds the number (alive or a zombie), and group membership counts only
    until a scan finds the group empty after the reap or the number held by another process
    (`GroupId::recycled`) — then the tag alone, each kill pidfd-verified. `exec`'s `GroupKillGuard`,
    the MCP sweep after a reap and a template transport's local group kill skip a recycled number the
    same way, and kill by pid only while the leader holds it
    (`bash_proc::tests::a_recycled_group_number_is_never_claimed`, which skips where `unshare` is
    unavailable).
    A full scan of `/proc` is cheap: 1,145 processes, 68 of them ours, read in 7 ms by an unoptimized
    Python probe on the dev box. It runs only when a shell exits, on a kill, and on each wake of an
    adopted job's wait.
  - **Waiting and killing.** After the shell exits, the pipes get the same 100 ms quiet grace as
    before, then the scan; with survivors, `on_orphans` tells `bash` at once and the runner keeps
    draining while it waits on a pidfd per survivor (readable when it exits; rescanned when all have,
    in case one forked) — no polling where pidfds exist. A kill (`ProcGroup::kill`) sends SIGTERM to
    the group and every scanned pid, waits up to `TERM_GRACE` (300 ms, returning as soon as the scan
    is empty), then signals the group with SIGKILL and sweeps the scan until it comes back empty,
    each pid signalled through a pidfd opened _before_ re-checking that it is still the process the
    scan saw (same start time), so a reused pid is never hit. TERM first because SIGKILL cannot be relayed: `sudo cmd` forwards a
    TERM to its root child (gone ~40 ms later on the dev box), while a KILL takes `sudo` down alone
    and leaves the child, which we may not signal, running. Stopping several jobs (`stop_all`,
    `end_turn`) goes through `exec::kill_all`, which spends one grace for all of them. A process
    that refuses the signal (`EPERM`: another uid) ends the sweep and is reported — in the
    `bash_job` kill's result (an error, not "killed") and as `survived` on the job's
    `bash_jobs_stopped` entry — instead of being claimed killed. No deadline bounds the
    wait: the job's `Kill`, or dropping the call, ends it. No name-based kill anywhere (`pkill -f` matching the harness is a known failure
    elsewhere).
  - **What escapes:** a process that clears its environment (`env -i`) or whose environment we cannot
    read (another uid, setuid, a process that made itself non-dumpable, e.g. `ssh-agent`), that left
    the group, **and** whose parent had already exited before any scan saw it. A `SIGKILL` of the
    agent itself runs no exit path, and a job's shell carries no parent-death signal (that would put
    the trampoline stdio MCP servers use in front of every `bash` call); the next process to open the
    session stops what it left running ("A killed process's survivors" above). Another unix falls back to
    the process group alone (liveness polled every 250 ms), which misses `setsid` and `timeout`.

### The agent as its descendants' subreaper (`subreaper.rs`, Linux)

`main` makes the agent a child subreaper (`PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER`) before anything is spawned, so
whatever a descendant orphans (a browser double-forked by a stdio MCP server, a `bash` command's
`nohup … &`) re-parents to the agent instead of init and stays in its tree. That has one
obligation: the agent must reap those orphans' zombies, or they accumulate (and count against
`RLIMIT_NPROC`) for the life of a daemon. A `waitpid(-1)` would also take exit statuses that tokio
and std `Child` handles are waiting for. So:

- **`main`'s work moves to a thread named `main`** (the main thread's 8 MiB stack, so nothing a deep
  future does can tell), which exits the process with the status `main` would have returned (101
  after a panic).
- **The main thread only reaps:** `waitpid(-1, __WNOTHREAD | __WALL)`, children of the main thread
  alone. The kernel re-parents an orphan to the subreaper's first live thread, which is the main
  thread, while every child the agent spawns is a child of the thread that spawned it, so this
  reaps orphans and never a handle's child. With no orphan to wait on it looks again every second
  (an orphan's arrival wakes nothing); with one it blocks in `waitpid`.
- **The invariant this rests on:** a thread that spawns a child outlives it or waits for it. Runtime
  threads live as long as the process; blocking-pool closures wait for what they start; stdio MCP
  servers come from the `mcp-spawner` thread. A child whose spawning thread exits first is
  re-parented to the main thread too, and its handle would then see `ECHILD`.
- **Nothing else is confused by it:** no code reads a child's parent pid (the `bash` tracker matches
  by tag, group and descent, and stops a descent walk at the agent itself); the `web` parser child,
  `bash` shells and exec-endpoint transports are the agent's own children, waited on by their
  handles as before.

`tests/mcp_stdio_orphans.rs` shows a server's `setsid` grandchild re-parented to `serve`, killed when
the idle server is reaped, and its zombie gone while `serve` keeps running. Elsewhere (macOS) the
module is a no-op and `main` runs as before.

---

## Interactive approval — the human-in-the-loop gate

`approval.rs` is the second consumer of `AgentHooks::before_tool_call`, alongside `ToolPolicy`'s static
deny-lists, and the second instance of this codebase's one human-in-the-loop seam pattern (the first is
`oauth::LoginCallbacks`): an abstract `ApprovalGate` trait, one implementation per host. `serve --approve`
installs `ServeApprovalGate`, which broadcasts an `approval_request` frame to every attached client,
parks a `oneshot` behind a drop guard, and resolves it from a later inbound `approve` command. Nothing in
`agent-core` changes. `run` has no gate: it has no client to ask.

The decision order in `gated_before_tool_call` is load-bearing:

1. **A static deny wins outright, with no round trip.** Asking a person to approve what the operator
   already forbade is pointless, and a way to social-engineer past the deny-list.
2. A tool outside the gated set (`--approve off|writes|all|tools:a,b`) runs unimpeded. An
   unrecognized value is a startup error, not a silently empty gate.
3. A remembered decision answers without asking.
4. Otherwise, ask.
5. **Every failure to get an answer denies.** Timeout, abort, and "no client attached" all produce an
   error `tool_result` the model reads, and the run continues. A gate that fails open on absence provides
   no security — and denying is what keeps a detached background session from blocking forever on a
   question nobody will ever see. (`running` stays `true` for the whole prompt, so a hang would pin the
   session against the idle reaper until an `abort`.)

"Always allow" is keyed on `(tool, scope_key)`, and `scope_key` is deliberately narrow: the **resolved
absolute path** for `write`/`edit` (same canonicalization the policy and the tools use, so `../` and
symlink spellings can't evade a remembered decision; a multi-file `edit` is keyed on its whole sorted
set of paths, so an "always" for one file never approves a call that also writes another), the
**verbatim command string plus its resolved working directory** for `bash` (the `cwd` argument
resolved like a `write` path, else the tool's root — `rm -rf *` approved in `build/` must not run
unasked in `$HOME`), the **method and URL origin** for `web` (`POST https://api.example.com`), and the
bare tool name otherwise. Not a command prefix: `git status` vs `git push` is not fixable with prefixes,
and exact matching fails safe — the only cost is re-asking when a command varies by a byte.

`web` is read-only (`READ_ONLY_TOOLS`) only while it sends nothing. A call whose method isn't
`GET`/`HEAD`, or that carries a body or custom headers (`approval::web_sends_data`), is gated as a
write by both `--approve writes` and `--approve all` (`GatedSet::is_gated_call`): reading a secret and
POSTing it out must not need zero prompts. A plain `GET` still doesn't ask.

Two implementation notes worth keeping:

- **Questions are serialized by a width-1 `tokio::Mutex` inside the gate**, not by
  `ToolExecutionMode::Sequential`. One sequential-requesting call reroutes the loop's _entire_ batch
  through its interleaved dispatch path — a cross-cutting change to execution semantics in service of a
  UI concern. Approved calls still run concurrently afterward.
- **A queued call re-checks the session memory before it is asked.** Same-key calls dispatched together
  all miss the memory before any of them is answered, so `ask_gate` checks it again once it holds the
  `ApprovalRuntime`'s `asking` lock, which spans the question and the remembering of its answer: an
  `allow_session`/`deny_session` given while a call was queued applies to it, and the user is asked
  once. The MCP-skill gate (`SkillSession::decide`) does the same with its own lock and memory. (`run`
  has no interactive gate: nobody can be asked there.)
- **`approval_resolved` has no OAuth analogue** because a login is a single-client RPC. An approval fans
  out to N attached clients of which exactly one answers; without a resolution frame the others keep a
  dead prompt on screen. The losing client's `approve` returns `accepted:false` — a race it can lose, not
  an error.

Subagent children inherit the gate for the same reason they inherit the deny-lists: a child that could
run `bash` without the human's approval _is_ the bypass. They share the parent's `ApprovalRuntime`, so
they queue behind the same one-question-at-a-time lock (eight parallel children must not raise eight
simultaneous prompts) and read the same `SessionMemory`. That sharing **widens privilege across the
tree** — an "always allow" granted to one child applies to its siblings and the parent for the rest of
the session. Intended, and load-bearing for "don't re-ask", but a real property. Each child stamps its
own `origin: {agent, spawn_id}` so a UI can say _reviewer#7 wants to run bash_ rather than _something
does_.

**The scope really is the session.** `new_session` and `switch_session` clear the `SessionMemory`,
alongside the `/session` memory re-point, the exec-endpoint detach and the MCP-kit reset they already
did. Without that, a decision the operator made about one conversation's commands and paths silently
pre-approved the next conversation's and the gate never asked. It is cleared **in place, through the
shared `Arc`** rather than swapped for a fresh one: the `ApprovalRuntime` is cloned by value into
every subagent, and a same-model `switch_session` skips `build_agent` entirely, so a swap would leave
live clones answering out of the old map. `fork`/`clone` deliberately do **not** clear it — unlike
exec and MCP, this is not a cross-tenant rule (a fork cannot cross a tenant), and a fork carries the
same conversation forward, so its remembered decisions still describe what is on screen.

## `structured_output` — the agent as a callable function

`tools/structured_output.rs` turns a run into something a script or a parent agent can call: a caller
supplies a JSON Schema, the tool advertises it **as its own `input_schema`**, and the model fills it in
the way it fills in any other tool call. The payload is validated (`jsonschema`), captured into a
host-owned `OutputSlot`, and the run ends via `ToolOutput::terminate`.

Three properties are load-bearing:

- **The slot is host-owned.** `serve` rebuilds its registry on every `set_model`/`set_thinking`, so a
  value captured into the tool itself would vanish on a mid-run model switch. The host holds the slot,
  clears it before each run, and reads it once the run drains.
- **Registration happens after `--tools`/`--exclude-tools` filtering**, like `subagent`. An allow-list
  scopes what the agent may _do_; silently stripping the one tool the invocation exists to add would
  leave a run that can never satisfy its own contract.
- **There is no `tool_choice` forcing.** It is per-request (so pinning it would stop the model doing any
  work before it answers) and the OpenAI Chat Completions dialect ignores it outright. The contract is
  carried by a system-prompt section — gated on `PromptOptions::has_structured_output` — plus
  `terminate`. A run that ends without a payload is reported as a failure rather than papered over.

A schema can be **model-authored** (a parent writing its child's), so nothing may panic on a hostile
one. It is compiled once at construction, never at first call, and a compile failure is returned to
whoever wrote it. `jsonschema` is built with `default-features = false`: that disables `$ref` resolution
over HTTP and the filesystem, so a schema cannot make the agent fetch a URL or read `/etc/passwd`.

Three hosts surface it, all reading the same slot:

| Host       | In                                                           | Out                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `run`      | `--output-schema` (inline or a file), `--output-description` | payload as the **last stdout line** (compact, so `… \| tail -1 \| jq` works); `--json` wraps it as one final `{"kind":"structured_output"}` line. Exit 1 if the model never produced one; exit 2 for an unusable schema, before any model call is billed.                                                                                                                                       |
| `serve`    | `prompt {output_schema, output_description}`                 | `data.structured_output` on the terminal `prompt` response — `null` when the model didn't answer, **absent** when no schema was asked for. Per-prompt, not per-session: installing, changing, or removing a schema rebuilds the tool set and the prompt section through the same path `set_model` uses.                                                                                         |
| `subagent` | a task's own `output_schema`                                 | `ChildOutcome.text` becomes the compact JSON instead of the child's last assistant message. A child that never calls the tool _fails_ its task — a paragraph is not the typed answer the parent asked for. A worktree note on a typed result travels beside it, `{"output": <payload>, "note": "…"}`, so the result stays one valid JSON value; without a note the payload is returned exactly. |

## `web` — a "curl for agents"

`tools/web/` gives the agent a window to the web: `fetch` (status + headers + body), `markdown`
(readable page text), and structured extraction — `outline`, `locate`, `extract`, `table` — that keeps
raw HTML _out of the context window_. It's modeled on [ax](https://github.com/yusukebe/ax), including
the `title=a, href=a@href` row spec (`a@attr` reads an attribute, else text) and the `--where` filter
grammar (`price > 100 && name ~ /^foo/i`, a hand-rolled panic-free evaluator in `whereexpr.rs`).
Dispatched by an explicit `mode` rather than ax's flag-inference — clearer for a model. Output is a
compact header-once TSV with a trailing `[N row(s); M more not shown]` note, since a tool has no stderr
the model reads. Body/time caps are ax's: 20 MB, 30 s.

**Egress safety is the load-bearing part** (`web/ssrf.rs`). ax is a local CLI a human runs; this is a
server fetching URLs the _model_ chose. Because a plain fetch is read-only (in `READ_ONLY_TOOLS`, so
`--approve all` never prompts on a `GET` — only a call that sends data is gated), the SSRF filter is the
**sole** boundary between the model and an internal fetch. So it **fails closed**: if the hardened client (resolver, timeout, no redirects) cannot be built — the builder errs or panics — the call fails and nothing is sent; there is no fallback to a default client (`a_client_that_cannot_be_built_fails_the_call_and_sends_nothing`). The MCP Events direct-HTTP client fails closed the same way. It is deny-by-default, in two layers:

- **A validating `reqwest::dns::Resolve`.** reqwest connects to exactly what the resolver returns, so
  checking every resolved `SocketAddr` validates the _actual_ connection IP — on the initial request and
  on every redirect hop — closing the resolve-then-reconnect (DNS-rebinding) TOCTOU gap a bare hostname
  check leaves open. Only if the client resolves the target at all: through a proxy it dials the proxy
  and hands over the hostname, so an ambient `HTTP(S)_PROXY`/`ALL_PROXY` would have the proxy fetch
  `localhost` for us. The client is built with `no_proxy()`, as are the grant-connector clients
  (`McpEgress` and the exit `DELETE`) — `tests/egress_proxy_env.rs`.
- **`validate_url` on every hop.** Non-http(s) schemes and literal-IP internal targets are refused
  before any DNS; redirects are followed manually (`Policy::none()`, capped at 5) so each hop is
  re-validated, which also blocks an `http → file:` scheme downgrade.

Each followed hop is rewritten the way the fetch spec (and browsers and curl) rewrite it
(`web::Hop::follow`): a 303, or a 301/302 answering a `POST`, becomes a `GET` with no body and no
`Content-*` headers, while a 307/308 keeps the method and body. When the scheme, host or port changes,
every caller-supplied header except `Accept`, `Accept-Language` and `User-Agent` is dropped for the rest
of the chain — an allow-list, because a header's name (`X-Api-Key`, a bespoke token header) says
nothing reliable about whether it carries a credential. And a hop that would still send data (a method
other than `GET`/`HEAD`, or a body) to a different origin is **refused**, with an error naming the new
URL: approval for a data-sending call is keyed on the origin the model named (`approval::scope_key`),
so following a cross-origin 307/308 would deliver the approved body somewhere nobody approved. The
model calls the new URL itself, as its own call, through the gate. (Carrying the approval forward per
hop was rejected: the tool would need the gate inside it, and a human asked mid-call about a URL the
model never chose has less to go on than the model's own explicit retry.)

Every blocked range is an explicit octet/segment check rather than a std helper, following the IANA
IPv4/IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries: every block that isn't globally reachable is refused —
v4 `0.0.0.0/8`, loopback, RFC-1918, link-local incl. `169.254.169.254`, CGNAT `100.64/10`,
`192.0.0.0/24`, documentation, `192.88.99/24`, benchmarking `198.18/15`, multicast and `240/4`; v6
loopback/unspecified, ULA `fc00::/7`, link-local, deprecated site-local `fec0::/10`, multicast,
local-use NAT64 `64:ff9b:1::/48`, discard-only `100::/64`, `2001::/23` (incl. Teredo), documentation
(`2001:db8::/32`, `3fff::/20`) and SRv6 `5f00::/16`. IPv6 forms that embed an IPv4 — mapped
`::ffff:a.b.c.d`, compatible `::a.b.c.d`, NAT64 `64:ff9b::/96` and 6to4 `2002::/16` — are unwrapped
and re-checked as their embedded v4 (`[64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe]` is the metadata endpoint through a
DNS64/NAT64 gateway); a public embedded v4 passes, as an IPv6-only host needs. MCP's HTTP egress
(`McpEgress`) uses the same `EgressPolicy`, so the same table. `--web-allow-private` and
`--web-allow-host <host>` open it back up; the allowlist is also what makes a loopback test fixture
reachable. The tool owns its own `reqwest::Client` (the gateway's `shared_http` is h2-pinned with a
10-minute timeout, the wrong shape), and subagents inherit the parent's egress policy via
`ChildToolConfig` — a child that could reach internal URLs the parent couldn't is the same bypass class
the deny-list/approval inheritance already guards.

Deferred (not v1): a disk/parse cache (ax's ~2 min) — the registry is rebuilt on every `set_model`, so a
tool-held cache would reset mid-session, the same gotcha `todo`/`structured_output` documented; revisit
as host-owned. And JS rendering — ax doesn't either; static DOM only.

## MCP tool names

Every MCP tool, resource and prompt is registered as `mcp__<server>__<name>`,
`mcp__<server>__resource__<name>` or `mcp__<server>__prompt__<name>` (`tools::mcp::registered_name`).
That name is what the model sees and calls, and Anthropic and OpenAI both require
`^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$` of it: one bad name in the tool list fails every turn, deferred or not (native
deferred loading still sends the definition). Servers name things freely — server-postgres's
`"users" database schema`, server-everything's `Resource 1`, the TypeScript SDK's `README.md` — so:

- **Normalised.** Each character outside the set becomes `_`; valid names are untouched. A name past
  64 keeps its `mcp__<server>__[kind__]` prefix, is cut to 55, and gets `_` plus an FNV-1a hash of the
  remote name — fixed by definition, so a transcript names the same tool in every build.
- **Never parsed back.** Each tool keeps the name the server knows beside the registered one
  (`McpTool::remote_name`, the resource's URI, `McpPromptTool::prompt_name`; MCP Apps keeps a
  registered → remote map), and calls go out under that.
- **Collisions are skipped.** Two remote names that normalise alike (`get.file`, `get file`): the first
  listed keeps the name, the rest are skipped with a warning; a skills server's
  `mcp__<server>__skill__read` is taken first.
- **Server names are checked** (`tools::mcp::server_name_error`): 1–32 of `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`, no `__`, not
  starting or ending in `_`. The server is read back by splitting on the first `__`
  (`server_name_from_registered`, used by the enable switches, tool search, Apps and the skills gate),
  so `a__b`'s `c` and `a`'s `b__c` would otherwise be one name credited to the wrong server. A
  configured server with a bad name is skipped with a warning before anything is dialed; a grant
  connector with one is a 400.

`tests/mcp_names.rs` drives the real names through `run`.

## Deferred MCP tools — tool search, no interpreter

By default MCP tools are not sent to the model up front. Three typical servers (playwright 25 tools,
github 26, filesystem 14) cost 16,225 Claude / 6,002 GPT tokens of schemas in every request when sent
eagerly, before the model does anything — and each MCP name used to be repeated once more in the
system prompt's `with tools: …` line (another ~925 tokens; that line now lists built-ins only, in every
mode). Instead the model sees one tool, `tool_search`, whose description is a compact catalog of
server and tool names, and loads what it needs.

**The pieces.**

- `ToolRegistry::register_deferred` ([`agent_core::tool`](../agent-core/src/tool.rs)): a deferred tool
  is callable by name like any other but absent from `definitions()`. Its definition travels separately
  on every request as `ModelRequest::deferred_tools` (sorted, so byte-stable).
- [`tools/tool_search.rs`](src/tools/tool_search.rs): the tool. Its description is the catalog (one
  line per server listing tool names, within 4 KB; past that a server collapses to its count). A
  query is keywords, a server name, or exact names; results are the tools matching the most query
  terms (so "github add" is github's `add`, not every github tool and every `add`), best first, at most
  `limit` (5 by default). Stateless, like `todo`. Matching (`tool_search::Index`, shared with Code
  Mode's `tools.search`) is on normalized words, not phrases: names and descriptions are split on
  `_`, `-`, `.` and camelCase humps, lowercased and plural-folded, so "get file contents",
  `getFileContents` and `get-file-contents` all find `get_file_contents`, "list issue" finds
  `list_issues`, and a word only the description has still matches (weakest). Deterministic: no
  embeddings, ties in name order. An earlier Code Mode search matched the whole query as one
  substring and returned `[]` for "get file contents"; `tests` in `tool_search.rs` pin these cases
  against the real catalogs in `eval/mcp_catalogs/`.
- [`agent_core::deferred`](../agent-core/src/deferred.rs): **a successful `tool_search` result loads
  every deferred tool it names.** The model read those names, so the transcript is the one record of
  what is loaded: it survives a resume, a `serve` reattach and a switch of dialect mid-session with
  nothing extra persisted. A compaction that summarizes the result away unloads the tool again; the
  model searches again if it still needs it.
- Each dialect puts a loaded tool in front of the model the cheapest way its vendor allows, below.

`--mcp-tool-loading` / `AI_AGENT_MCP_TOOL_LOADING` (`run` and `serve`, inherited by subagents) picks
`search`, `eager`, or `auto` (the default): `search` once the MCP tools' serialized definitions pass
`AUTO_SEARCH_MIN_BYTES` (8 KB, about ten typical tools). `--code-mode` takes precedence over all three.
A server's skill loader (`mcp__<server>__skill__read`) is never deferred, since `<available_skills>`
tells the model to call it by name. Filtering: a deferred tool rides with `tool_search` — an allow-list
that keeps `tool_search` keeps the catalog behind it (minus `--exclude-tools`), `--tools read,bash`
drops both (as it drops eager MCP tools), and when `tool_search` itself is filtered out the deferred
tools an allow-list named explicitly are advertised instead (`tool_search::refresh`). `get_mcp` and
`--export` still list deferred tools.

### Per provider: how a load reaches the model, and the prompt cache
