| Route                                                                                                        | Mechanism                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Cache across a load                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Anthropic Messages, Claude Opus/Sonnet/Haiku 4.5+ and Fable/Mythos — direct, through the gateway, or Bedrock | Every deferred definition rides in `tools` with `defer_loading: true` (out of the model's context and the billed input); the cache breakpoint stays on the last advertised tool (a deferred one can't carry it). The `tool_search` result becomes `tool_reference` blocks only — a result holding one may hold nothing else — which the API expands in place. | Intact: `tools` never changes. Measured: the request after a load read the full prefix from cache and wrote only the new tail (11,425 read, 0 written in a probe). |
| OpenAI Responses, GPT-5.4+ through OpenAI itself (direct or the gateway's byte relay)                        | Deferred definitions are not sent up front; an `additional_tools` developer item right after the `tool_search` output carries the loaded ones.                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Intact: the item is conversation, not prefix. Measured: 7,590 of 7,763 input tokens cached on the request after a load.                                            |
| Everything else — Chat Completions, aggregators, older Claude, Codex/Copilot/Azure routes                    | The loaded definitions join `tools` from the next request on (`deferred::with_loaded`).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | One full rewrite per load, `tools` being the front of the prompt: 0 read / 11,416 written on Claude, 0 of 7,665 cached on GPT in the same probe.                   |

The gateway's Messages → Chat Completions failover (OpenRouter) applies the fallback itself: a
`defer_loading` tool goes on once a `tool_reference` loaded it, and the reference reads as
`Loaded tool: <name>` (see the gateway's ARCHITECTURE.md). Every search costs one extra model round
trip on every route.

**Why a client-side `tool_search`, not the vendors' hosted search.** Anthropic's server-side tool search
(`tool_search_tool_regex/bm25_20251119`) and OpenAI's hosted `tool_search` run the search inside the
same response and so save that round trip (~1 s), but return `server_tool_use` /
`tool_search_tool_result` (or `tool_search_call` / `tool_search_output`) items the message model would
have to carry, replay verbatim, and drop on a dialect switch — a new block type through every dialect,
compaction and the session format. A plain function tool needs none of that, works on every provider,
and both vendors document a client-side path that keeps their cache benefit: Anthropic expands
`tool_reference` blocks returned by a custom search tool, OpenAI accepts `additional_tools` anywhere in
the input. Anthropic's `mid-conversation-tool-changes` beta (`tool_addition`) was not needed either.

### Measured (2026-10-11, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol)

[`eval/mcp_loading.py`](eval/mcp_loading.py) reproduces every number here against release builds; it
replays real servers' captured `tools/list` ([`eval/mcp_catalogs/`](eval/mcp_catalogs)) for the token
and cache runs and runs the real servers for the tasks.

**First request** — the agent's real first request, billed by the real API; MCP tokens are the total
minus a run with no MCP server (4,614 Claude / 2,344 GPT):

| MCP servers                     | Eager: Claude / GPT | Tool search: Claude / GPT | Code Mode: Claude / GPT |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| 1 (github, 26 tools)            | 6,532 / 2,109       | 567 / 263                 | 1,502 / 903             |
| 3 (+playwright, filesystem; 65) | 16,225 / 6,002      | 848 / 416                 | 1,583 / 924             |
| 7 (+4 more incl. notion; 112)   | 54,984 / 11,776     | 1,249 / 663               | 1,583 / 924             |

Code Mode's catalog is capped at 4 KB, so at 7 servers it lists a subset and points at
`tools.search()`; tool search's catalog lists every tool name up to its own 4 KB budget.

**Cache over a session** — four user turns over the three replayed catalogs, the second and third each
needing a tool from a server not yet used:

| Model / mode         | Requests | Uncached in | Cache read | Cache write | Read share | Cost    |
| -------------------- | -------- | ----------- | ---------- | ----------- | ---------- | ------- |
| Claude / eager       | 7        | 22          | 146,332    | 2,033       | 0.986      | $0.0252 |
| Claude / tool search | 9        | 26          | 51,889     | 2,629       | 0.951      | $0.0190 |
| Claude / Code Mode   | 8        | 24          | 52,323     | 2,576       | 0.953      | $0.0181 |

| GPT / tool search    | 9        | 3,902       | 25,180     | —           | 0.866      | $0.0137 |
| GPT / Code Mode      | 10       | 4,986       | 36,534     | —           | 0.880      | $0.0176 |

Eager's Claude prefix was already warm from the first-request run, so its first request read rather
than wrote 19,464 tokens — the comparison flatters eager.

**Live tasks on the real servers** (2 runs each; each task needs a tool tool search has not loaded):

| Task / model                | Mode        | Success | Requests | Wall   | Prompt tokens | Cost    |
| --------------------------- | ----------- | ------- | -------- | ------ | ------------- | ------- |
| github issue title / Claude | eager       | 2/2     | 2.0      | 3.1 s  | 43,545        | $0.0078 |
|                             | tool search | 2/2     | 3.0      | 4.2 s  | 18,756        | $0.0062 |
|                             | Code Mode   | 2/2     | 3.0      | 4.0 s  | 21,247        | $0.0063 |
| github issue title / GPT    | eager       | 2/2     | 2.0      | 4.9 s  | 17,953        | $0.0204 |
|                             | tool search | 2/2     | 3.0      | 5.9 s  | 9,994         | $0.0099 |
|                             | Code Mode   | 2/2     | 5.0      | 9.4 s  | 20,026        | $0.0137 |
| playwright JS link / Claude | eager       | 2/2     | 8.5      | 48.8 s | 190,924       | $0.0380 |
|                             | tool search | 2/2     | 7.5      | 32.1 s | 56,726        | $0.0208 |
|                             | Code Mode   | 2/2     | 6.5      | 27.8 s | 48,185        | $0.0203 |
| playwright JS link / GPT    | eager       | 2/2     | 8.0      | 35.0 s | 88,916        | $0.0394 |

The github task isolates the latency of a load: one extra request, +1.1 s on Claude and +1.0 s on GPT.
The playwright task's wall time is dominated by the browser (its first navigation fails in every mode
and the model retries), so its timings are noisy; its costs are not.

**Memory** — release builds, one MCP call through each path against a scripted local model, three
replayed catalogs, transparent huge pages off for the measured process, median of 15:

| Mode        | Idle anon | Peak anon | Peak file-backed | Peak total |
| ----------- | --------- | --------- | ---------------- | ---------- |
| eager       | 5.54 MiB  | 5.64 MiB  | 18.15 MiB        | 23.84 MiB  |
| tool search | 5.64 MiB  | 5.84 MiB  | 18.39 MiB        | 24.31 MiB  |
| Code Mode   | 4.88 MiB  | 5.18 MiB  | 19.76 MiB        | 24.97 MiB  |

Heap is a wash (within the run-to-run noise). Code Mode's cost is code: +958 KB of `.text` in the
binary (23.49 → 24.45 MB), +1.4 MiB of it resident once an `execute` has run, plus up to its 4 MiB JS
heap cap while a program runs. Tool search adds no code worth measuring and no runtime.

**Where `auto` switches.** A load costs one extra request: about a tenth of the cached prefix (~6k
tokens → ~600) plus ~50 output tokens, roughly 850 input-token-equivalents on Claude and ~1 s. Eager
costs 1.25× the schemas at every cache write (session start, after a 5-minute idle, after compaction)
and 0.1× on every request. On cost alone search wins from ~500–700 Claude tokens of schemas (~1.5–2
KB) in a 10–30 request session; `auto` waits until 8 KB (~2,800 Claude / ~1,000 GPT tokens) so a
setup of a few small tools keeps its first call one step and ~1 s shorter. Every real server measured
except sequential-thinking (one tool, 4.8 KB) is past it.

### Choosing

- **Default (`auto`)** — right for nearly everyone: big catalogs are searched, a couple of small tools
  stay eager.
- **`--mcp-tool-loading eager`** — a few small MCP tools the model uses on most turns, or a latency-
  critical first call; also the A/B baseline.
- **`--mcp-tool-loading search`** — force it for any catalog, e.g. many servers whose tools are rarely
  needed in one session.
- **`--code-mode`** — when one step should chain or fan out many MCP calls and filter their results
  before the model sees them. First-request cost is close to tool search; it needs a
  `--features code-mode` build and costs ~1 MB of resident code.

Tests: [`tests/mcp_tool_search.rs`](tests/mcp_tool_search.rs) (found, loaded and called on Anthropic
and on OpenAI Responses; prefix byte-stable across turns and runs; eager unchanged),
[`tests/code_mode_eval.rs`](tests/code_mode_eval.rs) (Code Mode wins over `--mcp-tool-loading
search`, unchanged), and the dialect and `deferred` unit tests in `agent-core`.

## MCP Apps (SEP-1865) — a pass-through host

`tools/mcp_apps.rs` implements the host side of the MCP Apps extension
(`io.modelcontextprotocol/ui`), pinned to the **stable 2026-01-26 revision**
(`modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps` → `specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx`). A server ships an
interactive view as a `ui://` resource (`text/html;profile=mcp-app`), links it from a tool's
`_meta.ui.resourceUri`, and the host renders it in a sandboxed iframe that speaks JSON-RPC back over
`postMessage`. The agent is headless and can never render, so — exactly like elicitation — the host
role is split between the agent and the `serve` client that renders:

| Host duty (spec)                                   | Who                                                |
| -------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Negotiate the extension with the server            | agent, only for a session that declared it         |
| Hide `visibility: ["app"]` tools from the model    | agent, in every session and in `run`               |
| Hide `ui://` resources from the model              | agent (never wrapped as resource tools)            |
| Read the view (cached by URI), run the tool        | agent (`AppTool`), concurrently                    |
| Sandbox + CSP the iframe, `ui/initialize`, theming | client, from `mcp_app_open.resource._meta`         |
| `tool-input` / `tool-result` / `tool-cancelled`    | client, from `mcp_app_open` / `mcp_app_result`     |
| `ui/resource-teardown`                             | client, from `mcp_app_teardown`                    |
| Proxy the view's `tools/call` / `resources/read`   | agent (`mcp_app_request`), gated like a model call |
| `ui/update-model-context`                          | agent: request-only block on the next user turn    |
| `ui/message`                                       | client: sends it as an ordinary `prompt`           |
| `ui/open-link`, display modes, size changes        | client (renderer-only)                             |

**Negotiation is per session, and connections come in two flavors.** A client declares it renders
apps with `set_mcp_apps {enabled: true}` (optionally `mime_types`: an array of strings that must
include `text/html;profile=mcp-app`). Nothing else ever advertises the extension: headless `run` never
does, and a `serve` session whose client did not declare sees what it saw before (minus app-only
tools, below). `--no-tools` refuses the declaration outright. The extension is negotiated once, on a
connection's handshake, and a server may answer `tools/list` differently once it is advertised — so
an apps-flavored connection can never be shared with a session that did not ask. `McpAppsPool` dials
the same servers a second time with the extension in `capabilities.extensions` (`Dial::apps`, carried
into every redial after an idle reap). Outside service mode the pool is **process-wide**
(`ServeConfig::mcp_apps`, shared by every daemon session that declared, as the plain connections are
shared by every session); in service mode it is per session (above). A stdio server used by both
kinds of session therefore runs as two processes, each reaped on its own idle window. The apps flavor
has its own manifest file (`~/.beyond/mcp-manifest-apps.json`, `ManifestDir::for_apps`) recording
each tool's `_meta.ui`, so a restarted daemon answers `set_mcp_apps` without starting any server.

**Dialing never blocks, and a failure is not sticky.** `set_mcp_apps` installs the session's view at
once and answers from a task of its own when the pool has dialed what was due, so the command loop never waits on a dial. Every `set_mcp_apps` and session switch bumps an epoch; the deferred answer is checked against it and sent under the same lock a withdrawal answers under, so a declaration that was withdrawn (or switched away from) answers `superseded` and never `enabled: true` after its withdrawal. The pool dials per server (`connect_each` / `connect_granted_each`): a server
whose apps dial fails is listed in the response's `failed: [{server, error, attempts, retry_in_ms}]`
and retried in the background with backoff (1 s doubling to 5 min) by a task that holds the pool
weakly, and that pauses once no session wants apps any more (every session view holds the pool's interest token; the next declaration redials what is due and restarts it). Until a server's apps connection is up, a declared session keeps that server's **plain**
tools (`AppsView::tools_over`): it never loses a server because its apps dial failed. Every change
bumps the pool's generation, and the next idle `prompt` rebuilds the agent onto whatever is up.

**App-only tools are hidden everywhere.** `_meta.ui.visibility` is parsed on both flavors of
connection (and recorded in both manifests, `MANIFEST_VERSION` 3), because servers send it whether or
not it was negotiated — the official SDK's `registerAppTool` always does. A tool whose visibility
omits `"model"` is never advertised, in a declared session, a plain one, or `run`. A `resourceUri`
that is not `ui://` (spec MUST) is ignored, so its tool is an ordinary tool.

**The session view.** The `AppsView` lives on the session's `McpEnabledSet` (the same
session-scoped "which MCP tools this session sees" seam as `set_mcp_enabled`). `filter_by_enabled` —
the one place every registry build, subagent and Code Mode gets MCP tools from — returns
`tools_over`: view-bearing tools of the servers whose apps connection is up, wrapped in an `AppTool`
holding this session's frame sink (a weak handle on its out-fanout); plain tools for the rest. An
`AppTool` call races a `resources/read` of the view (its own task) against `tools/call`:
`mcp_app_open` (the resource content item verbatim — HTML, `mimeType`, `_meta.ui` CSP/permissions —
plus the tool definition and input, keyed by `app_id` = the model's `tool_use` id) goes out as soon as
the HTML arrives, so a slow tool renders in progress; `mcp_app_result` carries the server's whole
`CallToolResult`. The model gets the same text it always did (`tool_output_from_result` reads only
`content`), so `structuredContent` and `_meta` reach the view and never model context. **The model's
result never waits for its view**: when the call finishes first it returns at once, and the view
(if it loads within 10 s) follows as `mcp_app_open` then `mcp_app_result`. A view over 4 MiB (`MAX_VIEW_BYTES`) — refused **unread** when the server advertised its `size` in `resources/list` (recorded in both manifests), refused at the transport when it did not, without the whole message ever being held: the stdio pump (`mcp_stdio::read_capped`) caps every inbound message at 64 MiB (`BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES`) and the answer to a `ui://` `resources/read` it wrote at `MAX_VIEW_BYTES`, keyed by that request's id. The id is read by walking the top-level object's members in the message's first 4 KiB (`mcp_stdio::scan_head` — never a text search, which a nested `"id":` would match), and an over-cap message is answered with a JSON-RPC error only when that prefix proves it is a response to a host request (a top-level `id` before a top-level `result`/`error`, and no `method`); anything else over the cap — a server→client request or notification (its id is the server's and can equal a host request's), or a message whose id comes after its body — is dropped with a warning, and its request, if any, times out; over streamable HTTP a view read goes through `mcp_wire::HttpClient::post_bounded` — the request path `skills/*` takes, with rmcp's own status handling (401/403 `WWW-Authenticate` → `AuthRequired`/`InsufficientScope`, a 404 on a session → `SessionExpired`) and an SSE response handed to rmcp as a stream, so every other event on it is routed — refused on its `Content-Length` before the body, or as soon as the streamed body or one SSE event passes the cap (the event replaced by the refusal and the stream ended); every other streamable-HTTP POST goes through `post_bounded` too, under the general per-message cap (rmcp's own `post_message` is no longer used — see `mcp_wire.rs` below) — with the wrong mime type, or missing costs only its frames — the spec's own text
fallback. The CSP of every view that opens is logged (spec SHOULD). An aborted call sends
`mcp_app_result{cancelled}`; its reason goes through service mode's path redaction.

**The view cache.** The view HTML is read once per connection and cached by URI on the connection's
`McpHandler` (`McpServerHandle::read_view`) — the spec lets a host cache view templates, and a
single-file view is commonly a few hundred KiB. The server's `notifications/resources/list_changed`
clears it (`on_resource_list_changed`), and so does any redial, since the cache lives with the client
a reap drops. A view over `MAX_VIEW_BYTES` is never cached. The bridge's own `resources/read` is
never cached.

**Reconnect replay.** `mcp_app_open`/`mcp_app_result` go through `OutFanout::broadcast_app`, which
keeps each view's frames — as their final JSON text, so `OutFrame::approx_len` is exact and a replay is
a copy — for the 16 newest views within 8 MiB, beside the session's attached-connection set, and
replays them, marked `replay: true`, to every connection that attaches, inside the same critical section as the catch-up: a view opened by a call in the turn being replayed goes **right after that call's `tool_start`**, so a renderer never meets a view before its call; a view from an earlier turn (whose `tool_start` is in the catch-up's history) goes right after the `catchup`. Every seeded frame — catch-up, views, turn replay — is queued outside the connection's backlog cap (`ConnTx::seed`, see [Why a slow connection is closed](#why-a-slow-connection-is-closed-not-backpressured-or-silently-dropped)), so none can be refused and none is delivered twice. A client that reconnects after the run reopens the view
and gets its result; one that attaches while the view's tool runs gets the open view replayed and its
result live. View frames are deliberately not recorded into the turn replay, which is dropped when
the run ends while the view lives on. No single view can exceed the budget (`MAX_VIEW_BYTES` is under
it). The store is also persisted beside the session (the views sidecar, below), so it survives a daemon restart: it is restored, re-bounded by the same budget, when the session loads (and replayed to any connection already attached), and a fresh `set_mcp_apps` seeds its open-view map with the restored views' `(app_id, server)`, so a restored view's bridge requests still bind.

**Teardown.** `set_mcp_apps false` and a session switch (`new_session`/`switch_session`/`fork`/
`clone`) close the view (`mcp_apps::close`): its bridge requests are cancelled, each open view gets
an `mcp_app_teardown {app_id, server, reason}` frame (for the client's `ui/resource-teardown` — spec:
the host MUST send it before tearing a view down), its model context is dropped, and the replay store is emptied. A view still loading (or a call still running) when its view closes emits nothing afterwards. The replay store is emptied explicitly (`clear_app_views`) as well as view by view by the teardown frames: the open-view map the teardown walks holds the 64 newest views and the store the 16 newest, so today the teardown alone covers it — the explicit clear keeps that true without depending on the two caps' relation.

**The bridge.** `mcp_app_request {server, app_id, request: {method, params}}` carries one request
the view sent its host. The agent binds it: `app_id` is required, must be a view this session opened
(the open-view map, the 64 newest), and `server` must be the server whose tool opened that view — a
request naming any other server, or a view that never opened, is refused. That server must have a
live apps connection and be enabled by `set_mcp_enabled`; a `tools/call` must name a tool that server
listed whose visibility includes `"app"` (the spec's MUST-reject), and must pass **exactly the
model's tool filter** (`tools::filter_allows`, the predicate `apply_filter` uses: `--tools`,
`--exclude-tools`, `--no-tools`) and `--deny-tool`. Then it goes through the **same `--approve` gate as
a model call** (`approval::ask_gate`, the gate/memory half of `gated_before_tool_call`): the same
`approval_request` frame, with `origin: {app: {server, app_id}}`, the same session memory (an "always
allow" given to either the model's or the view's call of a tool answers the other), and the same
fail-closed outcomes (no client, timeout). Bridge requests run scoped to the session's MCP host (`tools::mcp::with_session_host`), and a view's `tools/call`, `resources/read` and view reads are registered as calls in flight like any model call (`track_call` / `call_tool_tracked`), so a nested elicitation or sampling request the server raises during one is attributed to that session — or refused when it is ambiguous. They are spawned, so they work busy or idle and
block neither loop, and bounded: at most 8 in flight per session (the ninth is refused), each under a
deadline (300 s; `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_APP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`), cancelled by `abort`, by the view
closing, and when every client has detached. Proxied: `tools/call`, `resources/read`, `ping`,
`notifications/message` (logged). `ui/message` is refused with a pointer to `prompt`: the client
already has that path, with its busy/steer semantics. Other `ui/*` methods are renderer-only and
refused.

**Model context is untrusted data, not the user's words — and never in the system prompt.**
`ui/update-model-context` is held per view (each update replaces that view's last; at most 8 views,
16 KiB each) and rendered as one `<mcp_app_context>` block labelled as untrusted view output: every
value a view or client chose — its text, the server name, the `app_id` — sits inside one JSON object
per view whose `<`, `>` and `&` are `\u`-escaped, so nothing can close the block, forge an attribute,
or continue as the user. New context is taken once and attached to the **user turn about to start**
as a **request-only block** (`agent_core::Session::attach_request_block`): a content block of its own
after the user's text, added to that turn in every later request but never to the session's
messages — so it is not persisted, not in the transcript or `get_messages`, never in a title request,
and never concatenated into the user's text. The idle `prompt` attaches it to the new user turn; a
run in flight attaches it at its next turn boundary (`Steering::set_turn_context` — the tool-results
turn, or the follow-up/steer turns a stop boundary injects; a plain stop with nothing queued does not
pull it, so a context update alone never makes the model answer again). It stays on that turn in
every later request, so the model keeps it (spec: "used in future turns"), and the request's system
prompt and history are byte-stable across updates — the prompt cache's prefix is never churned. The
block is kept across a restart and a session switch: `serve` writes each session's attached blocks to
a sidecar beside its transcript (`mcp_apps::Sidecar`: `<session>.mcp-app-context.json`, or
`mcp-app-context.json` inside a service-mode session directory; the replay store goes to
`mcp-app-views.json` beside it) — never into the transcript or the session tree — each record naming
the message it rides by a fingerprint of that message's content (not a tree id, which compaction
reissues), and re-attaches them when the transcript is loaded, so the request after a restart is
byte-identical to the one before. Only blocks whose message is still in the session are recorded, and
only the newest 1 MiB of them (`MAX_SAVED_CONTEXT_BYTES`): past it the oldest blocks are not
re-attached after a restart, like a block whose message was summarized away. In service mode both
sidecars are sealed with the tenant's
transcript key (`TenantCodec::seal_sidecar`, AAD bound to the session id and the sidecar kind, so one
can be neither read in the clear nor swapped for another session's or kind's), and a store another
replica took over is never written. A `fork`/`clone` carries the records of the turns it copies
(`mcp_apps::carry_context`) into the new session and its sidecar.

The views sidecar holds every kept view's HTML and its full tool result (`structuredContent` the
model never sees included), so both sidecars are written the way a transcript rewrite is
(`session_store::write_private_atomic`): a `0600` temp file created exclusively (a planted temp file
or symlink is replaced, never written through), `fsync`ed, renamed over the old file, the directory
`fsync`ed — in the transcript's own directory. They are written from the idle loop only when their
content changed (at most once per pass, never per frame). A single-file session's sidecars
(`session_store::SESSION_SIDECARS`, with the MCP Events state) move into `.trash/` with it on
`delete_session`, come back on `restore_session`, and are removed with it by the hard-delete
fallback; a segmented session's live inside its directory and move with it.

**MCP Events stays on the plain connections.** Events subscriptions (`mcp_servers[].events`, see the
MCP Events section) are owned once per daemon by the events session, over the operator's **plain**
connections (`ServeConfig::mcp_catalog`). The apps pool's connections are a separate catalog that the
events hub never sees: they never subscribe, and their `NotificationRouter` stays empty, so no
`notifications/events/*` is ever routed from them. A session declaring apps therefore changes nothing
about events — one event is still one model run (`tests/mcp_apps_events.rs`).

**Out of scope by the spec** (the stable revision does not ask them of a host, or they are
draft-only): `tools/list` and `sampling/createMessage` from a view (draft), host-registered app
tools, and `ui/notifications/tool-input-partial` (MAY).

Proved against the real daemon (over a Unix socket of its own per test) and
`src/bin/mcp_apps_fixture_server.rs` — which, as the spec asks of a server, lists UI metadata only when
the extension was advertised (over both the `2026-07-28` per-request and the legacy `initialize`
lifecycle), and lists one app-only tool unconditionally, as the official SDK does — in
`tests/mcp_apps.rs` (negotiation, frames, bridge rules, manifest/reap, `run`), `tests/mcp_apps_session.rs`
(approval, replay, mid-run context, the view cache), `tests/mcp_apps_security.rs` (context escaping,
view binding, the tool filter, caps, `mime_types`, `ui://` and size limits, CSP logging) and
`tests/mcp_apps_resilience.rs` (dial failure and retry, redials pausing when no session wants apps, superseded declarations, abort mid-run, oversized views refused unread or uncached, app-only tools from the cached manifest, non-blocking declaration, bridge bounds and
cancellation, replay behind a long turn, results not waiting for views, teardown on session switch,
service mode's per-session pool), `tests/mcp_apps_durable.rs` (sealed sidecars surviving a service
replica restart, views replayed and still bound after a daemon restart, fork/clone carrying context,
unadvertised oversized views refused at the stdio and HTTP transports, an ambiguous nested question
refused), with `tests/common/mcp_apps_http.rs` as its HTTP Apps server).

## Subagents — in-process delegation with worktree isolation

The `subagent` tool (`tools/subagent.rs`) lets the model delegate a task to a nested `agent_core::Agent`
that runs **in the same process** with its own context window. The reference agent (pi) ships this as an
extension that spawns a subprocess per child; we own the loop, so a child is an in-process `Agent`,
which keeps the shared HTTP/connection pool, avoids reconnecting every MCP server per child, and makes a
child's progress stream into the parent's own observers for free.

**Agent definitions** (`agents.rs`) are markdown files — `~/.claude/agents/*.md`, `~/.agents/agents/*.md`
(user, ungated), and `<cwd>/.claude/agents`, `.agents/agents` ancestors (project, trust-gated exactly
like skills, because a definition body is injected verbatim as a child's system prompt). Frontmatter:
`name`, `description` (required); `tools` (comma-separated allow-list), `model`, `isolation`
(`none`|`worktree`), `skills` (names, or `all`), `memory-index` (`true`) (optional); the body is the
child's system prompt. **A child's prompt is lean by default**: no skills listing unless `skills:`
names some (Claude Code's subagent key; `read skill:<name>` still loads any skill), and the `memory`
guidance without the parent's `MEMORY.md` indexes unless `memory-index: true` (the child keeps the tool
and the shared `/session`, and can `view` an index). Both re-ship uncached on every spawn: on this repo
with a 23-skill Claude Code HOME, a child's first request went from 8,655 to 5,492 Claude tokens
(17,345 before the skills and memory budgets). Discovered like skills/prompts,
reusing `skills::parse_frontmatter`/`xml_escape`/`Collision`. When at least one definition exists, the
tool is registered and an `<available_agents>` block is added to the system prompt; otherwise neither
appears.

**Three modes, one tool call** — `single {agent, task}`, `parallel {tasks:[…]}` (≤8, 4 at a time, order
preserved, no early abort), `chain {chain:[…]}` (sequential; each step's `{previous}` is replaced by the
prior child's final assistant text). Parallel fan-out lives _inside one call_ deliberately: the tool
returns `conservative_exclusive() == true` (a child's blast radius is opaque, like `bash`'s), and the
loop caps an exclusive turn's concurrency at 1 — so N separate `subagent` calls would serialize. The
array shape is what gets real parallelism.

**Four invariants the implementation exists to hold:**

1. **Policy inheritance.** `Agent::new` installs `NoHooks`, so a child is built with the parent's
   `ToolPolicy::from_lists(deny_tool, deny_bash_pattern, deny_path)` — otherwise `subagent` would be a
   sandbox escape (a child running a `bash` command the parent's `--deny-bash-pattern` forbids). Covered
   by `tests/subagent_policy.rs`, which must never regress.
2. **Write serialization.** Every child shares the parent's `WriteLockRegistry` (`Agent::new`'s default
   is a private one), so same-path `write`/`edit` across parent and children serialize.
3. **Parallel writers need worktrees.** `bash` reports no `write_target`, so the lock registry provably
   cannot serialize two children's shell commands. In parallel mode, a write-capable agent
   (`write`/`edit`/`bash`) _must_ declare `isolation: worktree` or the call is rejected.
4. **Recursion bound.** Depth is carried in the `Subagent` instance (there is no ambient context in
   `Tool::run`). A child gets its own `subagent` tool only if its definition lists it _and_
   `depth+1 < max_depth` (default 1). A child with no `tools:` inherits the parent's effective set minus
   `subagent`.

Each child gets a **distinct `cache_key`** (`{parent}:sub:{seq}`): the parent's would poison the
Anthropic prompt cache and contend the Codex WebSocket pool, which is keyed on it. Children get **no
checkpoint hook** (`Agent::new`'s `NoCheckpoint` default) so their turns don't leak into the parent's
session store. The transport is built per child via a **factory closure** (`TransportFactory`), not by
cloning the parent's — credentials/routing are model-keyed, so a child naming its own `model:` must
re-resolve. A child with no `model:` inherits the parent's **current** model through
`SubagentCtx::parent`, a shared `ParentCell` read at each dispatch. `serve` builds its ctx once per
session and keeps it across every rebuild, so a copied startup model went stale on the first
`set_model`/`cycle_model`/resume/branch; `build_agent` — which every one of those reaches — now writes
the cell with the model it is building for.

The same cell carries the parent's **loop configuration** (`ParentLoop`): `--max-steps`, the compaction
flags (resolved against the _child's_ model, so an explicit `--context-window` carries over and an unset
one takes the child model's own window) and whether compaction is on, the effective thinking budget and
reasoning effort, `--block-images`, and the rate-limit retry budget. `run` writes it once its own agent
is built; `serve`'s `build_agent` on every rebuild, so `set_thinking`/`set_auto_compaction`/
`set_block_images` reach the next child too. A raw thinking budget only applies to a child on the
parent's own model; one on a model of its own gets the parent's effort (and, on a budget-shaped model,
the budget that effort maps to there). Children used to run on `Agent::new`'s defaults: unbounded steps
under a `--max-steps 20` parent, no thinking, the default compaction and rate-limit patience.

A child whose run ends `Ok` but **unfinished** is a failure, not a result: its last assistant message
stopped on a `Refusal`, or on `MaxTokens` with nothing left to recover (a length stop with tool calls
continues the loop, so a final one means the reply itself was cut). A worktree child's half-done edits
are then preserved, never merged.

Every model request a child makes, and every request its own children make, is reported up through
`ToolProgress::report_usage`, so the parent's totals are the whole tree's: `run`'s `[done in …]` line,
`serve`'s live stats and `get_session_stats` (whose message-derived totals add `Message::delegated_usage`),
and an export. Per request rather than once at the end, so a failed or cancelled child's spend counts.

Child `AgentEvent`s are folded into `ToolProgress::emit` as a **coalesced, throttled** status snapshot
(≥100 ms between emits; raw token deltas are never forwarded) — `serve`'s outbound channel is unbounded,
and eight streaming children would otherwise flood it.

### Worktree isolation and merge-back (`worktree.rs`)

A `worktree`-isolated child runs with its filesystem tools rooted at a private `git worktree`. This is
**conflict avoidance, not containment** — the same contract as Claude Code's `isolation: "worktree"`; an
absolute path still escapes, and that's fine. The point is that two parallel writers don't stomp each
other.

- **Rooted tools.** `Read`/`Write`/`Edit`/`Ls`/`Grep`/`Find`/`Bash` each carry a `root` (see
  `tools::ToolConfig`); a relative path resolves against it via `tools::resolve_against`, and
  `canonical_write_target(root, path)` keys the write-lock on the _resolved_ path — so two worktrees'
  `src/lib.rs` are correctly two different files. An empty root means the process cwd (the pre-subagent
  behavior every non-child caller keeps).
- **Seeding.** `git worktree add HEAD` checks out HEAD, not the developer's uncommitted work, so
  `Worktree::create` copies the parent's tracked modifications and untracked-but-not-ignored files into
  the worktree and commits them as a throwaway baseline. `child_delta` diffs against that baseline, so
  the patch is _only_ what the child changed — the parent's own WIP isn't replayed onto it. The
  baseline's id is recorded at creation and the delta is `diff --cached <baseline>`, not `HEAD`: a
  child that `git commit`s moves `HEAD`, and a delta from there was empty — work dropped, checkout
  auto-removed. The seed's reads of the parent run `--no-optional-locks` so they never rewrite its index.
  The untracked copy is one batch, never a call per file: one blocking task locally, and in a sandbox
  one fixed `sh` script per argv-sized chunk of paths. Per-file backend calls were four sandbox round
  trips each, so seeding cost grew with the untracked count times the exec latency (`benches/worktree_seed.rs`).
- **Merge-back.** On child success, `apply_patch` re-checks every path in the diff against the parent's
  `--deny-path` globs (mapped back to the main tree: a relative pattern is re-anchored at the main
  tree and at the parent's root, `ToolPolicy::denied_paths_at`) — `git apply` is not a tool call and never reaches
  `ToolPolicy`, so this is the only place that check can live — then applies to the parent's **working
  tree only**: a plain `git apply` first, and when hunks no longer apply as-is, `git apply --3way` against
  a private temporary index (`GIT_INDEX_FILE` under the git dir, removed afterwards) seeded by
  `update-index --add --remove` with just the touched paths as the working tree has them. The user's
  index is never read for the merge or written by it. (`--3way` on the user's index implied `--index`:
  it refused files edited but not staged — every file our `edit` tool touches — and files not yet added,
  and on success staged the child's work.) A clean apply removes the worktree; a conflict leaves
  markers in the main tree, preserves the worktree, and names it in the tool result for the parent (or
  the user) to resolve; a policy refusal rejects the whole patch (all-or-nothing).
  The preserved path rides every mode's result — `single` and a stopped `chain` included, success or
  failure — not just `parallel`'s sections: it is the only pointer to the child's work.
- **Cleanup.** `Drop` removes a worktree best-effort, but a `process::exit`/SIGKILL runs no destructors,
  so worktrees live under `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/beyond-agent/worktrees/<repo-id>/<pid>-<label>-<seq>` (on
  disk, not tmpfs — a checkout in RAM would exhaust it) and a startup `sweep` reaps any whose owning PID
  is gone. Keyed by PID so a sweep never deletes a concurrently-running session's work; `<seq>` is a
  per-process spawn counter, because a daemon's sessions share one PID and a retry re-spawns the same
  agent at the same index. `create` never removes an existing path (it skips to the next `<seq>`): that
  path may be a live sibling's, or a preserved checkout holding the only copy of a child's work.
  `sweep` takes any directory in the repo and keys on `rev-parse --show-toplevel`, so a run from a
  subdirectory reaps the same base `create` writes to.
- **Preserved worktrees are kept.** A conflicted, refused or failed child's checkout is moved
  (`git worktree move`) to a `kept-<leaf>` name and that path is reported. Neither the local PID sweep
  nor the sandbox's owner sweep ever reaps a `kept-` entry: it is the developer's to remove.
