## State Machine — `serve` session lifecycle

```
spawn ──► Booting ──writer task up + "ready" frame sent──► Ready
                                                               │
                                 stdin "prompt" line           │ stdin "get_state"/"get_messages" line
                                                               ▼                        │
                                                         RunningTurn                     │ (no transition)
                                                   (Agent::run_events;                  │
                                                    until the model ends its turn,       │
                                                    or ≤ max_steps when opted in)        │
                                                               │                          │
                                       turn ends / MaxSteps / transport error             │
                                                               ▼                          ▼
                                                             Ready ◄─────────────────────┘
                                                               │
                                                   stdin "new_session" line
                                                               ▼
                                                 Ready (fresh Session, new session_id)
                                                               │
                                         stdin EOF  or  stdout write fails
                                                               ▼
                                                            Closed
```

| From              | Event                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | To          | Guard                         | What Actually Happens                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Booting           | writer task spawned, `ready` frame sent                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Ready       | `out_tx.send` succeeds        | `Session` restored from persistence (file/dir/none); `session_id` minted; static system prompt built                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Ready             | `{"type":"prompt"}`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | RunningTurn | —                             | `ack` frame sent immediately; message pushed as a user turn; `Agent::run_events_steered` streams `event` frames live                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| RunningTurn       | `{"type":"abort"}` / `"stop_after_turn"` / `"steer"` / `"follow_up"`                                                                                                                                                                                               | RunningTurn | —                             | cancels the run / requests a graceful stop at the next turn boundary / queues a mid-run steer / queues a stop-boundary follow-up — the run keeps going until its current turn's tool calls (if any) finish                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| RunningTurn       | `{"type":"prompt", streaming_behavior:"steer"\|"follow_up"}`                                                                                                                                                                                                       | RunningTurn | —                             | accepted (not rejected as busy) and routed through the same `Steering` queue as an explicit `steer`/`follow_up`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| RunningTurn       | `"compact"` / `"switch_session"` / `"fork"` / `"clone"` / `"new_session"`                                                                                                                                                                                          | Ready       | —                             | self-abort-and-proceed: the run is cancelled exactly like an `abort`, and the command runs its ordinary idle-path logic once the run has gone idle (its idle response doubles as the ack). In service mode `fork`/`clone` are instead refused as busy, since there they derive a new session and leave this one running                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| RunningTurn       | read-only commands (`get_state`/`get_session_stats`/`get_messages`/`get_commands`/`list_branches`/`get_tree`/`list_sessions`/`list_all_sessions`/`get_available_models`/`get_todos`), `approve`/`elicit`/`sample`/`mcp_app_request`, `abort_retry`, `switch_model` | RunningTurn | —                             | answered while the run continues (from live sources or a snapshot where `&session` is borrowed); `switch_model` queues a model switch for the next turn boundary                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| RunningTurn       | any other command                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | RunningTurn | —                             | rejected: `response{success:false, error:"busy…"}` — the session is borrowed by the in-flight run                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| RunningTurn       | model ends turn (no more `tool_use`, not a refusal)                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Ready       | persist succeeds              | session persisted (rewrite/rewrite_compacted if compaction fired); `response{success:true, data:{steps,…, refused:false}}`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| RunningTurn       | model ends turn, but persisting the transcript fails (disk full, permission error, …)                                                                                                                                                                              | Ready       | —                             | `response{success:false, data:{steps,…}, error:"run completed but failed to persist: …"}` — the run itself is not retried or lost, but the client is told the transcript may not be durable yet, rather than a false success                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| RunningTurn       | model refuses (`StopReason::Refusal`)                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Ready       | —                             | run ends immediately _without_ draining queued steering; `response{success:true, data:{…, refused:true}}`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| RunningTurn       | `Error::MaxSteps` / transport error                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Ready       | —                             | session still persisted; `response{success:false, error}` — the process keeps serving                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Ready             | `{"type":"new_session", parent_session?}`                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Ready       | on-disk reset/create succeeds | history replaced; `steering.clear()`; `response{success:true, data:{session_id,…}}` — `parent` in the response is `parent_session` when given, else whatever was active before this call. An **addressed** session (`--session-id`, the daemon's `?session_id=`) keeps its own id instead of minting one, since something is routing on it: the outgoing conversation is archived into a sibling session (`parent` = this id) and this one is blanked in place, so "start a new session" is never also "destroy the old one" |
| Ready             | `{"type":"new_session"}`, on-disk reset/create fails                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Ready       | —                             | `response{success:false, error}` — the _previous_ session stays active (nothing is swapped for an empty in-memory session that was never actually persisted, which would otherwise desync `SessionStore`'s persisted-message count from what the caller believes is live, silently dropping the next turn's `append_new`)                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Ready             | `{"type":"switch_session"}` / `"fork"` / `"clone"` / `"switch_branch"`                                                                                                                                                                                             | Ready       | —                             | history replaced/switched; `steering.clear()` — a message queued for the old session's next turn can't leak into the new one                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Ready             | `{"type":"set_model"}` / `"cycle_model"` / `"set_reasoning_effort"` / `"cycle_thinking_level"`, recording the change fails to persist                                                                                                                              | Ready       | —                             | `response{success:false, error}`; the live model/thinking-level is _not_ switched either — a failed persist never leaves live state ahead of what's durably recorded                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Ready             | invalid JSON / unknown `type`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | Ready       | —                             | `response{success:false, error}`; loop continues, no state change                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Ready/RunningTurn | stdin EOF                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Closed      | —                             | `out_tx` dropped → writer drains its queue → awaited → process returns `Ok(())`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| any               | stdout write fails (broken pipe)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | Closed      | —                             | writer task `break`s its receive loop; the next `emit!` send fails → main loop `break`s                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

## State Machine — daemon session slot (Starting / Live / Stopping)

The daemon (`serve_ws`) keeps one map entry per session id, and that entry lives exactly as long as
the id's session task: "the id has an entry" means "a task owns this id's session file". It used to
mean only "attachable": the reaper removed an entry and _then_ its task persisted and exited, so a
reconnect landing in between found the id free and spawned a second `serve_session` on the same
append-only file while the first was still writing it — and the store's `append_new` is count-keyed,
so two writers corrupt the transcript rather than conflict. Graceful shutdown racing a new connection,
and `pin` replacing a handle whose loop had ended, had the same shape.

```
            pin, id free
(absent) ─────────────────► Starting ──── task runs: go_live ────► Live
   ▲                           │                                    │
   │           reap / shutdown │                  reap / shutdown / │
   │         (before go_live)  ▼          pin finds its input closed│
   │                        Stopping ◄──────────────────────────────┘
   │                           │
   └── task ends: ExitGuard removes its own incarnation's entry, then fires `exited`
```

| From            | Event                                                                | To        | What Actually Happens                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| absent          | `pin`                                                                | Starting  | next incarnation stamped; input channel, fan-out, and `exited` latch created; entry inserted under the map lock, task spawned after it is released; the caller is attached (`attached = 1`)                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Starting        | the task first runs (`go_live`)                                      | Live      | the task runs its body (`serve_session`). Start-up work that must finish before the session touches storage (e.g. a lock on its session file) goes just before `go_live`, awaited on the task with the map lock **not** held — the `Starting` entry already keeps a concurrent `pin` from spawning a rival meanwhile                                                      |
| Starting / Live | `pin`                                                                | unchanged | attached: `attached += 1`, detach clock cleared. Commands queue on the input channel even while `Starting`, exactly as they do while `serve_session` opens persistence                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Starting / Live | idle reaper (`is_reapable`), or `pin` finding the input closed       | Stopping  | the retained input sender is dropped → the session observes EOF (once no attached connection holds a clone), cancels any in-flight run, persists, and exits. `list_daemon_sessions` now reports it `live: false`                                                                                                                                                          |
| Starting        | `go_live` finds the entry already `Stopping`                         | (removed) | the body never runs: a session stopped before going live never touches storage                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Stopping        | `pin`                                                                | unchanged | the pin waits on `exited`, bounded by `JOIN_GRACE` (10 s), then looks again — normally finding the id free and spawning the next incarnation. Past the grace (a wedged task) the attach is refused — WebSocket close `1013 Try Again Later`, HTTP `503` — never doubled                                                                                                   |
| any             | graceful shutdown                                                    | Stopping  | the table is closed first (every later `pin` is refused), every entry is stopped, and shutdown waits on every `exited` latch under `JOIN_GRACE` — including sessions the reaper had already stopped                                                                                                                                                                       |
| any             | the task ends (body returned, panicked, or dropped with the runtime) | (removed) | `ExitGuard` removes the entry **only if it is still this incarnation's**, and only then fires `exited`, so whoever that wakes finds the id free. Every attached connection ends with it: each watches its own input sender for the session's receiver going away, flushes what the session broadcast last (typically the `error` frame saying why), and closes the socket |

A connection ends when its session does, and it has to watch for that explicitly. Its only other
notice is its own next `send` into the input channel failing — which is reached only when the
_client_ happens to send something else. A client that asked a question and is waiting for the answer
sends nothing else, so before the connection watched `input_tx.closed()` it held a live, silent
socket for as long as it was willing to wait, and the replica held the connection task and its
buffers for exactly as long. A session that fails to start (an unreachable sandbox, sealed storage
that will not open with the key in the grant) broadcasts one `error` frame and ends, so that was the
common case, not a corner. The teardown **flushes rather than cancels** in this direction: the queued
`error` is written out and the socket closed with a `Close` frame, bounded by `JOIN_GRACE` so a client
that has stopped reading cannot hold the task open. Two orderings could still lose the `error`, both seen only under load: the session's loop drops its input (waking the connection) _before_ its task broadcasts why, so a connection that flushed at the first sign closed ahead of the frame — it now waits for the task's `exited` latch, bounded by `JOIN_GRACE`, before flushing; and a connection whose upgrade was answered while the session was starting can register its output _after_ the session failed — the fanout keeps the terminal frame (`OutFanout::end`) and hands it to any sink that registers later. `tests/serve_service_session_end.rs` pins all three, the late cases with seams (`BEYOND_AI_AGENT_TEST_SLOW_SESSION_END_MS`, `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_TEST_SLOW_ATTACH_MS`); `crates/fleet-sim` found the original.

`unpin` is incarnation-scoped for the same reason: a connection that outlived its session (the loop
ended, and a reconnect has since spawned the next incarnation) must not decrement the new session's
attach count, or the reaper would take a session with a connection still attached. The regression is
pinned deterministically at the supervisor level (`serve_ws.rs` tests), with a test-only session body
standing in for `serve_session` so the test decides exactly when an exiting task finishes.

---

## Why It Behaves This Way

### Why the process tokio runtime is single-threaded

`serve --listen` looks concurrent, so a work-stealing runtime feels like the obvious default —
`#[tokio::main]` builds one, and that's what this binary used to inherit. Session tasks now share
that process runtime (`serve_ws` `tokio::spawn`s each `serve_session`; the future is `Send`).
CPU-bound tool work (`grep`/`find`/image resize) is `spawn_blocking`, which a current-thread
runtime still has a blocking pool for. So is anything that blocks the thread without using CPU: `web` builds its client and spawns and waits on its isolated parser child there, `bash`'s stale-spill sweep of the system temp directory runs there, `memory` merges and renders large search results there, and Code Mode evaluates there. `tests/tool_reactor_stall.rs` holds every tool that needs no external service to it with two probes on a `current_thread` runtime — the CPU the runtime thread spends inside the tool's polls, and the worst gap of a ticker task on the same runtime with run-queue wait (`/proc/thread-self/schedstat`) taken out, so wall-clock blocking (a sleep, blocking disk or NFS I/O, a contended `std` mutex) is caught and host load is not. Extra workers cost per-thread stacks and mimalloc heaps, on
a binary whose idle RSS in a 768 MB guest is already the density budget.

**The default now splits by mode** (`main.rs::build_runtime`): `current_thread` for a local daemon,
one worker per core for a `serve --service` replica. `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_TOKIO_WORKER_THREADS` overrides
either direction, and `=1` is how an operator pins a replica back onto the single thread without a
rebuild. The decision itself is `runtime_workers`, split out and unit-tested because `=1` and _unset_
both parse to `None` and an operator's explicit pin must not read as silence.

This is the re-run the paragraph below asked for, and it changed the answer for replicas. The
original A/B ran **one session**, where nothing contends for the thread: the two schedulers tied on
throughput, and per-worker stacks and mimalloc heaps were essentially the whole memory delta. Asked
again through `crates/fleet-sim` at **120 sessions across 3 replicas** on a real NFS mount, with
chaos off so recovery cost is not folded in:

```
workers   turns/s   vs 1     peak RSS   per replica   MB per turn/s
   1       274.2    1.00x      649 MB       216 MB        2.37
   2       385.1    1.40x      854 MB       285 MB        2.22
   4       514.1    1.88x      774 MB       258 MB        1.51
   8       619.6    2.26x     1168 MB       389 MB        1.88
  16       674.6    2.46x     1362 MB       454 MB        2.02
```

**Up to 2.46x the throughput, and memory grows sub-linearly in the worker count.** Even at one
worker per core on a 16-core host a replica sits at ~454 MB while serving 40 concurrently active
sessions.

A first pass capped this at four — the best throughput _per megabyte_ — which was the wrong frame.
The per-thread stacks and mimalloc heaps that argued for a single thread are a density budget from
the **in-VM** agent, which shares a 768 MB guest with the tenant's workload. A replica outside the
sandbox has its own task allocation and nothing to share it with, so trading 19% of throughput to
save ~120 MB is a bad deal there. Four workers is still the most efficient point if a deployment is
genuinely memory-tight: pin it with `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_TOKIO_WORKER_THREADS=4`.

The mechanism, which is why this hid for so long: the single thread was **87% of all CPU a replica
spent**, and a turn costing ~7 ms of CPU took ~311 ms of wall time. A turn crosses that thread a
dozen-plus times — read frame, build the request, poll the HTTP call, parse SSE, hand off
persistence, write the response — and each crossing queues behind every other session on the
replica. Small CPU, large queueing, and nothing ever _looks_ saturated: storage was ruled out (tmpfs
within 10% of NVMe, NFS in the same band), memory was flat, and chaos recovery accounted for only
14%.

A laptop daemon keeps `current_thread`, because there the single-session measurement is the accurate
one.

Numbers from the older topology, kept as history — note that every session had its own OS thread
then, so this is not a measurement of the current one:

```
                idle RSS   peak RSS   threads   rpc rps   rpc p95   prompt rps   prompt p95   CPU
multi_thread     16.84      216.8      36        5115      11.4      710          48.2        58%
current_thread   16.50      205.9      33        5124      10.8      722          47.8        55%
```

### Why session storage I/O runs on the blocking pool

That single runtime thread is also the reason no session may do synchronous filesystem work on it.
Session tasks, the accept loop and the idle reaper all share it, so a session that blocks it blocks
the whole replica — and in service mode the session directory is a **network mount**, where an
`fsync` or a `readdir` costs tens of milliseconds rather than tens of microseconds.

Three paths therefore go through `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`, all built the same way — the value is
moved **into** the blocking task and handed back **out**:

| Path                                               | Helper                                | Why it is the one that matters                                                                                                                                                 |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Session start (`Persistence::open`)                | `serve.rs::open_persistence_blocking` | Directory resolve + a **full transcript replay** — O(the conversation so far), on the reconnect path, and reconnects are correlated (a deploy or an LB rehash lands N at once) |
| Every session write (`persist`/`persist_messages`) | `serve.rs::persist_blocking`          | Runs after every turn, every manual `compact`, every mid-run checkpoint, and the host `bash` RPC                                                                               |
| Session listings                                   | `serve.rs::scan_session_dirs`         | `read_dir` **and** the per-file listing parse, both inside the closure — on a network mount the `read_dir` is the half with the latency                                        |

Awaiting a `spawn_blocking` suspends the calling session's own task at the await point either way, so
the win is never that session's own responsiveness. It is that everything else on the replica keeps
running while one session writes, opens or scans.

**The ownership invariant.** There is exactly one `Persistence` per session, on that session task's
stack. Moving it by value into the blocking task means that while the task holds it the session
cannot reach it — that ownership _is_ the per-session serialization of session writes. So a persist
is never `tokio::spawn`ed (the handle would outlive the await, which is exactly what lets a second
write start) and `Persistence` never goes behind a shared lock: `SessionStore::append_new`'s dedup
guard is count-keyed (`messages.len() <= self.persisted`), so it cannot see a _shrink_ — two writers
that desync it silently drop history rather than erroring.

`session_store.rs` stays fully synchronous throughout. It is the thing being wrapped, not the
wrapper. `switch_branch` is the one deliberate exception to the by-value pattern: it is `async` and
holds `store.as_mut()` across a summarization `.await`, so it cannot express a move-in/move-out at
all. The human-frequency whole-session commands (`new_session`, `delete`, `fork`, `restore_session`)
and the header-append mutators (`set_label`, `record_model_change`, …) are deliberately left inline —
one 5 ms `fsync` at human frequency is not the constraint, and wrapping it would only add noise.

`tests/serve_startup_stall.rs` pins the start-up half: with one session's open stalled for 3 s, a
different session's RPC answers in **731 µs** — against **2.70 s** when the open runs inline. The
stall comes from `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_TEST_SLOW_SESSION_OPEN_MS`, a seam compiled into debug builds only
(`serve.rs::simulated_slow_open`), because the property being pinned is _where_ the open runs, not
how long it takes.

### Why a single writer task with an unbounded channel

`Agent::run_events`'s event sink is a synchronous `FnMut` — the producer can't `.await` mid-callback
to apply backpressure. A bounded channel would force `try_send`, which silently drops frames on
backpressure and corrupts the NDJSON stream for a protocol where every frame matters. The channel is
unbounded instead, with the backlog naturally bounded by one in-flight turn's events; if a client
stops reading, stdout's write eventually fails and the writer tears down,
surfacing the stall as a closed session rather than masking it with dropped frames or unbounded
buffering. Every frame — events and responses — flows through this one task, so output is FIFO and
never interleaves even though tool execution itself is concurrent.

### Why a slow connection is closed, not backpressured or silently dropped

Each network connection (WebSocket, UDS, HTTP POST) has its own outbound queue between the session's
broadcast and the task that writes its socket (`serve::ConnTx`/`ConnRx`). That queue has to be bounded
— a locked phone or a dead tunnel must not make a still-running session buffer without limit — and the
bound is **bytes of live output not yet written** (`CONN_BACKLOG_MAX_BYTES`, 8 MiB), not frames.
Every frame is charged its real serialized size: `OutFanout::broadcast` serializes a `Value` frame
once, and those bytes are what each queue is charged, what the turn replay keeps and what every
connection is sent (a refcount bump per sink). `Value` frames used to be charged a flat 256 bytes, so
a run's worth of ~1 MB `get_messages` replies slipped past the cap (fifty were charged 12,800 bytes).

- **Bytes, because a frame count measures the wrong thing.** The queue used to be a 1024-frame
  channel. The daemon's runtime is single-threaded by default, so the session's writer moves everything
  one model read delivered into the queue before the socket writer gets a turn: a 3000-delta burst
  measured 252 KB queued at once, and a client that never stopped reading was dropped after ~1000
  frames. 8 MiB is ~33× that burst and still bounds what a wedged connection can pin.
- **Not backpressure, because nothing upstream can wait.** The agent's event sink is synchronous; the
  session's one writer task feeds every attached connection, so awaiting a slow one stalls the others;
  and approval, elicitation and app frames are broadcast from synchronous code under the fanout's lock.
  A frame that does not fit can only be lost, and a lost frame is a silent hole in the client's stream —
  so the connection goes instead.
- **Dropped means closed.** Refusing a frame cancels the connection's `dropped` token. Its send task
  stops writing at once (even mid-send to a socket nobody reads), sends `Close` `1013 Try Again Later`
  (bounded by `CLOSE_HANDSHAKE_WAIT`), and its read loop stops taking commands and unpins, so the idle
  reaper's clock starts. The client reconnects and is caught up from history plus the turn replay; the
  frames seeded on attach do not count against the cap (`ConnTx::seed`), so a reconnect is never
  dropped for its own replay. An HTTP POST dropped this way answers `503`. Before, a dropped sink was
  only unregistered: the connection's own reply handle kept the socket open, so the client kept getting
  pings and its commands kept running, but it never received another frame, never reconnected, and its
  session counted as attached forever.

`tests/serve_slow_client.rs` pins both halves end to end: a reading client gets every frame of a
3000-delta burst, and a client that stops reading during a 24 MiB turn sees its socket close and
re-attaches.

### Why the stdout guard is a compile-time lint, not a runtime patch

A stray line on stdout (a debug `println!`, a misconfigured logger) corrupts the NDJSON stream a
client reads line-by-line — `tracing`'s subscriber is already pinned to stderr (`main.rs`) for exactly
this reason, but that only covers _our own_ `tracing::warn!`/`info!` calls, not a direct `println!`/
`print!`. pi's equivalent (`output-guard.ts`'s `takeOverStdout`) closes that gap at runtime: it
monkey-patches `process.stdout.write` globally, transparently redirecting _any_ code's stray write
(including a dependency's own stray `console.log`) to stderr, leaving its own `writeRawStdout` as the
only sanctioned path back to the real stdout. There's no honest equivalent here — that requires
reopening/redirecting the raw fd, and this workspace's `[workspace.lints.rust] unsafe_code = "forbid"`
rules out the FFI that would take, categorically, not for lack of trying. `serve.rs` instead carries
`#![deny(clippy::print_stdout)]`: since nothing in that module has ever needed `println!`/`print!`
directly (the single `tokio::io::stdout()` writer task is already the only sanctioned path), this
costs nothing today and turns any future stray one — the realistic risk, since idiomatic Rust crates
overwhelmingly log through `tracing`/`log` rather than raw stdout writes, unlike the Node ecosystem
pi's version targets — into a hard compile error instead of a corrupted protocol stream discovered in
production.

`run`'s own `run_turn_once` (both its `--json` NDJSON path and its default text-streaming path) _does_
write to stdout directly — that's the whole point of `run`'s output — so it can't carry the same
`#![deny(clippy::print_stdout)]` lint `serve.rs` does. Task #10 (pi-parity fix) closes a different gap
those direct writes had: `println!`/`print!` panic internally on any stdout write error, including
`EPIPE`, so `beyond-ai-agent run --json "task" | head -1` used to crash with "Broken pipe" (exit 101) the instant
`head` closed its end, instead of exiting cleanly the way a well-behaved Unix producer should.
`write_stdout_or_exit` (a locked `std::io::stdout()` handle, `write_all`+`flush`, matched `Result`)
replaces every such call site in `run_turn_once`; on `ErrorKind::BrokenPipe` it calls
`std::process::exit(0)` immediately rather than propagating an error `run_task` would otherwise try to
persist/report — mirroring `serve.rs`'s own writer task, which already exits its loop gracefully on a
write failure instead of panicking, just reached by a simpler direct exit here since `run_turn_once`
runs inside a synchronous callback with no `select!` loop to fall out of cleanly.

### Why `is_compacting` is event-driven, and why `is_streaming` isn't

`get_state`'s `is_streaming`/`is_compacting`/`session_file` mirror pi's `RpcSessionState` fields of the
same name. `is_streaming` needs no tracking at all: it's simply `true` in the busy-loop's `get_state`
arm and `false` in the idle one — architecturally, those are the _only_ two places `get_state` can ever
run from, so which arm answered already says everything. `is_compacting` is different: `Agent::compact`
runs _inside_ the busy loop's own event stream, so its state has to be tracked live. It's set on the new
`AgentEvent::CompactionStart` (emitted once `compact` confirms a worthwhile prefix exists, right before
its first summarization call) and cleared on literally the next event of any kind, not specifically
`Compacted` — `compact` can end without ever emitting `Compacted` at all (an empty-summary no-op, or a
propagated error), and its own summarization call passes a discarding inner sink, so nothing else can
possibly arrive between `CompactionStart` and whatever naturally follows it (`Compacted` on success,
`CompactionFailed` when an automatic compaction's summary call fails, the next turn's `TurnStart`
otherwise). Clearing on "anything else" is therefore exact, not a conservative
guess, and never leaves the flag stuck `true` past the compaction attempt that set it. A manual
`compact` runs its summary call inside a select, the same shape as the host-`bash` loop, so the session
keeps answering while it waits (up to the stream idle timeout per call): `abort` cancels it (the
compaction ends unapplied and `abort` is acknowledged after the `compact` response), shutdown and stdin
EOF cancel it, `get_state` (`is_compacting: true`, `message_count` as it stands until the compaction
lands), `get_session_stats` and `get_messages` are answered from a pre-compaction snapshot, MCP Events
injections are deferred, and every other command is refused as busy. Branch summarization
(`switch_branch`'s `summarize?`) still runs inline from the idle loop. `session_file` is a plain accessor (`Persistence::session_file`) — repo and
single-file modes both populate `Persistence.store`, so one method covers either without needing to
distinguish them, and it's `None` only for true in-memory (`--no-session-persistence`) runs.

### Why `get_state` carries `cwd`/`git_branch` (Task #25, pi-parity fix)

Neither existed on `get_state`'s response at all before this fix — a real gap specific to this crate,
not a pi-parity gap in the usual sense: pi has no headless RPC protocol whose _whole point_ is letting a
client with no shared filesystem drive the agent remotely, so pi's own equivalent state never needed
this. `cwd` is the live process working directory (`serve`'s own `cwd` variable), not
`persistence.meta.cwd` — the session's _recorded_ directory, already separately surfaced via
`cwd_stale` whenever the two disagree — since `cwd` answers "what will `bash`/`read`/`write` actually
operate against right now," not "what did this session start in." `git_branch` is a lazily resolved,
best-effort `git symbolic-ref --short HEAD` (`serve::git_branch`) run fresh on every `get_state` call —
no filesystem watcher or caching, since a plain request/response poll has nothing to invalidate and a
`git` invocation is cheap enough to just redo — via the async `tokio::process::Command` rather than a
blocking `std::process::Command`, so a `get_state` answered from inside the busy loop's own
`tokio::select!` (while a `prompt` is streaming) doesn't stall that task's own forward progress the way
a blocking subprocess wait would (a strictly stronger property than `persist_blocking`'s: an inline
`std::process::Command` has no await point at all, so it pins this task _and_ the shared runtime
thread, while awaiting a `spawn_blocking` suspends the caller either way and only ever frees the
thread — see "Why session storage I/O runs on the blocking pool"). `None` — never a failed `get_state`
call — outside a git repo, on detached `HEAD` (matching `git symbolic-ref`'s own behavior: it resolves
a real branch ref only, never a raw commit), if `git` itself isn't installed, or for any other lookup
failure.

### Why `session_stats`'s token totals are recomputed from message history, not `Session`'s own counters

`Session::input_tokens`/`output_tokens`/`cache_read_tokens`/`cache_write_tokens`/`cache_write_1h_tokens`/
`reasoning_tokens` (`agent_core::Session::record_usage`) are a _process-lifetime_ running total — they
only ever accumulate for as long as the current process has been alive, and `SessionStore::open` never
restores them from disk (only `session.messages` itself is reconstructed on reattach). `session_stats`
(shared by the `prompt` response, `get_state`, and `get_session_stats`) used to read those counters
directly, so a resumed session's reported totals covered only activity since the _current_ process
started — silently resetting to whatever this run alone has produced, with no signal that anything from
before the restart was missing. Task #6 (pi-parity fix) instead sums each message's own per-turn
`usage` (`Message::usage`/`Message::with_usage`, populated on every assistant turn by
`Agent::run_events_steered`, and persisted automatically — `Message` derives `Serialize`/`Deserialize`
directly, so no session-file format/version change was needed, and `#[serde(default,
skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]` means an older file with no `usage` on any message just
deserializes it as `None`, fully backward-compatible) — `serve::message_usage_totals`, computed fresh on
every `session_stats` call, mirroring how `message_type_breakdown` right next to it already derives its
own counts fresh from `session.messages` rather than a running counter. The same fix applies to
`LiveStats::from_session` (the mid-run "busy" snapshot `get_state`/`get_session_stats` answer from
_inside_ a streaming `prompt`), which seeds from the identical per-message sum instead of the same stale
counters. Same accepted limitation as `message_type_breakdown`: a compacted-away message's `usage` is
gone along with the rest of its content, so this reports what's still visible on the active path, not a
truly unbounded historical total — inherent to deriving anything from `session.messages` at all, not a
regression this fix introduces. Session-restore also got more precise for the same reason: reopening a
session now seeds `Session::last_input_tokens`/`last_output_tokens`/`last_usage_message_count` (the
proactive-compaction trigger signal) from the most recent message's own exact `usage`, when one exists,
instead of always falling back to a whole-transcript estimate that remains the fallback for a session
with no `usage`-carrying message at all (one written before this field existed) and for one reopened
between a compaction and its next reply (whose kept usage measured the pre-compaction prompt) —
`agent_core::Session::restore_usage_snapshot`, which sizes every persisted
`Message::prior_turn_tokens` turn exactly.

Fix 6 (pi-parity gap) reuses this same message-summing approach one layer further out:
`serve::message_export_usage_totals` reshapes `message_usage_totals`'s result into
`crate::export::UsageTotals`, giving the standalone `export` subcommand (`main.rs`, no live
`Agent`/`Session` at all — just a freshly `SessionStore::open`ed one) the same usage figures `serve`'s
own `export_html` RPC and `run --export` already derive from a live `Session`'s running counters, instead
of the `usage: None` it used to pass unconditionally.

Fix 8 (pi-parity gap): `get_session_stats`'s idle response (`session_stats`) never carried
`session_id`/`session_file` even though `get_state`'s sibling idle arm trivially adds both from the same
`Persistence`; its busy-mode response was the raw `LiveStats::snapshot()` verbatim, dropping
`session_id`/`session_file` _and_ the whole `user_messages`/`assistant_messages`/`tool_calls`/
`tool_results`/`total_messages`/`context_usage` breakdown outright, unlike `get_state`'s own busy arm,
which at least backfills what it can from live sources. Fixed by a shared `insert_session_identity`
helper (`session_id`/`session_file`, called from all four `get_state`/`get_session_stats` idle/busy arms)
plus, for `get_session_stats`'s busy arm specifically, explicit `null` placeholders for the
six session-derived fields that are genuinely unavailable while `&session` is exclusively borrowed by the
in-flight turn — present as `null` rather than silently absent, so a client sees the same field _set_
idle or busy, values aside (mirroring how `get_state`'s own `message_count: null` already handles the
identical "genuinely can't answer this precisely mid-run" case).

### Why tool results batch into one user message, not one per tool

(Enforced in `agent_core`, but it constrains how this crate's tools must behave.) Anthropic rejects
consecutive same-role messages; if a model batches N tool calls in one turn and the loop emitted N
separate `user` messages, the next request would 400 whenever N > 1. All of a turn's `tool_result`
blocks are gathered onto a single `user` message instead, rebuilt in call order after the concurrent
join so the transcript stays deterministic regardless of which tool actually finishes first. The
events are not held back for it: `ToolStart` is emitted for the whole batch up front, in call order,
and each `ToolEnd` live, the moment its own call's result is known, so a client sees completions in
finish order.

### Why `edit` demands a unique match

A non-unique `old_string` means the model under-specified the change — `edit` refuses rather than
guessing which occurrence was meant, forcing the model to add surrounding context (or pass
`replace_all` for the explicit bulk case) before any byte of the file is touched. This trades one
extra round-trip for never silently editing the wrong occurrence.

### Why `edit`'s result carries no diff/patch data

pi's own `edit` tool computes a `diff`/`patch` alongside its result, but doesn't send either to the
_model_ — the model-facing text is the same bare `"Successfully replaced N block(s) in {path}."`
confirmation `edit.rs` returns here (`"edited {path} (N replacements)"`). pi's `diff`/`patch` exist
purely for its interactive terminal UI (`renderResult`'s `renderDiff`), a client-side rendering
concern this crate has no equivalent live surface for: `AgentEvent::ToolEnd` (`agent_core::agent`)
carries only `{id, name, result, is_error}` — no structured `details` channel a `serve` client could
even receive one through (unlike `ToolProgress`, which does carry `details: Option<Value>` for a
tool that streams incremental state). And where a diff actually gets _rendered_ today —
`export.rs`'s `render_edit_call` — it already reconstructs the old/new pair independently from the
tool _call's `input`_ via `parse_edits`, the same parser the tool itself runs, not from anything
carried on the result. Computing a `diff`/`patch` on every `edit` result would mean real CPU work
(diffing, unified-patch formatting) with, today, no reader on either end: not the model, not the one
existing renderer, not the wire protocol. Revisit if `serve` ever grows a `ToolEnd.details` channel
with a real client consuming it — until then this is deliberately not built, per this repo's own
"don't design for hypothetical future requirements."

### Why grep is parallel and find is sequential

See the Core Mechanism numbers above — this isn't a stylistic choice, it's the benchmark result.
`grep`'s bottleneck is per-file regex scanning (parallel walk gave 3.8×); `find`'s bottleneck is the
directory traversal itself, and its per-file cost (one glob test) is too cheap to amortize
`WalkParallel`'s thread-coordination overhead. Applying the same "parallelize it" instinct to both
would have made `find` slower, not faster — the Theory-of-Constraints discipline of profiling before
optimizing, then only investing in the part that's actually the bottleneck.

### Why there's no `warn_deprecation`-style utility

pi has one (`utils/deprecation.ts`'s `warnDeprecation(message)` — dedupes by message, warns once via
`console.warn`), but it has zero call sites anywhere in pi's own current source; the only _actual_
deprecation warnings pi emits are `migrations.ts`'s own, narrowly specific to migrating its legacy
`hooks/`/`tools/` directories to `extensions/` — a directory structure this crate never had, so there's
nothing to migrate away from here either. Matching `warnDeprecation` itself would mean adding a
generic utility with no current caller in either codebase — this repo's own "don't design for
hypothetical future requirements." Add one (a small, message-deduped `tracing::warn!` wrapper is the
natural shape here, consistent with `session_store.rs`'s corrupt-line warning and `skills.rs`'s
discovery warning) when an actual deprecated flag/RPC command/config value first needs one, not before.

### Provider keys: managed vs. BYO vs. OAuth subscription

This section is about gateway mode. With a gateway configured (see "Provider routing — the gateway
is optional" above), `GatewayClient` (in `agent_core`) never picks a provider or decides routing
itself — it sends a Bearer token to the gateway and lets the gateway decide authentication, routing,
and key-swapping. Centralizing that in the gateway means this crate (and every other agent harness)
doesn't duplicate Ed25519 verification, deny-set checks, or per-provider auth schemes. The exceptions
are credentials that carry a `DirectRouting` (`Credential::with_direct_routing`): direct mode, a
`models.json` `base_url` override, and a GitHub Copilot login all dial their provider without the
gateway.

There are three distinct shapes that token can take, and the gateway already treats two of them
identically:

- **Managed** — a `bai_v1…` virtual key. The gateway verifies it, swaps in its own pool credential,
  and meters usage against the tenant it identifies.
- **BYO** — any other string, forwarded to the upstream provider _unchanged_
  (`crates/gateway/src/proxy.rs`'s "leave the user's own auth header exactly as presented" comment) —
  no pool-key swap, no per-tenant billing record (there's no Beyond identity to attribute cost to).
- **OAuth subscription** (`crate::oauth`/`crate::auth_store`) — a Claude Pro/Max, GitHub Copilot, or
  ChatGPT Plus/Pro login. From the gateway's perspective this is **just another BYO token** — the
  gateway needed _zero_ changes to support it. The insight that made this the right design: a
  subscription-authenticated request is paid for directly by the user, not by Beyond's pool, so BYO's
  existing "no billing record" behavior is exactly correct here, not an accident of reuse.

`agent_core::client::CredentialSource` is the seam that makes this work without `agent_core` ever
learning _how_ a token was obtained: `GatewayClient` resolves a fresh `Credential` immediately before
every request (`client.rs`'s `stream()`) rather than holding one fixed at construction. The trivial
`StaticCredential` (managed/BYO) ships in `agent_core`; the OAuth-aware
`crate::auth_credential_source::OAuthCredentialSource` — which transparently refreshes an expiring
token via `AuthStore`'s locked, cross-process-safe `refreshed()` — lives in `agent`, which depends on
`agent_core`, never the reverse. `agent_core` still never _holds_ a provider key of its own; it only
ever borrows one fetched through this trait for the span of one request, the same rule that governed
it before OAuth existed.

**Identity headers — a confirmed, deliberate divergence from an earlier version of this document.**
Anthropic's and GitHub Copilot's OAuth-gated endpoints check for identity headers naming their own
first-party client before serving a subscription-authenticated request: Anthropic wants
`anthropic-beta: claude-code-20250219,oauth-2025-04-20,…`, `user-agent: claude-cli/<version>`, and
`x-app: cli`; Copilot wants `Editor-Version: vscode/…`, `Editor-Plugin-Version: copilot-chat/…`, and
`Copilot-Integration-Id: vscode-chat`. An earlier version of this document declined to send these,
calling it "false attribution, not parity." That call has been revisited and reversed, on the user's
explicit, informed decision: this crate now sends the real headers — full pi parity, matching pi,
opencode, and other OSS coding agents that all do the same thing. Presenting this tool as Claude
Code/VS Code Copilot Chat to those providers' servers is a real tradeoff (a gray area against both
providers' subscription terms, with some risk of account action if a provider decides to enforce
against it) that the user chose to accept in exchange for the feature actually working end-to-end.
See `client.rs`'s `CLAUDE_CODE_BETA`/`CLAUDE_CLI_IDENTITY` constants for where Anthropic's headers are
attached (gated on `Credential::is_oauth` and on the request having no direct route or one that points
at Anthropic itself, so a Claude model reached through a Copilot login never claims to be Claude Code;
threaded through `send_with_retry` alongside the existing `is_anthropic` bool) — `CLAUDE_CLI_IDENTITY`
in particular is a moving target, not a one-time constant: if Anthropic starts rejecting a stale
`claude-cli/<version>`, it needs bumping to whatever the real Claude Code CLI currently reports.
GitHub Copilot's own identity headers ride a different path: Copilot's proxy endpoint
(`api.{individual,enterprise}.githubcopilot.com`) is not the gateway, so `crate::oauth::github_copilot`'s
credential source tags each credential with a `DirectRouting` to that host carrying the static
editor-identity headers (`static_headers`) and `copilot_dynamic_headers`, and `GatewayClient` sends
them through `send_with_retry`'s `direct_headers`. Its own direct HTTP calls (the token exchange)
attach the same headers.

**Deliberate divergence: no `api_key` credential type in `AuthStore`.** pi's own credential store can
also hold a plain API key per provider, as an alternative to OAuth. This crate already has a working
static-credential mechanism for exactly that job — the `--key`/`AI_AGENT_KEY` flag, resolved through
the gateway's managed/BYO path above — so a second, parallel place to store a static key would be two
mechanisms for one job. `crate::auth_store`'s `StoredCredential` (wrapping `oauth::OAuthCredential`) is
OAuth-only by design.

## Session grant (`bsg_v1`)

A multi-tenant `serve` fleet sits behind an edge that authenticates the user. On every connection the
edge presents a **session grant**: one signed token that tells the replica which tenant and session it
is serving, where that session's workspace, exec endpoint, and MCP connectors are, and — sealed — the
credentials to reach them. [`grant`](src/grant.rs) verifies it offline and opens the secrets.

**Ownership.** This crate owns the spec (this section), the verifier, and the golden vectors
(`tests/fixtures/grant/v1.json`). The control plane mints, and its Go minter must reproduce the
vectors byte for byte. Production code here never mints; the only minter is `#[cfg(test)]` and exists
to pin the vectors.

**Why two asymmetric keys.** Each one makes a trust split structural rather than a convention:

- **Ed25519 signs the claims.** A replica holds only the control plane's _public_ keys, by `kid`, so
  it verifies with no lookup and no round trip — and a compromised replica still cannot mint a grant
  for another tenant. An HMAC would put the minting key on every replica. Same shape as the gateway's
  `bai_v1` virtual key and the control plane's `bagt_v1`.
- **X25519 seals the secrets to the fleet.** The minter needs only the fleet's _public_ key, so the
  edge that relays a grant, a proxy log, or a captured token never sees an exec header, gateway key,
  or DEK. Only a holder of the fleet secret (`--seal-key`) can open them.

### Wire format

```text
bsg_v1.{kid}.{payload_b64}.{sig_b64}

kid         decimal u32, canonical (digits only, no sign, no leading zero)
signed      ASCII "bsg_v1.{kid}.{payload_b64}"   (version and kid are signed: no downgrade, no swap)
sig         Ed25519(signed)
payload     compact JSON, keys in this order:
            {"tenant":str,"session_id":str,"home_shard":str,"workspace_root":str,"exec_url":str,
             "mcp":[{"name":str,"url":str},...],"exp":u64,"code_mode":true,"sealed":str}
exp         unix seconds; the grant is valid while now < exp (no leeway: the minter's TTL absorbs skew)
code_mode   optional; present only as true (a grant that doesn't ask for Code Mode omits it, so it mints
            byte-for-byte as before the claim existed); absent means off

sealed      eph_pk (32) ‖ nonce (24) ‖ XChaCha20-Poly1305 ciphertext ‖ tag (16)
shared      X25519(eph_sk, fleet_pk)          — an all-zero result (low-order eph_pk) is rejected
key         HKDF-SHA256(ikm = shared, salt = eph_pk ‖ fleet_pk, info = ASCII "bsg_v1 seal"), 32 bytes
aad         ASCII "bsg_v1.{kid}"               — the seal is bound to the signing kid
plaintext   compact JSON, keys in this order:
            {"exec_headers":[{"name":str,"value":str},...],
             "mcp_headers":{"<connector name>":[{"name":str,"value":str},...],...},
             "gateway_key":str,"dek":str}
dek         standard base64 (padded) of exactly 32 bytes
```

`payload_b64`, `sig_b64`, and `sealed` are base64url without padding. The minter draws a fresh
ephemeral key and a random 24-byte nonce per grant; the vectors fix both so the output is
deterministic.

The verifier parses the JSON — it never re-serializes it — so any valid JSON verifies. Byte-exact
encoding only matters for reproducing the vectors: compact, keys in the order above, `mcp_headers`
keys sorted bytewise (Go's map marshal already does this), and **no HTML escaping** (Go:
`json.Encoder` with `SetEscapeHTML(false)`, trailing newline trimmed). The vector's MCP URL carries
an `&`, so a minter that escapes it fails the byte comparison instead of shipping.

### Verification

`GrantVerifier::verify(token, now)` runs these stages in order and fails at the first with its own
[`GrantError`](src/grant.rs) variant. Nothing in the payload is read before the signature checks
out, and no crypto runs for an untrusted kid.

| Stage             | Rejects                                                                                                      | Variant                |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- |
| Parse             | wrong prefix or field count, a non-canonical kid, a signature that isn't base64url of 64 bytes               | `Malformed`            |
| Kid               | a kid not passed as `--grant-key` — usually a rotation gap                                                   | `UnknownKid(kid)`      |
| Signature         | Ed25519 `verify_strict` over the literal signed bytes fails: tampered, or signed by another key              | `BadSignature`         |
| Claims            | the payload isn't base64url JSON of exactly the v1 fields (`deny_unknown_fields`)                            | `BadClaims`            |
| Expiry            | `now >= exp`                                                                                                 | `Expired { exp, now }` |
| Unseal: structure | `sealed` isn't base64url, is shorter than `eph_pk ‖ nonce ‖ tag` (72 bytes), or carries a low-order `eph_pk` | `SealMalformed`        |
| Unseal: AEAD      | the tag doesn't verify: sealed to another fleet key, under another kid's AAD, or altered                     | `SealOpenFailed`       |
| Unseal: contents  | the plaintext isn't exactly the v1 secrets shape, or the DEK isn't 32 bytes                                  | `BadClaims`            |

An unknown claim is refused, not ignored: a v1 replica that silently dropped a claim it didn't
understand — a future restriction, say — would fail open. Any change to the format is `bsg_v2`.

**Secret hygiene.** Error text is static apart from a kid or timestamps. Every secret — header
values and the gateway key (`auth_store::Secret`), the DEK (`grant::Dek`) — redacts in `Debug` and
is zeroized on drop, as are the decoded seal blob and the derived AEAD key. The AEAD opens in place
inside the decoded blob, so the plaintext never gets a second buffer. `--seal-key` errors name the
path, never the file's contents.

### Keys and flags

`serve --grant-key <kid>=<Ed25519 public key>` (repeatable; comma-separated in `AI_AGENT_GRANT_KEY`)
and `--seal-key <path>` (`AI_AGENT_SEAL_KEY`; a file holding base64 of the 32-byte X25519 secret,
whitespace trimmed — `wg genkey` output, with `wg pubkey` giving the public key the minter seals to).
Keys may be standard or url-safe base64. Both flags or neither: one without the other, a duplicated
kid, or an unparseable key fails `serve` at startup. Neither flag leaves `serve` exactly as it was.
The parsed verifier lands in `ServeConfig::grant_verifier` (an `Arc`, shared by every session).
`serve --service` is what consults it: see "Service mode" below.

Signing keys rotate without a gap: trust the new kid beside the old, move the minter to the new kid,
and drop the old one once every grant it signed has expired. The fleet seal key is one secret at a
time, so rotating it is a coordinated switch: a grant sealed to the old key fails `SealOpenFailed` on
a replica that already holds the new one, until it is re-minted.

### Golden vectors

`tests/fixtures/grant/v1.json` holds the inputs (signing seed, kid, fleet secret, ephemeral secret,
nonce, `now`, claims, secrets), every intermediate (shared secret, AEAD key, plaintext JSON, `sealed`,
payload JSON), the expected token, the flag-format keys, and ten negative cases — wrong prefix,
tampered payload, tampered signature, unknown kid, expired, wrong seal key, truncated seal, low-order
ephemeral key, unknown claim, short DEK — each with the variant it must fail with. `grant.rs`'s unit
tests assert that the test-only minter reproduces every token byte for byte, that the verifier yields
exactly the fixture's claims and secrets, and that each negative fails with its own variant. A
deliberate change regenerates the file with `UPDATE_FIXTURES=1 cargo test -p beyond-ai-agent grant::`
(then `dprint fmt`); the control plane's minter must then match it again.

## Session storage — single file, or epoch segments

`session_store.rs` writes a session through one private seam, `Log`, which has two shapes. The tree
logic above it — ids, branches, compaction, labels — never learns which one it is on.

|               | `Layout::File` (default)           | `Layout::Segmented`                          |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| on disk       | `<dir>/<created_at>_<id>.jsonl`    | `<dir>/<id>/`                                |
| append        | `O_APPEND` write, `fsync`          | append into the segment this process created |
| replace       | temp file + `rename` + dir `fsync` | a new **base** segment                       |
| memory        | `<...>.memory/` sibling            | `<id>/memory`                                |
| who may write | whoever holds the file             | whoever created the newest epoch             |

`SessionRepo::open` gives the single-file layout with no id prefix, and is byte-for-byte what it
always was. `SessionRepo::open_with(dir, RepoOptions { layout, id_prefix })` selects the other.
`SessionStore::open(path)` probes with `is_dir()`, so `main.rs`, `fork_from_path` and export keep
handing a bare path over without knowing which shape it names.

### The segmented layout

```text
<dir>/<id>/
  .beyond-lock    advisory, liveness only (OFD lock; see Locks)
  lock            the legacy flock older binaries take, kept for a mixed rollout
  000001.jsonl    epoch 1 — created with O_EXCL; the session's existence fence
  000002.jsonl    epoch 2 — created by the next owner, sealing epoch 1 where it stopped reading
  ...
  memory/         this session's /session working memory
```

**Segment header** — the plaintext first line of every segment:

```json
{ "type": "segment", "epoch": 2, "sealed": { "1": 728 }, "base": false }
```

`sealed` maps an epoch to the byte offset it is readable up to; it carries **every** seal since the
last base, so a reader starting at that base can bound each segment between without opening headers
it may no longer be able to read. `base` says the segment's content is a full rewrite.

**Base trailer** — the plaintext line that closes a base's own content:

```json
{ "type": "base_complete" }
```

A base counts only once its trailer is on disk. Lines after the trailer are ordinary appends. Epoch 1
is written as a complete base holding the session header, so a replay always has somewhere to start.

**Sealed transcript line** — every other line, when a codec is configured:

```text
e1.<kfp8>:<base64url(nonce(24) ‖ ciphertext ‖ tag(16))>
```

`kfp8` is eight hex digits of key fingerprint, for rotation. A plaintext line starts with `{`; a
sealed one never does, which is how a reader tells them apart with no state.

### Effective view

1. Start at the newest **complete** base (header says `base`, and its trailer is present), else at
   the oldest segment there is.
2. Read each segment from just past its header up to its seal; the newest reads to the length the
   scan observed.
3. A segment whose header is torn or missing counts as empty, sealed at 0. A `base` segment newer
   than the start never had its trailer land, so its content — a partial rewrite of the whole
   transcript — is skipped entirely, while its header's seals still count.
4. A torn final line is dropped, but only at the end of a segment's range. A sealed line that fails
   to open anywhere is a hard error: the bytes are not this session's, and presenting a truncated
   view would let the next write overwrite real history.
5. Every descriptor is opened up front, so an unlink underneath the reader is harmless; `ENOENT`/
   `ESTALE` restarts the whole read.

### Ownership: the epoch fence

There is no lease and no clock. A writer owns a session because it created a file nobody else could
have created.

- **Create** — `create_dir_all(<id>)` (idempotent, so the lock can live there), then
  `000001.jsonl` at mode 0600, created **whole** (`create_whole`): the complete base goes to a hidden
  temp file beside it, `fsync`ed, then `link`ed into place — `link` refuses an existing name, so it
  is still the exclusive-create fence, but the name never exists with less than its header — then
  `fsync` of its directory and the parent. A directory with no segments is not a session. The
  single-file layout creates its `.jsonl` the same way. A crash between an O_EXCL create and the
  header write used to leave an empty first file that bricked the id for good — not openable (no
  header) and not creatable (it exists); `open_or_create_id` now treats such a file, left by an older
  build, as absent: one that is empty, or has no newline and only the start of a header line
  (`is_headerless`), is renamed aside, judged again (and put back if a creator raced it), then removed
  and the id created (`tests/session_create_recovery.rs`).
- **Open** — record the newest epoch `N` and the offset `L` the replay consumed. Nothing is created
  until the first write.
- **First write** — if `len(N) ≠ L`, `Superseded`. Otherwise O_EXCL-create `N+1` with the seals so
  far plus `{N: L}`; `EEXIST` is also `Superseded`. A store that just created a segment (a fresh
  create, a fork, a base) appends into it rather than rolling another.
- **`Superseded` poisons the store.** Every later write fails, whatever kind — a title, a label, a
  model change, a rewrite. `SessionStore::superseded()` is what an owner checks after each write;
  `session_store::is_superseded(&err)` classifies the error.
- **A stale writer's bytes are harmless to a reader.** They land past the seal the new epoch
  recorded, so no replay reaches them. They are _not_ harmless to the writer's own client, which is
  a separate problem with a separate fix — see below.
- **Every committed batch re-checks.** The rules above fence an owner that is _rolling_. An owner
  that already holds an open target appends straight to it, so without a second check it never
  learns it was fenced: its appends keep succeeding (they are ordinary appends to a file it can
  still write), the successor sealed that segment at the offset it read, and the owner goes on
  telling its client that turns committed which no reader will ever replay. So after each committed
  batch — once per turn, not per line, next to an `fsync` that costs far more — the segmented log
  `stat`s the epoch after its own. If it exists, someone else claimed it and the store is poisoned.
  This does not close the window entirely: a successor that reads this segment's length and creates
  its epoch _after_ the check has passed still seals away an acknowledged line, and a network
  filesystem's negative-lookup cache bounds detection from below. It reduces the exposure from
  unbounded to one round trip; closing it completely needs a fencing token in the write itself,
  which the format has no room for today. Measured with a partitioned owner against a real NFSv4
  lease: the successor took over at 102 s, and before this check the old owner then committed a turn,
  answered `success`, and that turn was absent from the transcript the successor replayed.
- **Deployment invariant: the shard's NFS mount (`shard_mount`).** The re-check is a lookup of the
  next epoch's name, and an NFS client may answer a lookup from cache: a negative dentry is trusted
  until the directory's cached attributes expire, up to `acdirmax` (with the default
  `lookupcache=all`). The fence holds anyway because a successor can only take a session from a
  partitioned owner after the owner's NFSv4 lease expires — at least one lease after the owner's
  last contact, which is no earlier than any attribute it cached — so once the owner can reach the
  server again, every cache that could hide the successor's segment is already older than a lease.
  That needs `acdirmax` (and `acdirmin`; `actimeo` sets both) shorter than the lease, and
  close-to-open consistency so a successor's open of the predecessor reads its real length.
  `serve --service` checks this at startup: it reads `/proc/self/mountinfo` and finds the mount each
  `--shard` path lives on (resolved through symlinks, deepest and latest mount wins). It refuses to
  start, naming the shard and the option, when an `nfs`/`nfs4` mount has `nocto`, or has
  `lookupcache=all` with a directory attribute timeout of 80 s or more (the assumed 90 s lease less
  a 10 s margin). `lookupcache=none`/`pos` never caches negative lookups, so `acdirmax` is not
  limited there. A shard that is not on NFS passes, and if `mountinfo` cannot be read startup fails
  (fail closed). The kernel prints only non-default timeouts; its defaults (30 s/60 s) are what
  ECS/Fargate mounts EFS with, so the shipped deployment passes. The lease belongs to the server and
  no client interface exposes it, so 90 s (EFS's, and Linux `nfsd`'s default) is assumed: a server
  set to a shorter lease needs a correspondingly smaller `acdirmax`, which this check cannot see.
- **An append that fails** seals the segment at its last good offset and rolls on the next write, so
  one `ENOSPC` can't brick a session with an unbounded torn line mid-segment.

### Bases, consolidation and deletion

`replace_all` (compaction's path) O_EXCL-creates a new base segment, writes the seals, the content
and the trailer, and `fsync`s. That segment becomes the append target. Above **K = 8** segments since
the last base, the next persist writes a base instead of rolling — which bounds the growth a
reap-and-reattach cycle causes. Consolidation copies the current view's bytes rather than
re-serializing the in-memory tree, so the model/title/label/leaf records that live only on disk
survive it.

A new base deletes only the segments **older than the base it supersedes**, so a reader that already
started at that base still has every file it needs. Epoch 1 is never deleted: it is the O_EXCL fence
that says the session exists.

### Sealing

`TenantCodec { tenant, dek }` holds one tenant's keys — not one session's. A listing, a fork and a
preview all open _other_ ids, so the session id is mixed in as associated data per call instead of
being baked into a key. Three HKDF-SHA256 subkeys, XChaCha20-Poly1305, nonces from `getrandom::fill`:

| surface          | HKDF `info`         | AAD                                                     | shape      |
| ---------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- |
| transcript lines | `bsg_v1 transcript` | `tenant ‖ 0x00 ‖ session_id`                            | per line   |
| `.listings.json` | `bsg_v1 listing`    | `tenant`                                                | whole file |
| memory documents | `bsg_v1 memory`     | `tenant`                                                | whole file |
| session sidecars | `bsg_v1 transcript` | `tenant ‖ 0x00 ‖ session_id ‖ 0x00 ‖ "sidecar:" ‖ kind` | whole file |

Segment headers and base trailers stay plaintext, so a reader can bound a file it cannot open.
Memory documents are bound to the tenant and **not** to their path, because `rename` moves a document
without rewriting it. The grant's `dek` is per-tenant and stable, which is what makes all of this
coherent across a tenant's sessions.

### Locks

`acquire_session_lock(path)` is `file_lock::try_lock` on the session — `Target::Dir` for a session
directory, `Target::File` for a `.jsonl`. The MCP manifest's write lock and the memory store's lock
are the same primitive, `Target::File` on the manifest file and on `<memdir>/.memory`; the memory
store's legacy `flock` is the `.memory.lock` older binaries took. The settings, trust, auth and
MCP-auth stores lock with `file_lock::lock_store_file` — `Target::Beside` on the store file
(`settings.json.beyond-lock`, …), waited on for up to 5 s and then `TimedOut`, with no legacy half.
They used to lock with a create-new `<file>.lock` deleted on release and broken by age after 10 s, so
a writer that crashed while holding it made every write to that store fail for those 10 s; a dead
holder's kernel lock is already released. The old `<file>.lock` is neither taken nor deleted — a
