leftover one is ignored — so during a rollout an old binary and this one do not exclude each other
on these stores: a concurrent read-modify-write of the same small config file by the two can lose one
change. `Ok(None)` means someone holds it right now. It is **liveness only** — correctness is
the epoch fence, which needs no lock — so a lock lost to a crash or a partition costs a retry, never
history.

**An open file description (OFD) lock** on Linux: exclusive, non-blocking, whole file
(`fcntl(F_OFD_SETLK)`, through `nix`), on a lock file only `file_lock` names (`<dir>/.beyond-lock`,
`<file>.beyond-lock`). It belongs to the one `open` that took it, which settles the two ways a lock used
to be lost:

- **Another descriptor of the same file** — a file tool, the memory tool, an `@file` read, reaching it
  by name, through a symlink or a hard link — is a different description: opening and closing it
  neither releases this lock nor shares it. (A POSIX record lock belongs to the process, so closing
  any of its descriptors of the file dropped it; that made every in-process opener a hazard.) Two
  descriptions conflict even inside one process, so a second acquire here, under any spelling of the
  path, is refused by the kernel — there is no in-process registry.
- **A forked child.** A child forked by any thread (a `bash` call, an MCP stdio server) shares the
  description until it execs. The lock is released with an explicit `F_UNLCK` on its descriptor before
  that descriptor closes, which drops it whatever copies a child holds. (`flock` released by closing
  is what made a just-released lock look held 180 times in 3000 while other threads spawned
  processes — the root cause of `serve_ws::tests::a_session_directory_with_a_segment_is_left_alone`
  flaking under load.)

Off Linux there are no OFD locks; there it is `flock`, which also belongs to the description, released
the same way with an explicit `LOCK_UN`.

**On NFS/EFS** the Linux client sends an OFD lock to the server as a POSIX byte-range lock owned by the
open file description, so the same two properties hold there. Verified against a loopback NFSv4.2
mount (`local_lock=none`, so every lock goes to the server): the `file_lock` tests and the session-lock
probes below all pass with their files on the mount. (`flock` on NFS is emulated with a process-owned
POSIX lock, which is why it is not the authoritative half.)

Nothing else needs guarding: the only remaining hazard is _replacing_ a lock file, which an atomic
write (`tools::write_atomic`) could do by renaming over it — it refuses a lock file as its target
(`file_lock::is_lock_file`, applied after resolving a symlink). **It never opens the target and never
locks it — it only `stat`s.** Opening a FIFO with no writer blocks forever, opening a device can act,
and a test lock makes another program's own non-blocking lock fail while it is held (2071 of 20000
attempts, measured). So a target is a lock file only when one of three things says so:

- **Its name**, compared without regard to ASCII case: a record lock file, or a legacy `lock` /
  `<f>.lock` beside one.
- **It is a lock this process holds.** `try_lock` puts the (device, inode) of each lock file in a
  small counted set **before** it tries to lock it, takes it out again if the attempt fails, and
  `Drop` takes it out only after unlocking — so no moment exists when a lock is held but reads as not
  held (a brief false "held" mid-acquire is the safe direction). `write_atomic` looks the target's
  `stat` up there. That covers a journal key held through `Target::Itself` under any name, a hard link
  to one of our own lock files, and a spelling a case-insensitive filesystem folds onto one.
- **An old binary's legacy lock with no record lock file beside it**, by where it sits: a `lock` in a
  session directory (one holding `000001.jsonl`, which is never deleted), or a `<f>.lock` beside a
  session file (`*.jsonl`), the MCP manifest or the memory store's `.memory`. Whether anyone holds it
  is not asked.

Anything else is an ordinary file and an edit of it goes through: a SQLite database another program
holds mid-transaction, a daemon's pid file, an unrelated `Cargo.lock`, a `lock` in a directory that
holds no session. (Verified on a casefold ext4 directory as well as here.) A worktree seed leaves
record lock files behind (a copy of a lock is no lock). A failed session start's directory is taken
back through `file_lock::dir_holds_only_lock_files` and `FileLock::release_and_remove_files`, which **closes** the
lock files' descriptors before the directory is removed: an NFS client turns the unlink of a file it
still has open into a rename to `.nfs*`, which stays until the last close and makes `remove_dir` fail
with ENOTEMPTY (`serve_ws::tests::an_empty_session_directory_is_taken_back_with_its_lock` fails on a
loopback NFS mount with the old unlink, remove, close order, and passes with this one).

A small file whose holder writes it under its own lock — the MCP task journal key — is locked
**itself** (`Target::Itself`): no lock file beside it, and the key is re-read and written through the
locked descriptor (`FileLock::file`). No legacy `flock` there: no released binary took one, and an
`flock` on the same file would conflict with the process's own OFD lock on NFS, where `flock` is a
process-owned POSIX lock.

**Mixed rollout.** Binaries before this one took only an `flock` on `<dir>/lock` / `<file>.lock`. So
`try_lock` also takes that `flock` (its own descriptor, close-on-exec, released with an explicit
`LOCK_UN`), and a held one means held: an old binary still excludes this one and the other way round.
It is retried for up to 250 ms, since an old binary's own fork→exec window can hold it briefly. **The
legacy `flock` half is removed in a later release, once no older binary can run against the same
files.**

Pinned by `session_store::tests::a_released_session_lock_is_free_at_once_while_other_threads_spawn_processes`
(0 of 3000 with 8 threads spawning),
`every_in_process_reader_reaching_the_lock_file_leaves_it_held` (read, write, edit, search, the memory
tool's view and an `@file` read, through a symlink and a hard link: still held for another process,
refused a second time here, the file untouched), `reading_a_locked_session_through_any_public_api_leaves_it_locked`,
and `file_lock`'s own tests (another descriptor neither releases nor shares it, a child holding the
description cannot keep a released lock, one holder per process, an old binary's `flock` excluding this
one). After locking, `fstat` on the held descriptor is compared with `stat` of the path, catching a
directory renamed into `.trash/` between the open and the lock.

`SessionRepo::delete` on a segmented repo takes that lock first and refuses if it is held, then
renames `<id>/` → `.trash/<id>.<unix_ns>`. The timestamp suffix is what makes repeated deletes of one
id work, and the rename carries `memory/` along with the segments.

### Listings

The sidecar `.listings.json` cache is keyed by a stamp: `(size, mtime)` for a file, and the **newest
segment's** `(len, mtime, epoch)` plus the **segment count** for a segmented session, so a roll, an
append, a base or a prune all invalidate it. It is a cache and only a cache — a blob that will not
open is treated as no cache at all.

The stamp has to be cheap, because it is the validator: the scan computes it for **every** candidate
path, on a cache hit as much as a miss, so it is the floor on the cost of listing a shard. It is one
`readdir`. It used to also `File::open` and header-parse every segment of every session just to learn
which one carried the base, which made a 100%-warm cache pay O(shards × sessions × segments) opens
for an answer it then threw away. Dropping the base epoch is safe because a base is never written in
place — `SegLog::write_base` creates `pred + 1` with `create_new`, so a base always _advances_ the
newest epoch, and the prune that retires what it superseded moves the count. Narrowing the size from
the directory total to the newest segment's length is safe for the same kind of reason: an older
segment only ever changes by a stale writer appending past its seal, and those bytes are ignored by
every reader, so the listing they would invalidate is still correct. `LISTING_INDEX_VERSION` is
bumped whenever the stamp's or the cached fields' meaning changes (it is at **3**: v2 was this stamp,
v3 dropped the cached `search_text`), since an index at an unknown version is discarded wholesale
rather than validated against a stamp that means something else.

### Derived ids

`RepoOptions.id_prefix` makes every id the repo _mints_ — a fork, a clone, an archive —
`<prefix>.<opaque>`, so a derived session stays on its parent's shard and every path built from it
is still rooted at the same tenant. An id the caller supplies is never rewritten.

`SessionStore::memory_dir()` is the only correct way to find a session's `/session` directory:
`memory::session_dir`'s `with_extension` would turn a dotted `<shard>.<opaque>` id into one shared
`<shard>.memory` directory for every session on the shard.

## Service mode — one replica, many tenants

> **Operating a fleet of these, and building the edge in front of them, is
> [FLEET.md](FLEET.md).** This section is the mechanism: what a replica does and why. That one is the
> contract and the operations — the routing obligations the agent cannot enforce, replica sizing and
> blast radius, what to alert on, how it scales, and what it costs against the alternatives.

`serve --listen … --service` turns the daemon from "a headless agent for whoever is on the other end
of this socket" into a **fail-closed multi-tenant service**. Every connection presents a
[session grant](#session-grant-bsg_v1) in the `x-beyond-grant` header (or, for a browser
`WebSocket`, which cannot set headers, as `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: beyond.grant, <grant>`); that grant says which tenant
and session it is, where the session's sandbox and workspace are, and — sealed — the credentials to
reach them. [`service.rs`](src/service.rs) is the seam: it turns a token into a `ServiceSession`, and
everything `serve` used to answer from the replica host it now asks that.

**The rule the whole mode exists for: nothing of the replica's reaches a tenant.** Not its `$HOME`
(`~/.claude` skills, prompts, agents, `SYSTEM.md`/`APPEND_SYSTEM.md`, CLAUDE.md), not its stored
settings (`settings.json`, `models.json`, `auth.json`, configured MCP servers), not its cwd, not its
ambient provider environment, not its filesystem as a fallback for an unset exec endpoint. Where a
host default would have applied, service mode **refuses** instead. The operator can still pass
`--system-prompt`/`--append-system-prompt` explicitly — those are the operator's, not another
tenant's.

The sections below are one per landing change; each fills in its own.

### The connection: grant → `ServiceSession`

`handle_connection` verifies **before** the method branch, so the WebSocket and POST paths cannot
diverge on who is allowed in. The `x-beyond-grant` header is taken off the `HttpHead` the moment it
is read (`HttpHead::take_grant`): the head is handed to tungstenite's `create_response`, which echoes
request headers into the handshake, so a grant left in place would be reflected straight back to
whoever sent it. A value over **12 KiB** is dropped unread — the whole header block is capped at
16 KiB, so a larger one cannot be a grant this fleet minted. The subprotocol form is parsed as an RFC 6455
comma-separated list and accepted only when it is exactly the `beyond.grant` marker followed by one token;
the marker with anything else is a 400, a list without the marker is some other negotiation and is left
alone, and a grant in **both** carriers is a 400 (even if they agree) rather than a silent choice. The
whole `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` header is stripped from the head, and the 101 answers
`Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: beyond.grant` only, never the token. `now` comes from `SystemTime` with
`unwrap_or(u64::MAX)`: a clock the process cannot read at all expires every grant rather than
accepting every expired one.

| Condition                                                                               | Status                  |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| no grant, or one that does not verify (unknown kid, bad signature, expired, unsealable) | 401 Unauthorized        |
| no `?session_id=` in the URL                                                            | 400 Bad Request         |
| `grant.session_id` ≠ the URL's id                                                       | 403 Forbidden           |
| the id is live under **another tenant**                                                 | 403 Forbidden           |
| tenant, shard name or connector name not a path segment; `workspace_root` not absolute  | 400 Bad Request         |
| the id's shard, or `grant.home_shard`, is not mounted here                              | 421 Misdirected Request |

421 rather than 404 is deliberate: the grant is fine, this replica is the wrong one, and the edge
should route it to a replica that mounts the shard.

**Pin before the upgrade.** `handle_websocket_upgrade` pins the session slot and _then_ writes the
101. The tenant check and the still-stopping wait both live on the slot, and both of their answers
are HTTP statuses (403, 503) — past the upgrade the only vocabulary left is a close code, which no
HTTP client, proxy, or retry policy can read as "wrong tenant" or "try again". POST maps the same
`PinError` enum.

**A grant is per connection; a session's secrets are not.** The connection that _spawns_ a session
hands its `Arc<ServiceSession>` to that session's task, where it fixes the tenant, storage, sandbox
and gateway credential for the task's life. Every later attach still needs its own valid grant for
the same `(tenant, session_id)` — `SessionHandle.tenant` is what enforces that — but does not
re-point any of it. `exp` is therefore checked per connection, not per session.

### Shards and the tenant layout

`--shard <name>=</absolute/path>` (repeatable) names a tenant-data mount. A shard is a storage
domain, not a tenant: many tenants live on one shard.

```text
<shard root>/<tenant>/sessions/     the tenant's transcripts on this shard
<shard root>/<tenant>/memory/       the tenant's durable memory (on its home shard only)
```

A session id carries its shard as a `<shard>.` prefix, so an id alone says which mount to open — no
lookup, and a session for an unmounted shard is a routing answer (421) rather than a 404. An id with
no prefix belongs to the grant's `home_shard`. Shard names are letters, digits, `-` and `_` — no
`.`, so `<shard>.<opaque>` splits unambiguously.

From that, one connection's `ServiceSession` derives `session_dir = <id's shard>/<tenant>/sessions`
and `memory_dir = <home shard>/<tenant>/memory`. Durable memory follows the _home_ shard so a
tenant's memory does not fragment as its sessions spread across mounts.

### Startup

`--service` requires the grant verifier (`--grant-key` + `--seal-key`), at least one `--shard`, and a
listener (`--listen`, `--listen-uds`, or systemd socket activation). Stdio `serve --service` is
refused: stdio has no place to carry a per-connection grant. Every shard's NFS mount is checked
before anything is served (`shard_mount::check_shards`; see the epoch fence's deployment invariant).

These flags are **refused**, not ignored — an operator who passes one must find out at startup rather
than from an audit later: `--key`, `--session-file`, `--session-dir`, `--session-id`, `--continue`,
`--name`, `--no-session-persistence`, `--memory`, `--trust-project`, `--force-untrusted`,
`--exec-url`, `--exec-cmd`, `--exec-header`, `--web-allow-private`, `--web-allow-host`,
`--code-mode`, `--skill`, `--prompt-template`, `--bash-shell-path`. Each has an env var, and the env
var is refused the same way (`AI_AGENT_KEY` is `--key`). Worktree isolation is not in that list
because it is not a flag: a subagent asks for it in its own definition, which service mode discovers
only from the tenant's sandbox (see "Sandbox discovery"), and it runs there.

Three host contributions are skipped outright rather than refused, because they are defaults rather
than requests: the stored-settings tier (`effective_settings_for_cwd` — so no persisted shell path,
skill/template paths, memory backend, session directory, model or gateway URL), the process-wide MCP
`connect_all`, and `ProviderEnv::from_process_env`.

### The session

`service.rs` answers each of these; `serve_session` delegates rather than branching inline.

- **Persistence** opens a repo at `service.session_dir` with **no fallback** — a `service_mode`
  config that reached a session without a grant is an error, never the per-cwd default repo.
  `SessionMeta.cwd` is the grant's `workspace_root`.
- **Exec, strict, and lazy.** `ExecCell::strict()` has no host fallback: an empty cell errors
  instead of running on `RealRunner`/`LocalFs`. On a replica that fallback is not stale config, it is
  a tenant's `bash` on the machine every other tenant shares. The target is built from `exec_url`
  plus the grant's `SecretHeader`s, then **probed**: `sh -c 'printf %s "$HOME"'`. Its output becomes
  the backend's home (`ShellFs::with_home`), so `~` expands inside the sandbox; a second
  `command -v bash` records which shell the remote `bash` tool should ask for. Exec headers are never
  persisted — `set_exec_endpoint`, the only writer of that record, is refused.

  The probe runs **when the sandbox is first needed, not when the session opens**: a sandbox sleeps
  when idle and any exec request wakes it, and a client reopening a chat to read it is no reason to
  wake one. `ExecCell::set_lazy` installs `ServiceSession::lazy_exec` as the cell's connector, and
  `CellRoute::resolve` runs it before the first call is dispatched — `CellRunner` and `CellFs` both
  wait on it, so no tool can run before the probe, and concurrent first calls share one probe (a
  `tokio` mutex, single flight). A failed probe is that call's error, worded as a failed start is
  (`service::UNREACHABLE`: "this session's sandbox is unreachable: …"), and is not remembered: the
  next call probes again. Until the probe has run, `CellFs::world` answers with the home the session
  last saw, so a `~` resolves the same way before it as after. `CommandRunner::ready` connects
  explicitly for the one synchronous question asked of a target (`sandbox_jobs`): `bash` calls it
  before anything else, so a probe failure is reported once, as the call's error.

  What a probe learned lives on the built target (`ExecTarget`: the runner, its lazily probed v1.2
  streaming and v1.3 jobs capabilities, the `ShellFs` capability rung) and on the `ServiceSession`
  (`Sandbox`: home and shell). It is thrown away, and the next call probes again, when the target
  turns **suspect** — its runner raises a flag shared with the target (`HttpExecRunner::
  with_suspect_flag`, `ExecTarget::watching`) on a request the endpoint did not answer or refused
  with a non-2xx status, the signs of a replaced sandbox; a timeout does not count — and on a session
  switch (`reset_exec_endpoint!` installs a fresh connector). A grant's credentials are fixed for a
  session task's life, so a refreshed token arrives with a new task, which probes anew; the endpoint
  cannot be re-pointed (`set_exec_endpoint` is refused). A session with no [snapshot](#sandbox-snapshot)
  (a new one, or one saved by an older binary) connects at start, because building its prompt needs
  the sandbox anyway, and a probe that fails then ends the session as before.
- **Credentials.** `build_gateway_client` uses the grant's sealed `gateway_key` and skips the whole
  host ladder (`--key`, ambient provider env, `models.json` overrides, the OAuth store). The retry,
  shared-client and idle-timeout chain is unchanged.
- **Prompt.** `PromptOptions.disk_overrides = false` — the replica's own `SYSTEM.md`/
  `APPEND_SYSTEM.md` never apply, and a subagent inherits that. Everything the prompt _is_ made of
  comes from the sandbox instead; see "Sandbox discovery". No worktree sweep, no trust store, no
  untrusted-project warning — sandbox content is the tenant's own, so it counts as trusted.
- **Memory** is `FileBackend::at(service.memory_dir)`, sealed with the tenant's codec
  (`ServiceSession::memory_backend`).

### Commands

Gated at dispatch **and** at both busy-loop intercepts, so a refusal never costs a running prompt:
`fork`/`clone`/`new_session`/`switch_session` self-abort a run to make room for themselves, and a
command that was going to be refused must not get that far.

**Refused:** `set_exec_endpoint` (the grant fixes the endpoint), the whole login surface (`login`,
`submit_code`, `abort_login`, `logout`, `auth_status` — an operator credential store),
`switch_session` (connect at `?session_id=` with a grant for that session), and the MCP Events
commands (`mcp_events_list`/`_subscribe`/`_unsubscribe` — grant connectors carry no events).
`reload` and `fork`/
`clone`/`new_session` were each refused for a while — the first until sandbox discovery re-aimed it at
the tenant's own filesystem, the others until derived ids carried their shard prefix — and all of them
are allowed now.

**Changed:**

- `export_html` returns the document inline as `data.html` (`render_html_full`); `output_path` is
  refused rather than silently ignored.
- The settings toggles (`set_auto_compaction`, `set_block_images`, `set_image_auto_resize`,
  `set_steering_mode`, `set_follow_up_mode`) are session-local — the `SettingsStore` is not even
  opened, since it is the operator's file and shared by every tenant on the box.
- `list_sessions` drops its cwd filter (the directory is already tenant-scoped); `list_all_sessions`
  and `list_daemon_sessions` merge `<every mounted shard>/<tenant>/sessions`, and
  `list_daemon_sessions` also filters the live map by tenant.
- `delete_session`, `restore_session`, `list_trash` and `preview_fork` route by the **target id's own
  shard**, and match the id **exactly**: the repo's unique-prefix fallback is a convenience for an id
  a human typed, and a tenant's ids are minted — a miss must be an error, not a neighbour (and, for
  `delete`, not a silent `Ok`).
- `get_state` reports `cwd = workspace_root` and `cwd_stale = false`; `git_branch` runs in the
  sandbox through the session's runner (see "Sandbox discovery"), never against the replica's own
  checkout — and is `null` without asking while the sandbox is not attached yet, so a client's poll
  never wakes a reopened session's sandbox.
- Redacted: `session_file` is `null`, and `TrashEntry.original_path` plus every failed response's
  `error` have replica mount paths stripped (`ServiceSession::redact`, applied on the one frame
  funnel).
- Lifecycle events carry `tenant`, since one replica emits for many.
- A session that fails to start sends an `{"type":"error", session_id, error}` frame to its attached
  connections before closing. It used to write only to the replica's stderr, leaving the client with
  a socket that accepted commands and answered nothing.

### Remote-world tools

Paths resolve against the sandbox root in the backend's world (`tools::resolve_against_in`,
`fs::PathWorld`). The host-only checks are dropped in the remote world: `bash`'s `is_dir` on its
`cwd` and its shell probe (it uses the probed `remote_shell`, else `sh`), `root_is_inside_git_repo`
(only `LocalFs` asks it), and `display_base`'s process cwd (with no tool root, result paths print as
the search produced them). Oversized
`bash` output gets no host spill file (`OutputAccumulator::without_spill`).

### Sandbox discovery

Everything a tenant's prompt is made of comes from the tenant's own box, read through the session's
exec backend. `ServiceSession::resources` is the single seam that does it — session start, the
post-reopen refresh and `reload` all call it, which is exactly why `reload` is allowed here at all:
"re-walk the filesystem" now means the tenant's. A reopened session starts from its saved set
instead (see "Sandbox snapshot").

| Resource                            | Sandbox roots (ascending specificity — a later one shadows an earlier)              |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| skills                              | `<home>/.claude/skills`, `<workspace>/.agents/skills`, `<workspace>/.claude/skills` |
| agent definitions, prompt templates | `<home>/.claude/{agents,prompts}`, `<workspace>/.claude/{agents,prompts}`           |
| `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`             | `<home>/.claude`, then every ancestor of `<workspace>`, nearest last                |
| `SYSTEM.md`/`APPEND_SYSTEM.md`      | `<workspace>/.claude`, else `<home>/.claude`                                        |

`<home>` is the sandbox's own `$HOME`, from the startup probe — the tenant's home, not the
replica's. None of it is trust-gated: on this host that gate protects an operator from a checkout
they did not write, and inside one tenant's own box there is no second party to protect from.

The prompt overrides arrive as `PromptOptions::base`/`append`, **not** through
`PromptOptions::disk_overrides`, which stays `false`. That flag answers "may the replica's disk set
this prompt?", and the answer is never yes; routing the sandbox's own files around it keeps the two
questions from collapsing into one. An explicit `--append-system-prompt` still outranks the file,
matching the on-disk precedence.

**Skill bodies are prefetched at discovery.** `/skill:name` expansion (`expand_if_skill_invocation`)
is synchronous and sits five call sites deep on the prompt path, so there is no read to `await`
later; `Skill::body` carries the text for a backend-side skill and stays `None` for a host one, whose
progressive disclosure is the whole point. Advertised locations are sandbox paths — which is what
makes them usable, since the model opens one by handing the path back to `read`, and `read` runs
through the same backend.

Two deliberate narrowings against the on-host walks, both because a round trip is not a `stat`: only
the `SKILL.md`-per-directory shape is recognized (never `.claude/skills`'s loose single `.md` file),
and context files are tried by name rather than by listing each ancestor — a workspace root can hold
ten thousand entries, and moving that listing to answer a two-file question is not a trade worth
making. `tools::fs::read_text_capped` is the one stat-check-read spelling all of them share, so the
1 MiB cap lands before the bytes move in every case.

**Root, policy and shell.** `build_tools` sets `root = workspace_root`, so a relative path the model
writes lands in the tenant's workspace rather than wherever this replica's process was started, and
`remote_shell` to what `command -v bash` found. Every `ToolPolicy` construction site
(`build_agent`'s gate, the RPC `bash` gate, a subagent's) is rooted the same way and takes its world
from the backend via `ToolPolicy::in_world` — the backend is the authority on which filesystem a call
lands on, and a policy that decides separately is a deny-list that silently stops firing rather than
a visible error.

**Subagents** inherit all of it: the parent's `workspace_root` as their root, the parent's
already-fetched context files and skills (mandatory, not an optimization — walking `cwd` in a child
would read the replica), the probed `remote_shell`, and `--no-context-files`. `isolation: worktree`
runs `git` in the sandbox (`worktree::Git::Remote`; see "Worktree isolation in the sandbox") rather
than silently downgrading to `Isolation::None`, which would hand a write-capable child the shared
root — the one thing the field exists to prevent.

`get_state.git_branch` runs `git symbolic-ref --short HEAD` through the session's runner, in the
sandbox, with a 5 s timeout and `null` on anything unexpected — a slow or absent sandbox must make a
poll answer `null`, never hang it, and must certainly never answer about the replica's own checkout.
While the sandbox is not attached yet (a reopened session nothing has used) it answers `null`
without asking.

### Sandbox snapshot

**A reopened session makes no exec request until it needs its sandbox.** What a session learned
from its sandbox — the probe's `Sandbox` (home, shell) and the discovered `Resources` — is saved
beside its transcript as a `service::Snapshot`: `sandbox-snapshot.json` inside the session's own
directory (which moves, trashes and deletes whole), sealed under the tenant's transcript key and bound
to the session id and kind (`TenantCodec::seal_sidecar`), written atomically
(`write_private_atomic`). It is written at the top of `serve_session`'s loop whenever it is behind —
after a start that discovered, a `reload`, a refresh, or a transcript switch (the new id gets its own)
— and simply retried while the session's directory does not exist yet.

The next task to open the session (a replica restart, the 60 s reap, a deploy) loads it
(`ServiceSession::load_snapshot`: it must open, be this format, and match the grant's
`workspace_root` and the process's `--no-context-files`; anything else is ignored and the session
starts as a new one does). With one, start sends nothing: the cell is attached lazily with the saved
home, the `ServiceSession` is seeded with the saved `Sandbox` (so tools build with the probed shell),
discovery is skipped, and the prompt is built from the saved `Resources` — **the same system prompt,
byte for byte**, so the prompt cache keeps hitting. The bash jobs' read-back is deferred too (see
"Reattach" under "`bash` jobs").

**Freshness.** Discovery runs again at the first loop iteration after the sandbox has been woken by
real use (`sandbox_refresh`, checked while `!ExecCell::pending()`), so the refresh never wakes it
itself. An unchanged set leaves the prompt alone; a changed one goes through `apply_discovered!` —
the same rebuild `reload` does — so the change costs one prompt-cache miss on the next turn, as an
explicit `reload` would. `reload` itself always rediscovers (and so wakes the sandbox: it was asked
to). The first turns of a reopened session therefore use the set it had when it closed; an edit made
inside the sandbox while nothing was attached shows up after the first real use, or at a `reload`.

Tests: `tests/serve_service_lazy_sandbox.rs` (a reopen with a running job and discovered resources,
`get_state` and `get_commands`, then a detach: zero exec requests, probe included; the first tool
after a reopen probes exactly once and before its own request, also with three concurrent tools; a
probe that fails then reaches the tool call; the reopened session's system prompt equals the one
before the restart, with zero requests; a job that ended while detached), `exec_endpoint`'s
`lazy_cell_tests` (single flight, a failure not remembered, a suspect target probed again) and
`service`'s snapshot round trip.

### Storage: segmented, sealed sessions

A segmented on-disk layout with epoch fencing and per-tenant AEAD (`Layout::Segmented`,
`TenantCodec`), behind a `Log` seam inside `session_store.rs`. The layout is
[Session storage — single file, or epoch segments](#session-storage--single-file-or-epoch-segments);
how service mode opens it is "Storage wiring", next.

### Storage wiring

Service mode is the reason the [segmented layout](#session-storage--single-file-or-epoch-segments)
exists: a shard is one network filesystem mounted by every replica that serves it, so "which process
owns this session" cannot be answered by a process.

**What a session opens.** `Persistence::open`'s service arm opens the repo at
`service.session_dir` with `Layout::Segmented { codec: TenantCodec(tenant, dek) }` and
`id_prefix = <the session id's own shard>`. The DEK comes from the grant's sealed secrets, is derived
into subkeys once per connection (`ServiceSession::codec`), and is neither logged nor written
anywhere — `TenantCodec`'s `Debug` shows the tenant and a key fingerprint. Every other repo a command
reaches for opens the same way: `delete_session`, `restore_session`, `preview_fork` and `export` go
through `ServiceSession::repo_options_for(<target id>)`, which puts each one on **that id's** mount
with **that id's** prefix, and the listing scans (`list_sessions`, `list_all_sessions`,
`list_daemon_sessions`, `list_trash`) take the tenant's `Layout` so they read directories rather than
`*.jsonl` and open the sealed `.listings.json` cache. Both memory mounts are sealed with the same
codec: durable memory at `<home shard>/<tenant>/memory`, and the `/session` mount at the session's own
`memory/`, whose path is asked of the store (`SessionStore::memory_dir`) because deriving it from the
file name would collapse every session on a shard into one `<shard>.memory` directory.

**The session lock.** The task spawned by `Supervisor::try_pin` takes `acquire_session_lock` on the
blocking pool **before** `go_live`, holds it across the session body, and drops it **before** the
`ExitGuard` — the guard frees the id and wakes whoever is waiting for it, whose first move is to take
this very lock. It creates the session directory first (idempotent, and a directory with no segments
is not a session), because the lock lives inside it and `acquire_session_lock` falls back to a
`<path>.lock` sibling for a path that is not a directory — two replicas racing a brand-new session
would otherwise lock two different files. The spawning pin waits on a `oneshot` for the outcome, so
"open on another replica" is a **503 with `Retry-After`** answered before the WebSocket upgrade rather
than a session that comes up and immediately dies; a connection that attached to the `Starting` slot
meanwhile gets an `error` frame. The lock is liveness only — correctness is the epoch fence — so a
lost lock costs a retry, never history. Its one visible consequence: `delete_session` on a session
some task still holds is refused rather than renaming a directory out from under a live writer.

Acquiring it is **bounded at ten seconds**, and past that the connection is answered 503 with
`Retry-After` like any other transient refusal. The directory create plus the lock are filesystem
calls on the same mount as the session, so an unreachable mount would otherwise hold the HTTP
connection open indefinitely. Because `spawn_blocking` cannot be cancelled, the abandoned attempt may
still acquire the lock afterwards — so the result is delivered over a `oneshot`, and once the waiter
has given up, `send` hands it back to the blocking thread where the `SessionLock` **drops on the
spot**, closing the descriptor that holds it. The lock is never handed to the next attempt: that
would mean a registry of orphans, a second place to leak, and a second rule about who owns a lock.
The retry after the 503 simply takes it the ordinary way.

**What the edge must do with that 503, and why "retry the same key" is not enough.** A session is
pinned to whichever replica holds its lock, and after a failover that is the _substitute_, not the
replica the session id hashes to. The hash target has nothing to serve and cannot say where the
session went — deliberately, since an owner record on the mount would be service discovery living in
this repo, with a stale-record failure mode of its own. So it answers 503, and a strictly
hash-and-retry edge keeps asking the one replica that will keep refusing, until the substitute's idle
reaper frees the lock: **60 s** in service mode. That is an outage for every session a deploy moved.
After repeated 503s on the same key the edge must **walk the ring** — try the other replicas in the
slice — which finds the substitute on the first or second try and is safe by construction, because
only the lock holder can serve the session anyway. The fleet simulator routes exactly this way and
counts how many sessions needed the walk; in a run with rolling deploys it is most of the ones that
moved, not a rare case.

**Empty session directories.** `take_session_lock` has to create `<id>/` before it can know this
replica will own the session, because the lock lives inside it. A session that then never wrote a
segment gives that directory back on **its own exit path**, where it still holds the lock: if the
directory holds nothing but `lock`, the lock file is unlinked and `remove_dir` is attempted —
`ENOTEMPTY` being the atomic "someone got a segment in after all, leave it alone" check, since
`000001.jsonl` is created with `O_EXCL` before anything else and never deleted. This is the only
place the delete is safe. A would-be _creator_ evaluating the same predicate would race another
replica's `create_dir_all` + `O_EXCL`, and on NFS/EFS attribute staleness would let it delete a
directory whose fresh segment it had not yet seen. Everything outside that path — a lock that could
not be taken at all, a replica that died mid-start — is deliberately left to an **out-of-band sweep**
that does not exist yet; a leftover empty directory costs an inode and is not a session (nothing
lists it, and the next start reuses it).

**`--max-live-sessions`** (default 20,000; `0` turns it off) is checked under the table lock at the
moment a session would be spawned, so two simultaneous connections cannot both take the last slot.
Over the limit is a 503. A live session holds three descriptors — its newest segment and its two lock
files (the OFD lock and, during the mixed rollout, the legacy `flock`; see `file_lock`) — and two
locks, so the default is ~60,000 descriptors (inside a 65,535 `nofile` limit, not by much) and 40,000
locks (inside EFS's documented 65,536 per instance).

**Superseded.** An owner that has been fenced (a newer epoch exists, so every write now fails) ends
its session with a `{"type":"session_superseded", session_id, tenant}` frame. It is checked at the top
of the idle loop, which every write path returns through before the next command is read. The client
reconnects, which lands it on whoever owns the session now; carrying on would mean accepting turns
that can never be persisted.

**Derived sessions.** `fork`, `clone` and `new_session` are allowed here because the repo mints
`<shard>.<opaque>`. `fork`/`clone` **do not switch**: a daemon session's id is what its supervisor
slot, its lock and every attached grant are keyed on, so they create the derived session, answer with
its id and `switched:false`, and leave this session running. A `fork`/`clone` arriving mid-run is
answered "busy" instead of aborting the run to make room — it copies what is on disk, so there is
nothing for it to interrupt. `new_session` keeps its own id (the address a client routes on) and
archives the outgoing conversation into a derived session, exactly as an addressed session does
anywhere else.

### A dead MCP server is dialed again

A server's connection (`McpConnection`) caches one live client, shared by every tool, resource,
prompt, skill and events subscription of that server. A server that dies — OOM-killed, crashed,
`kill -9` — leaves that client cached with its transport closed: rmcp's service loop ends on the
EOF, and every later request fails "transport closed". So `McpConnection::client` checks
`is_transport_closed()` before handing the cached client out; a closed one is retired (its process
group swept) and the server dialed again, under the same lock, so concurrent callers make one
process. Every path to a server goes through `client()`, so tool calls, reads and the events poll
loop all recover without retry code of their own (`live_client`, which never dials, reports a closed
client as none). A call already in flight when the server died still fails: whether it reached the
server is unknowable, and re-sending a `tools/call` could do its work twice. The next call redials.
`tests/mcp_redial.rs` (tool, then resource, after `kill -9`) and `tests/mcp_events_redial.rs` (a
poll subscription resubscribes on the fresh process).

Every dial — first connect or redial, stdio or HTTP — is bounded (`connect_one_client`,
`handshake_timeout`). Servers connect concurrently but startup waits for all of them, so one that
starts and never answers `initialize` used to hold `run`/`serve` startup, and every other server's
tools, forever; on a redial it would hold the connection's lock, and every call to that server. A
grant connector gets 20 s; an operator's own server 60 s (a first `npx -y …` downloads the package),
or `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_HANDSHAKE_SECS`. On timeout the dial is dropped (a stdio child retired with
its transport) and handled like any failed connect: a warning, the server dormant, the rest loaded
(`tests/mcp_handshake_timeout.rs`).

### A server's tools can change

A server's tool list is not fixed at its first boot: one may add tools on request (an
`enable_toolset`) and say so with `notifications/tools/list_changed`, and one upgraded since the
manifest cache recorded it lists something new with no notification at all. So connecting yields a
live set, `McpTools`, rather than a fixed `Vec`, and each server's `Relist` brings its share up to
date: it lists the server's tools again and, if the answer differs from what is advertised, swaps
that server's tools in the set (bumping its generation) and amends its cached manifest
(`mcp_manifest::store_tools`). It runs on `notifications/tools/list_changed`, and after every real
start of the server's process — a cache-hit boot's first call, a redial after a reap or a crash. That
is the manifest's invalidation rule: the cache is only a hint for boot, the started server's own
listing wins, and the comparison is the listing itself rather than the version `initialize`
reported (a version can stay put while tools change). A listing that matches bumps nothing and
writes nothing. A `tools/call` that set off a re-listing is answered once the re-listing has
landed, so the model's next request already has the new tools.

A change reaches the model on the next request, whichever way it loads MCP tools: a running loop
pulls `Steering::set_tool_source` at every turn boundary, and the source `tools::mcp::tool_source`
installs answers with the run's registry rebased onto the live set (`tools::rebase_mcp`: every
`mcp__` tool and `tool_search` replaced, placed and filtered the way a fresh build places them —
a deferred server's catalog entry updated, a loaded server's tools registered), and nothing at all
while the generation has not moved. `serve` also rebuilds a session's agent before a `prompt` when
the generation moved since it was built; a subagent dispatched later gets the live set. The cost is
one prompt-cache miss per real change: tool definitions are sorted, so the new prefix is as stable
as the old one, but it is a different prefix. Not covered: Code Mode mid-run (its MCP tools live
inside `execute`; the next build picks them up), and MCP Apps connections, whose tools carry view
metadata of their own — both keep the listing they connected with until rebuilt or redialed.
`tests/mcp_list_changed.rs`: a tool added by `unlock` is callable, offered on the very next request
of the same run (`run` and `serve`) and on the next prompt; a stale manifest is corrected by the
server's first start.

### Per-session MCP

Outside service mode, MCP is a **process** fact: `main.rs` connects every server in the operator's
`settings.json` once at startup and every session shares those connections. On a replica that is
exactly wrong — those are the operator's servers, with the operator's credentials. Service mode
connects nothing at startup and instead dials **each session's own connectors, at session start**,
from its grant: `grant.mcp` names them (`{name, url}`), and `secrets.mcp_headers[name]` carries their
credentials. `service.rs` owns the seam (`ServiceSession::mcp`), `tools::mcp::connect_granted` does
the dialing, and `serve_session` puts the result in `cfg.mcp_tools`/`cfg.mcp_catalog` before the
first registry build — so `set_mcp_enabled`, `get_mcp`, Code Mode and `mcp_complete` work
unchanged, on a set that is this tenant's alone.

Four things a grant connector does **not** inherit from the host path, each one a way a host-wide
assumption would otherwise cross a tenant boundary:

- **Header resolution.** A configured `headers` value goes through `resolve_config_value` first: a
  leading `!` runs the rest as a shell command, and `$VAR` expands from the process environment.
  That is right for a value an operator typed into their own settings file and catastrophic for one
  that arrived over the network — `!curl …` would execute on the replica. A grant's headers become
  `tools::mcp::SecretHeader`s instead: validated, marked sensitive, taken byte for byte, and
  redacted in `Debug`. They are kept on the connection, so a redial after an idle reap sends the same
  credential without the grant still being in scope.
- **OAuth.** `mcp_oauth::ServerAuth::load` reads `~/.beyond/mcp_auth.json`, **keyed by server name**. A tenant
  connector called `linear` would otherwise be handed the operator's own `linear` token. Grant
  connectors never consult that store; a connector's only credentials are the ones in its grant.
- **The manifest cache.** `mcp_manifest` is keyed by name + url and shared by the whole replica, so
  grant connectors pass `manifest_dir: None` and always discover by connecting.
- **Transport.** HTTP only. A `stdio` connector would be a process on the replica.

**Egress.** Connectors dial through one process-wide `McpEgress` (`ServeConfig::mcp_http`), built
once by `main.rs`: its own client, not the gateway's h2c pool (a tenant's connector is not the
gateway), carrying the `web` tool's SSRF layers for the same reason the `web` tool has them — the URL
is not this process's to choose. `validate_url` rejects a non-`http(s)` scheme or a literal internal
IP before any DNS; `SsrfResolver` validates every address the client actually connects to (and the
client ignores ambient proxies, which would resolve the target in its place); redirects
are refused outright, since reqwest resolves a redirect target itself and a redirect to a literal IP
would never reach the resolver. So a connector cannot name the instance metadata service, a storage
mount target, or a peer replica. `--mcp-allow-private` opens the blocklist for a dev replica whose
connectors run beside it (this repo's own tests); a production replica never passes it, and no grant
can ask for it. URL **query strings are redacted** in every message, since a connector URL can carry
a credential in one. A connector that is refused, fails to handshake, or takes longer than 20 s to
do so costs its own tools and nothing else; the warning goes to the replica's stderr, not to the
tenant.

**Elicitation and sampling.** Every `serve` session has its own `McpHost` (the elicitation +
sampling hubs) and installs its `elicitation_request` and `sampling_request` gates into it, never into
a process-wide hub. A server's question reaches the session whose call raised it:

- A service session's own connectors are dialed with its host and consult it directly.
- The operator's servers are connected once and shared by every session of a daemon. Each session's
  runs (and resumed tasks) are scoped in a task-local (`tools::mcp::with_session_host`). A call reads
  it to answer in-task and MRTR input (`calling_host`), which is exact: our own code answers those,
  inside the call.
- A _nested_ request (one the server sends while a `tools/call` is outstanding) is routed by
  `McpHandler::route`, which never guesses. Each outstanding call is registered on its connection
  with its session's host and its JSON-RPC request id, for exactly as long as the request is out.
  - Over Streamable HTTP the request arrives on the SSE stream of the POST that raised it (rmcp's
    `InboundStreamOrigin::OutboundRequest`). It goes to that call's session, however many sessions
    have calls in flight.
  - Otherwise (stdio carries no correlation), it goes to the session with calls in flight if there
    is exactly one, and to the connection's own host if there are none.
  - With calls from more than one session in flight and nothing attributing the request, it is
    refused with an error that says so. It reaches nobody, and the asking call gets the refusal as
    its answer. Delivered to a possibly wrong session, one user would answer another's server, or
    spend tokens for it.

Before this, each session installed its gates into the process-wide hub. The last session to start
answered every session's servers, and once it detached, every session's questions were refused.
`tests/mcp_tasks_daemon.rs` proves the routing with two daemon sessions: in-task and nested requests
with one session in flight, attribution by HTTP stream with both in flight, and refusal of an
unattributable stdio request with both in flight.

Sampling is answered by the attached host. The agent never spends model tokens on a server's behalf
unasked:

- A `sampling/createMessage` (nested, MRTR, or an in-task `inputRequests` entry, which SEP-2663 says
  must be treated exactly like the standalone request) becomes a `sampling_request` frame carrying
  `request_id`, the asking `server`, and `params`.
- The host answers `{type:"sample", request_id, result}` with a `CreateMessageResult`, or
  `{type:"sample", request_id, action:"decline"}`.
- Every view then gets a `sampling_resolved` frame (`action`, and `reason` on a refusal), as with
  `elicitation_resolved`.
- No attached client, a decline, or the timeout (`--approval-timeout`, as for elicitation; 120 s when
  that is `0`) refuses the request.
- A request whose call is abandoned frees its pending slot.
- Headless `run` has no host to ask, so it refuses sampling as it declines elicitation.

**Durable MCP tasks (SEP-2663).** A task outlives the request that created it, so the client treats
the task, not the connection or the process, as the unit of work.

- **Connection trouble mid-poll.** A request that could not be delivered (`TransportSend`, e.g. an
  HTTP POST whose connection dropped) is re-sent on the same client after a backoff of 200 ms,
  doubling to 5 s. rmcp's HTTP client survives a failed POST: its worker only quits during
  initialization. A dead client (`TransportClosed`, e.g. a stdio server that exited) is dropped
  (`McpConnection::invalidate`, which takes the lock and so cannot be skipped) and the server
  redialed. Either way, the _same_ `taskId` is polled again, and a pending `tasks/update` is re-sent
  with the same answer rather than re-asked. The call survives eight consecutive losses and fails on
  the ninth. A JSON-RPC error is the server's answer and is never retried. A stdio server that died
  took its tasks with it: the respawned process answers `-32602`, which ends the call.
- **Waiting.** A single wait between polls is the server's `pollIntervalMs`, capped by the remainder
  of the task's latest `ttlMs` and by 60 s.
- **Cancel on abort.** Dropping an in-flight call cancels its task through the connection's _current_
  client, redialing for it if there is none. An abort during a redial still reaches a server that
  keeps tasks across its own restart.
- **Journal.** The tool emits its `McpTaskRecord` (`server`, `tool`, `taskId`, `createdAtMs`, the
  latest `ttlMs`, and the `inputRequests` keys already `answered`) in a `tool_progress`'s
  `details.mcpTask`. It does so when the task is created and again whenever any of that changes.
  `serve` journals each one with the session as an `mcp_task` custom entry, stamped with `toolUseId`
  and the owning `sessionId`. Journal writes come from the run's event sink and from the background
  resumer. They are drained by the idle loop, the busy loop and at run end, and a write whose
  `sessionId` is not the session being persisted to is dropped. The journal sits beside the
  pre-dispatch checkpoint, which already persisted the assistant's `tool_use`. Headless `run`
  journals the same entries with its persisted session (`RunJournal`, from its event sink).
- **Pending.** A journaled task is pending when three things hold: its record belongs to this session,
  its `tool_use` is anywhere on the active path, and nothing answers it, neither a `tool_result` nor
  a journaled `mcp_task_result`. Requiring this session's record means only the session that created
  a task may resume it. A fork copies messages, not custom entries, so it inherits no journal; a
  journal that does travel under another session id (a session file copied or restored under a new
  id) is ignored. The call then gets the generic "interrupted" repair. A record must also describe the
  call it names (`mcp__<server>__<tool>` equal to the call's tool) and name a configured server, and a
  client's `append_custom` cannot write the journal's kinds (`mcp_task`, `mcp_task_result`): a forged
  record would otherwise have the resumer poll a task id of the client's choosing.
- **Resume, in the background.** When a session is loaded, and the moment a command switches to
  another one (`switch_session`, `new_session`, `fork`, `clone`), `mcp_resume::Resumer` polls each of
  that session's pending tasks to a terminal status through its `McpCatalog`. The previous session's
  resumer is dropped. It never cancels a task, and from that moment nothing it still has in flight
  reaches the clients.
  - The `ttlMs` backstop counts from `createdAtMs`. A TTL that ran out while the agent was down
    resolves as expired without contacting the server, even if the server is gone.
  - A server that cannot be reached is not an answer. The resume redials a few times (250 ms
    doubling, about 5 s); if it still cannot connect, or the connection is lost for good mid-poll,
    the call gets a placeholder `tool_result` reading `[MCP task result pending] …` (the model is
    told the result is pending), no result is journaled, and an `mcp_task_placeholder` entry marks
    that call's `tool_result` as a placeholder, so the task stays pending. A placeholder is known by
    that mark, never by its text: a real result that happens to begin the same way is an answer. A
    later prompt (a fresh resumer, when the last one finished with a server unreachable) or start
    (`serve`, or `run --continue`) tries again, and the real result replaces the placeholder where it
    sits. A configured server that could not be dialed at startup is kept dormant in the catalog for
    this.
    Only a terminal status, a JSON-RPC error such as `-32602`, or an expired TTL resolves a call.
  - Answered keys are seeded from the record, so the user is never asked twice.
  - In-task input reaches the session's host.
  - Its progress streams as `tool_progress`, starting with a "resuming" notice. That notice is not
    a journal record: the task's record is already there, and a restart does not append another.
    Each result is journaled as an `mcp_task_result` the moment it lands, prompt or no prompt.
  - It never cancels a task. Dropping it on a switch, or when the session ends (it is dropped
    before the writer is joined, so the process can exit), stops its polling, but the tasks stay
    journaled for when the session is opened again.
- **Prompt policy.** A prompt that arrives while a resumed task is outstanding waits for it before
  its model call. The wait is visible: a `tool_start` and a "waiting … abort to skip" `tool_progress`
  per task, then the task's own progress. It is also abortable. An abort ends the prompt, not the
  task, which keeps polling and is waited on again by the next prompt. A `null` TTL can therefore
  hold a prompt for as long as the task runs, but never silently.
- **Splicing results.** Every resolved result, journaled or fresh, goes at the front of the first user
  turn after the assistant turn holding its `tool_use`. That is the new prompt's turn when the call is
  at the tip, or an aborted prompt's turn when one came in between. No turn is added, so role
  alternation holds. Each splice is reported through the run's own event sink as a
  `tool_start`/`tool_end` pair. The splice is part of the transcript, not only of the model request.
  The session store applies every journaled result on the active path when it materializes
  messages (`session_store::materialize`), so `get_messages`, the HTML export and `run --continue`
  show exactly what `serve` sent the model. The file stays append-only and ids stay stable.
- **`run --continue`.** `run` resumes too: before its turn, it polls each pending task of the session it
  opened (journaled by `run` or `serve`) to its result, in turn, with a line on stderr (it has no
  client to stream progress to; Ctrl-C ends the wait as it ends the run), journals each result, and
  splices it into the turn it sends.
- **Privacy.** Custom entries never reach the model. A task id can be a bearer token for the
  server's stored state. Resume needs it, so the session keeps it, exactly as private as the
  conversation it holds. A local session file is created `0600`, and every append tightens an
  existing file whose mode is looser (an older version's, a restore's, a `chmod`) before writing.
  In service mode the journal goes through the tenant-keyed sealed segments with the rest of the
  transcript (`tests/session_segments_sealing.rs`). The HTML export withholds `mcp_task*` entries.
- **Journal authentication** (`mcp_resume::JournalAuth`, held by the session's store, which seals
  what it journals and replays only what passes). The key goes where the session goes, never with
  the machine, so a session resumes on another replica, another machine, a fresh `$HOME` or after
  an upgrade.
  - Service mode (segments sealed under the tenant key): no MAC at all. The storage already
    authenticates every line, which is strictly stronger, and any replica holding the tenant key
    reads the journal (`tests/mcp_tasks_service.rs`).
  - Local: every entry carries a `mac`, an HMAC-SHA256 over its kind and content, keyed by 32 random
    bytes in a `0600` sidecar beside the session (`<session>.jsonl.mcp-task-journal.json`: a suffix
    on the whole file name, so `work.1` and `work.2` never share a key; or inside a segmented
    session's directory), made by the session's first journal write, so a session that never
    journals a task gets no extra file. Every first writer (threads, other processes) agrees on one
    key: it is made under an exclusive lock on the sidecar and re-read once the lock is held, and
    every journal write adopts the key on disk. The lock is an OFD lock on the sidecar itself
    (`file_lock::Target::Itself`), so another descriptor's open and close cannot release it, NFS
    included; the holder still re-reads and writes through its locked descriptor, so "re-read, then
    write" is one step. A key under the earlier `with_extension` name
    (`<session>.mcp-task-journal.json`) is read, and carried over by the next journal write. Both
    names are session sidecars, so the key moves, trashes and restores with its session. On replay an entry without a valid `mac` is ignored: a line appended to the
    `.jsonl` by a model with `write`/`edit` neither causes a poll nor is delivered as a result.
  - A session without a key (from before per-session keys, or that has not journaled yet) is read
    as before: its entries are accepted, and opening it writes nothing. Its next journal write makes
    the key and records the MACs of the entries already there as accepted, so a task that resumed
    before still resumes. Entries written after that must carry a `mac`.
  - The residual risk, honestly: locally the key is a file the agent's user can read, and a session
    that never journaled has no key yet, so a model that can also read files, or that targets such a
    session, can forge an entry. A model with `write` can also delete the key or corrupt it
    (overwrite it with anything that does not parse): the session is then keyless (what is there is
    accepted), and its next journal write makes a new key that accepts every line already in the
    file, planted ones included; and the transcript itself is unauthenticated (a model
    that can write the file can plant an ordinary `tool_result`). Locally the seal turns "append a
    line" into a deliberate read-then-forge; it does not close forgery. In service mode the store is
    out of the tools' reach (they run in the tenant's sandbox), and forgery is closed.

**MCP Apps.** A service session's apps pool (`ServiceSession::mcp_apps_pool`) dials the same grant
connectors a second time, with `io.modelcontextprotocol/ui` advertised, the first time the session's
client sends `set_mcp_apps` — per session, through the same egress, headers and hub as `mcp`, so an
apps-flavored connection is no more shared than the plain one. See "MCP Apps" below.

### MCP skills (SEP-2640)

A server that declares the Skills extension (`capabilities.extensions["io.modelcontextprotocol/skills"]`)
publishes Agent Skills as resources (`skill://<skill-path>/<file>`), enumerated by `skills/list` with a
complete `{uri, digest, size}` manifest per skill and answered one at a time by `skills/get`. The
client also declares the extension (SEP-2133 lets it; nothing requires it). `tools/mcp_skills.rs`
owns the integration; `tools/mcp.rs` only calls into it at connect.

**What is the server's, what is the session's.** `ServerSkills` (one per connection, shared by every
session on it) holds the listing and every entry learned since — facts about the server.
`SkillSession` (one per session, on its `McpEnabledSet`) holds what that session loaded, what its user
approved, and whom to ask. A `serve` daemon's sessions share connections, so a skill one session loaded
never stands for another: each session's registry rebinds the loading tools to its own `SkillSession`
(`filter_by_enabled`), a session switch resets it (`McpEnabledSet::reset_session`), and subagents share
their parent session's. **The acting window is rebuilt from the transcript** before every run
(`SkillSession::restore_from_transcript`, called by `serve`'s prompt arm and by `run` before its first
turn): a loaded skill enters context under a tag carrying its server, `SKILL.md` URI and manifest
fingerprint (`<skill name server location manifest>`), so a session resumed with `run --session-id`,
switched back to, forked, cloned, or reopened after a restart is still gated while that tag is in its
context. Only host-authored records count: a skill-tool result (matched to its `mcp__<server>__skill__read` call by `tool_use_id`, its tag naming that server and starting the result) or a user turn that is itself a `/skill:` expansion — never a tag some other tool's output, a file or the model reproduced, which would gate the session on a phantom skill.

- **Discovery reads the listing and nothing else.** At connect `skills/list` is paged and each entry
  validated (`SKILL.md` explicit in the URI, last skill-path segment == `name`, a `description`, a
  manifest that lists `SKILL.md` and only files inside the skill, and the per-skill limits: at most 512
  files and 16 MiB summed). No skill file is fetched — the spec forbids retrieving files "on
  connection, on listing, or at approval" — so MCP skills deliberately do **not** use the on-disk
  backend's prefetch-the-body shortcut (`Skill::body`). `"resources": "dynamic"` skills (no digests)
  and over-limit ones are declined, which the spec permits; every entry left out, a failed listing,
  and a listing cut off at the 64-page cap becomes a diagnostic (below).
- **Freshness.** A listing is re-fetched when it is needed (each `serve` turn, `McpSkills::refresh`)
  and due: its `ttlMs` ran out (absent or `0` reads as stale at once, per the caching rules), or the
  server sent `notifications/resources/list_changed` (skills are resources; SEP-2640 defines no
  skills-specific notification — `notifications/skills/list_changed` belonged to the first-class
  design the working group did not adopt, and is honoured too). Never on a timer, and only against a
  server that is up: starting a reaped one just to re-list would undo the reaping. A held entry past
  its `ttlMs` is re-fetched with `skills/get` before a load. A listing marked `cacheScope: "private"`
  is never written to the on-disk manifest (that file outlives the authorization context); the server is forgotten there instead, so the next boot asks it again. A listing re-fetched after connect is written back to that manifest at once (`mcp_manifest::store_skills`, amending only the skills fields of the invocation's recorded manifest) — or, if it is now private, the server is forgotten — so a restart answering from the cache does not advertise the listing the server replaced. A re-list that fails keeps the last good
  listing; a notification is a generation count the listing catches up with only once a re-list
  succeeds, so one cut short by the refresh deadline (30s, `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_SKILLS_REFRESH_TIMEOUT_MS`)
  leaves the notice pending.
- **One loading tool per server, `mcp__<server>__skill__read({uri})`.** A `SKILL.md` URI loads
  (activates) the skill — `skills/get` first for a URI never listed; a file URI reads a file of a skill
  this session loaded; a directory URI is listed from the held manifest. Per-server is what binds every
  read to the skill's origin (a skill from A can never cause a read against B), and the
  `mcp__<server>__` prefix is what `set_mcp_enabled` gates. A file of a skill the session has not
  loaded is refused without a request. A `SKILL.md` URI inside a loaded skill is a load request first
  (an unlisted nested skill activates by URI); only if `skills/get` answers `-32602` is it read as the
  enclosing skill's ordinary file.
- **Every read is verified** against the entry the skill was loaded under: byte length, then SHA-256
  of the raw bytes, and for `SKILL.md` a field-by-field comparison of its YAML frontmatter with the
  entry's — equality of YAML values, not of one JSON rendering (`1` = `1.0`, a YAML 1.1 boolean word = the boolean, null spellings = null), so an honest skill rendered by a YAML 1.1 parser is not refused. This deliberately loosens the spec's "identical in content" from bytes-of-a-rendering to values, and the host reads the fields it acts on (`disable-model-invocation`) with the same normalization, so what verifies as `true` is treated as `true`.
  A failure is refreshed once via `skills/get` and otherwise refused; unverified bytes never reach the
  model, an unlisted file inside a loaded skill is a verification failure, and a content block
  labelled as some other resource is refused.
- **Approval (the spec's "no implicit local execution").** MCP skill content may not drive host-side
  code execution without the user's explicit, per-skill approval:
  - _Activation._ A skill the model chose is loaded only once the user approves it — before
    `SKILL.md` is fetched, bound to the entry's manifest fingerprint (every `{uri, digest}`), so a
    changed skill is asked about again. A `/skill:` the user typed is that consent — for that invocation only, never remembered, so a later load the model chooses is asked about. A nested skill (its
    directory inside another skill's) is no exception: its approval is its own, never covered by the
    enclosing skill's, and the question names the enclosing skill. The question names the agent that chose the skill (`origin`: `"main"`, or the subagent's `{agent, spawn_id}`): a subagent's registry binds the loading tools in its own name (`filter_by_enabled_as`), the same provenance its code-execution questions carry.
  - _Code execution._ While the session is acting on any MCP skill (from load to the end of the
    session, and again whenever its transcript still holds the skill — the spec allows longer, never
    shorter), every `bash`/`execute` call needs approval, asked per call and naming the active skills;
    a "session" answer covers that exact call — the verbatim command in its named `cwd`, or a digest of the whole input
    (`execute`'s program) — under that exact set of manifests. The gate (`SkillSession::gate_tool_call`)
    is in every hook path: `serve`'s `ServeHooks`, `run`'s `RunHooks`, and subagents' `ChildHooks`.
  - _Cross-origin reads._ While acting on a skill of server A, a resource read from server B
    (`mcp__B__resource__…`, `mcp__B__skill__read`) needs explicit approval per call — never remembered —
    naming both servers.
  - _Who answers._ `serve` asks through its existing approval gate — always present now, independent
    of `--approve` — as `approval_request` frames carrying an `mcp_skill` object
    (`{purpose: "activate", server, uri, name, description, frontmatter, manifest, files,
    manifest_files, nested_in}` — the entry and its file manifest, so a client can show what would load
    before it is fetched; `{purpose: "execute", active_skills}`; or
    `{purpose: "cross_origin_read", from_servers, to_server}`), answered by the usual `approve`
    command. `run` has no one to ask and denies; `--approve-mcp-skills` (both commands) approves
    everything in advance. Without `--approve`, the only questions a `serve` session raises are MCP skills', so an `approve` naming none of its pending questions is refused (pointing at `--approve`) rather than acknowledged.
  - _Not persisted._ Remembered ("session"-scoped) decisions live in memory for the session's life in this process and are never written down or read back. Any approval on disk would be forgeable: the session file is the user's, and a model with file-write tools (`write`/`edit`) can append to it — and it knows the fingerprint a key embeds, which is in the loaded skill's tag — so a restored approval could be one the model planted, and an `execute` approval would then run code unasked after a restart. A resumed, switched-to or restarted session is therefore asked again. The `mcp_skill_approval` kind stays reserved (`session_store::HOST_CUSTOM_KINDS`, with the MCP task journal's kinds): a client's `append_custom` of a kind the agent writes itself is refused, so it cannot forge one (`tests/mcp_skills_resume.rs`, `tests/serve_session_tree.rs`).
  - `allowed-tools` and other declarative frontmatter are not honoured for any skill, so nothing an MCP
    skill declares can widen permissions.
- **Names are per origin**: `<server>:<name>`, or `<server>:<skill-path>` for two entries of one
  server sharing a name (both kept). `:` cannot occur in a valid on-disk skill name, so an MCP skill
  can never shadow a local one; should an on-disk skill nonetheless be literally named `docs:x`, the
  on-disk skill wins `/skill:docs:x`. The server label is the settings `name`, never `serverInfo`.
- **Surfaces.** A separate `<available_skills origin="mcp">` block (name, description, `SKILL.md` URI,
  server, tool) so MCP skills are never presented as local ones; loaded content is wrapped in
  `<skill name server location>` with the skill root and file list. `run` appends the block once;
  `serve` renders it in `full_system` on every rebuild and turn, through the live session gate; a
  subagent's prompt gets its parent session's. `/skill:<server>:<name>` loads the skill at the user's
  invocation (`expand_message` is `async` for this one case, bounded at 30s) and honours
  `disable-model-invocation` (expandable, never listed). A `/skill:` steered into a running prompt is expanded on its own task, never awaited inside the busy loop, which must keep polling the run and reading `abort`/`approve` (`PendingSteers`). Steers keep their arrival order — each takes its place at receipt and is queued and acked only after everything ahead of it — and are bound to their run: when it ends (finished, aborted, or cancelled by `new_session`/`switch_session`/`fork`/`clone`) an expansion still in flight is cancelled (and awaited) and acked as not queued, with the reason. What waits behind it is queued in order if the run finished; if the run was cancelled, which already dropped its steer and follow-up lanes (`clear_run_scoped`), it is acked as not queued too, like every steer the cancellation dropped. The expansion opens no acting window itself; the skill is activated only when its text is queued, so an expansion that finished but never reached the model — still waiting its turn when the run was cancelled — activates nothing, and nothing of it reaches a later prompt or another session.
  `--no-skills` suppresses MCP skills too (listing, expansion, `get_commands`). `get_commands` lists MCP skills with
  `scope: "mcp"`, `path` = the `SKILL.md` URI, and `server`.
- **Diagnostics.** `McpSkills::diagnostics` reports, in the on-disk skills' `Collision` shape: entries
  declined (invalid, dynamic, over the limits — with the reason, as the spec asks), a failed listing,
  a name one server lists twice, and an on-disk skill named like an MCP one. `serve` returns them in
  `get_commands`' `collisions`; `run` prints them as warnings. They survive a boot from the manifest
  cache (`skill_diagnostics`).
- **No bypass surface.** With the extension declared, `resources/list` entries that are files of a
  listed skill, files under a declined skill's root, anything under `skill://`, and any `.../SKILL.md` under any scheme together with everything under its directory are not wrapped as
  `mcp__<server>__resource__<n>` tools: a generic resource read opens no acting window and passes no
  gate, so it would be a way around everything above. A server without the extension is untouched —
  its `skill://` resources are ordinary resources.
- **Manifest cache.** `mcp_manifest` (version 3) records the entries (`None` = extension not
  declared) and their diagnostics, so a reaped or never-started server still lists its skills; the
  first load dials it (and re-fetches the entry, whose freshness a cache cannot vouch for). Every write is a read-modify-write of one file shared by all connections (a connect, a forget, a refreshed listing), so each runs under `file_lock::try_lock` on the manifest file — the OFD-lock primitive the session lock (`session_store::acquire_session_lock`) is also built on, a kernel file lock that dies with its holder, so a crashed writer's leftover file is simply unlocked and no two waiters can both take it — and renames a temporary of its own into place; concurrent refreshes lose nobody's update. Waiting for the lock blocks, so the public writers (`store`, `forget`, `store_skills`) are `async` and run it with `spawn_blocking`: a connection task never holds an async worker while another writer finishes. A write that panics leaves the file as it was and is logged at warn.
- **Nested-request attribution.** Every skills request (`skills/list`, `skills/get`,
  `resources/read`) goes through `mcp::request_tracked`, registered with `track_call` under the
  calling session's host for as long as it is outstanding, so a nested request the server raises
  meanwhile (an elicitation, a sampling call) is attributed to that session or refused — never sent
  to a shared connection's own host. A skill-tool call is scoped by its run; a `/skill:` steered into
  a running prompt is expanded as its session (`McpSkills::in_run`), whose live command loop can
  answer; a re-list or an expansion between runs runs under a host with no client
  (`McpSkills::outside_run`), so a nested request is declined at once rather than stalling the
  prompt on a command loop that is waiting on that very read (`tests/mcp_skills_steer.rs`).
- **rmcp workaround (one boundary: `mcp_stdio::rescue` / `unwrap_rescued`).** rmcp decodes results
  into an untagged union in which `CallToolResult` accepts any object with `_meta`; `2026-07-28`
  servers put `_meta` on every result, so a skills result would arrive as an empty tool result
  (upstream rust-sdk#1197, open). The same rescue that keeps MCP Events results intact keeps skills
  results intact: a lossy result is wrapped as `{"x-beyond-raw-result": …}` before rmcp parses it,
  and `custom_request` unwraps it. Stdio servers go through the one stdio transport
  (`tools/mcp_stdio.rs`: rescue on every line, non-UTF-8 lines skipped, exit grace and group sweep).
  The streamable-HTTP transport drives `mcp_wire::HttpClient`, which answers `skills/*` POSTs itself
  with the URI, session, auth and standard headers the transport hands it — reserved headers
  refused, 401/403/404-with-session mapped to the errors rmcp acts on, an SSE response handed back as
  a bounded stream rescued event by event (event boundaries found byte by byte across chunks, for
  `\n`, `\r\n` and `\r` alike), so rmcp reads it incrementally and routes anything else on it, and a
  JSON body read up to the same cap — and delegates everything else to `reqwest`.

### Metrics

`--metrics-listen <addr>` starts a second listener that answers `GET /metrics` in the Prometheus text
format and 404s everything else. Everything about it is shaped by one fact: **the tenant-facing
listener is reachable by tenants, and a scrape is not tenant-scoped.**

- **Loopback only.** `metrics::parse_listen_addr` refuses a routable bind outright rather than
  warning, because a warning in a log is not read before the port is already open. A scraper runs
  beside the replica — an ECS `awsvpc` task shares a network namespace across its containers, so a
  sidecar reaches `127.0.0.1` without the port existing anywhere else.
- **Its own registry.** Not prometheus' default one. `gateway/src/metrics.rs` uses the default
  because Pingora exposes exactly that; here it would mean anything a dependency happens to register
  turns up on a tenant-facing replica's scrape. The gateway's module is also typed against gateway
  types (`&crate::usage::Usage`, `crate::route::Provider`), so this copies the shape and shares no
  code.
- **No tenant, session, shard or workspace identifier in any label, ever.** Two problems at once:
  unbounded cardinality, and one tenant's session ids readable by whoever holds the scrape. Every
  label is a closed set fixed at compile time, resolved to its child once at boot so the hot paths
  take no map lookup. A unit test asserts no forbidden label name survives into an encoded scrape.
- **Every child exists at zero before first use.** "No data" and "zero" page differently.

| Instrument                        | Type      | What it answers                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| --------------------------------- | --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `agent_sessions_live`             | gauge     | What `--max-live-sessions` is checked against — and the blast radius if this replica dies                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `agent_runs_in_flight`            | gauge     | Prompts executing right now. **The one that predicts memory**: an attached-but-idle session costs a few hundred KB, a running one additionally holds its replay buffer (`TURN_REPLAY_MAX_BYTES`, 4 MiB) — and `--max-live-sessions` admits on the session count, not on this |
