## OAuth / Subscription-Credential Authentication

Full pi parity: logging in with a Claude Pro/Max, GitHub Copilot, or ChatGPT Plus/Pro subscription
instead of a metered API key. See "Provider keys: managed vs. BYO vs. OAuth subscription" above for
_why_ this needed no gateway changes at all and the identity-header tradeoff; this section is _what's
built_ and _where_.

**Protocol flows** (`crate::oauth`, one module per provider — `anthropic`/`github_copilot`/
`openai_codex` — plus shared `pkce`/`device_code`/`callback_server` helpers):

- **Anthropic**: PKCE + a local callback listener on the fixed port `53692`. A real quirk, replicated
  exactly: `state` is the raw PKCE verifier itself, not an independently generated CSRF token. No
  bind-failure fallback — a port conflict is a hard error, matching pi.
- **GitHub Copilot**: device-code (`Iv1.b507a08c87ecfe98`), waits one poll interval before its first
  attempt. `login` first prompts for an optional GitHub Enterprise domain (Task #4 pi-parity fix,
  matching pi's own `loginGitHubCopilot` prompt) — blank defaults to `github.com`; anything else must
  normalize to a real hostname (`github_copilot::normalize_enterprise_domain`, accepting either a bare
  host or a full URL) or the whole login fails outright — and threads the resolved domain through every
  device-flow/token-exchange URL, ending up recorded on the stored credential's own `enterprise_url`
  (previously always `None`, even though `refresh`/`base_url_from_token` already accepted one for a
  credential that had it set some other way). Refreshing re-derives a short-lived Copilot-internal proxy
  token from the long-lived GitHub device-flow token every time; `login` additionally does a
  best-effort, parallel model-"enable" fan-out and records which models are actually available —
  `refresh` re-checks availability but never repeats the enable step.
- **OpenAI Codex**: user picks browser PKCE (port `1455`, an _independent_ random CSRF state, unlike
  Anthropic) or a custom, non-RFC-8628 device-code flow (403/404 both mean "pending"; the token server
  issues its own PKCE verifier for this path, not the client's). No early-refresh buffer, unlike the
  other two providers' 5-minute buffer.

**Storage** (`crate::auth_store::AuthStore`, `~/.beyond/auth.json` by default): same shape family as
`SettingsStore`/`TrustStore` — the shared store lock (`file_lock::lock_store_file`), `mutate_locked`'s
re-read-fresh-under-lock discipline, tolerant of a missing/corrupt file on read. A write follows
`store_file`'s rule: entries this binary can't parse (an unknown provider, an unsupported credential
type, a newer shape) are written back untouched, so refreshing one provider never deletes another's
login, and a file that can't be parsed refuses the write instead of being replaced. `refreshed()` is the one
new piece of substance: double-checked-locked refresh (the lock is held across the _entire_ refresh,
including the network call, so two concurrent processes sharing a credential can't both consume a
single-use refresh token) that preserves the credential bit-for-bit and records
`last_refresh_error` on failure, rather than deleting it — a transient failure must never cost the
user their login. The file is created at `0600` atomically on first write, and every subsequent write
re-asserts `0600` via an explicit `chmod` afterward — `write_atomic` only ever _preserves_ whatever
permission bits the file already had, so this is what self-heals a mode ever loosened out-of-band
between writes, matching pi's own unconditional `chmodSync` after every `auth-storage.ts` write.

**CLI**: `beyond-ai-agent login <provider>` (blocks in-terminal, prints a URL/device-code, races a manual-paste
fallback against the local callback listener), `beyond-ai-agent logout <provider>`, `beyond-ai-agent auth-status
[provider]` — same dispatch shape as `beyond-ai-agent trust`/`beyond-ai-agent settings`.

**`serve` RPC**: `login`/`logout`/`auth_status`/`submit_code`/`abort_login` — see the wire-protocol
doc comment at the top of `serve.rs` for the exact frame shapes. `login` runs as a detached background
task (not an inline nested busy-loop like `prompt`'s), pushing `login_progress` frames and an
eventual `response`, precisely because a subscription login has nothing to do with `session`/`agent`
state — every other command keeps working while one is pending; only a second concurrent `login` is
rejected.

**The client-side credential seam**: `gateway_credential::resolve_gateway_credential` is the one
further fallback tier below `--key`/`AI_AGENT_KEY` — consulted only when both are absent, inferring a
provider from the resolved model id (Anthropic: any Claude-dialect id; Codex: a `"codex"`-containing
id; Copilot: _not_ inferred by model prefix at all, since its model set is dynamic — matched only
against a stored credential's own `available_model_ids`) and building an `OAuthCredentialSource` for
it. See `agent_core::client::CredentialSource` above for how that source plugs into `GatewayClient`.

Resolved fresh every time the active model changes, not once for the process's whole life: `run`
(never switches models mid-invocation) calls it exactly once, but `serve` calls it again — via
`serve::build_gateway_client`, which also applies the process's retry policy — at startup (against
whichever model actually ends up active after the anti-bleed session-restore check, not `cfg.model`
directly) and on every `set_model`/`cycle_model`/`switch_session`/`fork`/`clone`/`switch_branch` that
changes it thereafter, swapping the whole `Arc<GatewayClient>` rather than just rebuilding the `Agent`
around the same one. Previously this was resolved exactly once, before `serve` even started, and the
resulting client silently kept serving every later model switch regardless of whether the new model's
provider still matched — a switch from an Anthropic-OAuth model to a GitHub-Copilot- or
OpenAI-Codex-OAuth one sent that stale bearer token/routing to the new provider's endpoint instead of
its own. `set_model`/`cycle_model` fail the whole switch outright if credential resolution for the new
model errors (leaving `current_model`/the persisted lineage untouched, the same "don't fork live state
away from what's durably recorded" precedent `record_model_change` already sets); the four
session-restoration commands (`switch_session`/`fork`/`clone`/`switch_branch`) instead warn to stderr
and keep the previous client, matching their existing best-effort "restore whatever was recorded"
posture — the next `prompt` then surfaces its own clear transport-level error if that client genuinely
can't serve the restored model.

## MCP Server OAuth

A wholly separate OAuth mechanism from the section above — that one authenticates _this agent_ to a
_model_ provider (Anthropic/Copilot/Codex); this one authenticates it to a _configured MCP server_
(`tools/mcp.rs`'s `mcp_servers`, `http` transport only — `stdio` servers have no login of their own,
see that module's doc comment). Different protocol too: not each provider's own bespoke flow, but the
MCP spec's own standardized OAuth 2.1 (SEP-985 protected-resource-metadata discovery, RFC 7591 dynamic
client registration, PKCE) — implemented almost entirely by `rmcp`'s own `transport::auth` module
(`AuthorizationManager`/`AuthorizationSession`), not hand-rolled the way `crate::oauth`'s three
provider flows are (MCP servers don't each have their own bespoke client id/endpoint quirks the way
Anthropic/Copilot/Codex do — the whole point of the spec's own discovery + DCR is that a generic client
never needs provider-specific code).

**Storage** (`mcp_auth_store.rs::McpAuthStore`, `~/.beyond/mcp_auth.json` by default): same shape family
as `AuthStore`/`SettingsStore`/`TrustStore` (the shared store lock, atomic writes,
re-read-fresh-under-lock) but keyed by MCP server _name_ (`mcp_servers`' own `name` field) rather than
a fixed provider enum — a `ScopedMcpCredentialStore` implements `rmcp`'s own `CredentialStore` trait
scoped to one server's slot in the shared file, which is what an `AuthorizationManager` actually reads
and writes through; `rmcp` itself calls `save()` after both the initial token exchange and every later
refresh, so persistence is a side effect of driving the manager, not something this crate's own code
does explicitly.

**CLI**: `beyond-ai-agent mcp-login <name>` (blocks in-terminal, prints the authorization URL, waits on a local
callback) — `name` must already be a configured `http`-transport `mcp_servers` entry. Unlike `agent
login`'s three providers, each pre-registered against one _fixed_ callback port, `mcp-login` picks a
fresh local port every run and registers _that_ via dynamic client registration — there's no
pre-registered redirect URI to reuse, since MCP servers don't know about this client in advance.
Reuses `oauth::callback_server::CallbackServer` (the identical local-listener primitive `beyond-ai-agent login`'s
own PKCE flows use) for the actual wait; the CSRF `state` value needed to validate the callback is
extracted directly from the authorization URL `AuthorizationSession` generates (it doesn't otherwise
expose the raw token) rather than threaded through as a separate return value. `beyond-ai-agent mcp-logout <name>`
removes the stored credential; idempotent, matching `beyond-ai-agent logout`.

**`tools::mcp::connect_http`'s consumption side**: before connecting, checks
`McpAuthStore::has_credential` for the server's name — a plain file-existence check, so the common case
(no MCP OAuth login at all) costs nothing beyond that. When one exists, restores it
(`AuthorizationManager::initialize_from_store`) and calls `get_access_token()` (refreshing
transparently — `rmcp`'s own 30-second-early buffer means most real-world token lifetimes trigger a
refresh well before actual expiry) to get a current bearer token (`tools::mcp_oauth::ServerAuth::load`).
A missing/dead credential is never itself treated as fatal here — the
connect attempt proceeds unauthenticated (correct for the common case of a server that needs no auth
at all) and _that_ attempt's own failure (if the server does require it) is enriched with a hint to run
`beyond-ai-agent mcp-login <name>`, rather than this function pre-emptively deciding a server needs auth.

**Mid-session refresh** (`tools/mcp_oauth.rs`). The token is a `ServerAuth`, one per configured server
in the process, shared by every connection to it — the plain and apps-flavoured connections and direct
`events/*` requests. It is reloaded from the store at each dial **under the same lock a refresh
holds** (a refresh persists before releasing it, so the store read there is never older than the token
held; a reload that reads nothing keeps the token held). Every request rmcp's streamable-HTTP
transport makes goes through `OAuthHttp`, which attaches the server's _current_ token (the transport
carries no `auth_header` of its own); direct `events/*` POSTs (`mcp_events::wire`'s `Conn::send`)
likewise read the current token per request, not the one their headers were built with. **One rule
on both paths:** any **401** from a server with a login — with or without a `WWW-Authenticate`
challenge, whatever its body (every POST, for every server, is answered by
`mcp_wire::HttpClient::post_bounded`, which decides from the status — a deliberate divergence from rmcp's own client (see below), which reads a 401 carrying a JSON-RPC error body as an ordinary error
response; pinned in `an_ordinary_request_is_answered_as_rmcps_own_client_would`) — makes `ServerAuth::after_rejection` force a refresh through the same `AuthorizationManager`
and `McpAuthStore` `mcp-login` uses (so the new token is persisted), and the request is retried
**once**; a second 401 is returned as the server's answer, saying to run `beyond-ai-agent mcp-login <server>`
again — on a tool call as at connect, since only a new login helps once a refreshed token is refused
too. **The server's reason survives the 401:** when its small body (≤ 64 KiB) is a JSON-RPC error, the message — untrusted text from an external system — is cut to 1 KiB (with `…`) and fenced the way event payloads are (`<mcp_server_message untrusted>…`). The fence is a rule, not a list: every character in Unicode General_Category Cc (tab, newline, CR become spaces), Cf, Co, Cn, Zl, Zp or Cs is dropped, with the TAG block ("ASCII smuggling"), U+180E and the variation selectors; and any character whose NFKC form or UTS #39 confusable skeleton is a fence character — or whose Unicode name makes it a bare angle (a generated table, `tools/fence_tables.rs` from `scripts/gen_angle_lookalikes.py`: PRECEDES, the angle-bracket ornaments, arrowheads, …) — becomes `‹` `›` `/` or `'`, so nothing in the text can close its fence, however it is spelled, or end a quoted-string. `mcp_wire::fenced_server_message` is the one place server text crosses into model-visible errors: a JSON-RPC error's `message` and `data` (`tool_call_err`; MCP Events' `RpcError`, fenced where it comes in, its code and structured `data` kept for the decisions made on them), a challenge header among a failed call's causes (401 and 403), the post-refresh `beyond-ai-agent mcp-login` error, an authorization server's own text in a refresh failure, a non-JSON-RPC success's body, a legacy `server/discover` rejection's body. With a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge the 401 stays `AuthRequired`, carrying that challenge for whatever reads it (rmcp's auth client, `auth_challenge`) with the reason added as RFC 6750's `error_description`; without one it fails as rmcp's own bare-401 error does, `HTTP 401 Unauthorized: <fenced message> (JSON-RPC error <code>)`. Either way it is still a 401 to the refresh, and for a server with no login (a static key it stopped accepting, say) it is the tool error the model sees: a failed tool call prints its error's causes too, so a challenge and the reason in it are not hidden behind rmcp's "Auth required"; any other 401 is a bare `AuthRequired` (`tests/mcp_unauthorized.rs`). That covers `tools/call`, `resources/*`,
`prompts/*`, `skills/*`, MCP App view reads, the handshake, the standalone stream and `events/*`. A 403
(`InsufficientScope`) never refreshes.

**`post_bounded` answers what rmcp's client would, with two deliberate differences.** Since no server's POSTs reach rmcp's client any more, `post_bounded` carries its semantics: `Mcp-Session-Id`
in and out, a 404 on a session as `SessionExpired` (rmcp re-initializes and retries), an SSE response
handed back as a stream, 202/204 — or an empty 200 to a notification or reply — as accepted, a JSON 200
that is not a JSON-RPC message, for a notification or reply, as accepted, a non-JSON success as an
error (rmcp's unexpected content type), and a 4xx to `server/discover` as the legacy server's cue to
`initialize`. **The differences:** any 401 is a 401 (above; rmcp reads one with a JSON-RPC body as an error response — pinned in `an_ordinary_request_is_answered_as_rmcps_own_client_would`); and a JSON 200 that is not a JSON-RPC message, answering a _request_,
is an error here. rmcp calls it accepted and then waits for a response that cannot come (a request is
answered on its own POST, as JSON or an SSE stream carrying it) until the request's timeout; failing
at once with the body in the error is the honest answer. Pinned end to end against the OAuth fixture
— which speaks sessions (and their 404 expiry), SSE responses streamed event by event (a progress
notification and an `elicitation/create` on the call's own POST, the response held until the client's
answer has come back on another POST), the `GET` stream and `DELETE` — in
`tests/mcp_oauth_routing.rs` (a 401 with a JSON-RPC body through a real dial, the legacy
`server/discover` 4xx, an empty-200 notification, sessions with SSE, an expired session, an in-POST
question routed to the client and answered mid-stream, and a reaped connection's DELETE carrying the
bearer and session id), and the request/notification difference in `mcp_wire`'s
`a_json_success_that_is_not_json_rpc_is_accepted_for_a_notification_but_fails_a_request`.

**Sessions end on the way out** (`tools/mcp_http_exit.rs`). rmcp sends a session's `DELETE` when a
connection is closed while the runtime runs (the idle reaper, a registry rebuild); a process that
exits (`beyond-ai-agent run` finishing, a `serve` shutdown) never got that far. So every HTTP connection records
the session it opened (`OAuthHttp` sees each response's `Mcp-Session-Id` and each `DELETE` rmcp sends;
the process holds it only weakly, so a connection that goes away takes its entry with it — one that
goes with its session still open sends that `DELETE` at once on its runtime and is dropped once that
attempt is over, answered or timed out — kept for the exit only when dropped by the runtime's own
teardown),
and `mcp_stdio::sweep_before_exit` — every graceful way out, `exit_process` and `ExitSweep` alike —
first sends a `DELETE` for every session still open: in parallel, with the server's current bearer and
the connection's own headers, on a thread with its own runtime and a fresh pool-less client (the
process runtime may be gone, or blocked in the very call that is exiting; a grant connector's client
keeps its SSRF resolver), bounded by `CLOSE_DEADLINE` (1.5 s) overlapping the stdio grace. A server that
never answers costs at most the deadline. Pinned in `tests/mcp_oauth_routing.rs`: an `beyond-ai-agent run` sends
exactly one authenticated `DELETE` before it exits, and one whose `DELETE` is held for 30 s still
exits within its deadline.

**Single flight (refresh):** the refresh runs under the token's lock, and
a caller whose rejected token has already been replaced takes the replacement without refreshing, so
concurrent 401s cost one refresh (a second refresh with a rotated-away refresh token would fail). **A
failed refresh is remembered:** a _definitive_ one for good, with an error naming `beyond-ai-agent mcp-login
<name>` — any RFC 6749 §5.2 error code from the token endpoint (`invalid_grant`, `invalid_client`,
`unauthorized_client`, `unsupported_grant_type`, `invalid_scope`, `invalid_request`), a token endpoint
that is not there (404/405/410), or no refresh token, classified from the endpoint's own answer (the
OAuth HTTP goes through `RecordingOAuthHttp`, since rmcp's refresh error keeps neither status nor
code); a _transient_ one (the authorization server unreachable, a 5xx, a 429) for a backoff of 30 s
doubling to 5 min, after which a rejection refreshes again. A reload clears a remembered failure
only when the stored token actually changed. Tested in
`tests/mcp_oauth_refresh.rs` (a token revoked between two tool calls of one run, a failing refresh,
three concurrent 401s) against the shared fixture in `tests/common/mcp_oauth_fixture.rs`, and by unit
tests in `mcp_oauth.rs` and `mcp_events/wire.rs` (backoff, the reload race, a bare 401, a 403, the
events path's current token).

Tested end to end in `tests/mcp_oauth.rs` against a real, hand-rolled OAuth-protected MCP fixture
(metadata discovery, dynamic client registration, a real authorize-then-redirect exchange, a token
endpoint supporting both `authorization_code` and `refresh_token` grants, and _actual_ bearer-token
enforcement on the MCP endpoint itself) — the full login flow, a subsequent tool call authenticated by
the resulting token, transparent refresh, `mcp-logout`, and the clear-failure-naming-`mcp-login` path
for a server nobody has ever logged into.

## MCP Events (draft extension)

> **Draft.** Implements the MCP Triggers & Events Working Group's design sketch at commit
> [`6682596d65eec778fe0b8b1f43b4e89d2fe2c546`](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/experimental-ext-triggers-events/blob/6682596d65eec778fe0b8b1f43b4e89d2fe2c546/docs/design-sketch-proposal.md)
> (no SEP yet), cross-checked against OpenAI's MCP Events guide (ChatGPT ships a webhook-only
> client). The wire may change. Code: [`tools/mcp_events/`](src/tools/mcp_events) (`mod.rs` hub,
> subscriptions, coalescer; `webhook.rs` receiver and key policy; `state.rs` durable state;
> `wire.rs` transports) and [`tools/mcp_stdio.rs`](src/tools/mcp_stdio.rs).

A server emits, this agent subscribes. Subscriptions are declared per server in `settings.json`
(`mcp_servers[].events: [{name, arguments?, delivery?, action?, instructions?, max_age_ms?}]`)
and/or made at runtime per session (`mcp_events_subscribe` / `mcp_events_unsubscribe` /
`mcp_events_list`). A server with no `events` entry is never asked about events at all, and a
session with no connected MCP server wires nothing. A session with servers but no subscriptions
interposes on its command channel (so it can subscribe at runtime) and otherwise does nothing: no
requests, no state files. What _does_ change for every stdio MCP server, events or not, is its
transport — see "The stdio transport" below.

```
settings.json mcp_servers[].events ──► owned by ONE session: stdio serve's, or the daemon's
                                       --mcp-events-session (default `mcp-events`), booted at start
mcp_events_subscribe (any session) ──► owned by that session
                       │
           McpEventsHub ── events/list (cached; list_changed invalidates)
                       ├─ poll    : events/poll {cursor} every max(nextPollMs, floor)
                       ├─ push    : events/stream ─► notifications/events/* (router, never lossy)
                       └─ webhook : events/subscribe {url, whsec_ secret, ttlMs} ─► refresh loop
                                      ▲  /_beyond/mcp-events/<token> on serve's listener
         occurrence ─► dedup(eventId) ─► appended to <session>.mcp-events.log, fdatasync'd ─► ack/advance
                                      ─► `mcp_event` frame
         coalescer ─► commit ─► {"type":"prompt","mcp_events":<batch>,…} on the session's channel
         model received it + transcript persisted ─► `done` appended ─► out of pending
         run failed / steer dropped by an abort    ─► pending again (re-injected; dropped after 3)
```

- **Ownership and routing.** Configured subscriptions belong to exactly one session per process:
  the stdio `serve`'s only session, or the daemon's events session (`--mcp-events-session`, default
  `mcp-events`), which `serve_ws` starts at boot (pinned and at once unpinned, as if a client had
  come and gone) whenever anything is configured. Every event from a configured subscription is
  delivered to that session and nowhere else — one event, one subscription, one model run, however
  many clients are connected. A client watches it by attaching to that id. Any session may also
  subscribe at runtime; it alone then owns that subscription.
- **Delivery modes.** Negotiated from the event type's advertised `delivery` and what this process
  can receive, preferring webhook > push > poll (the draft's order); `delivery` forces one, and an
  impossible choice is an error naming why. **Webhook** needs `serve --listen`/`--listen-uds` _and_
  `--mcp-events-callback-url` (`main.rs` refuses the flag without a listener). Each subscription gets
  a random token path and a fresh `whsec_` secret (32 CSPRNG bytes); the token is registered _before_
  `events/subscribe` is sent, so the server's verification challenge and first delivery always find
  their route. The token and the last confirmed secret persist in the state file, so after a restart
  the same callback URL is registered again before anything is sent — a delivery the server retries
  while the daemon was down (a crash leaves its subscription in place) still lands and verifies.
  Persisted tokens of every subscription the session will subscribe again — configured ones, and
  runtime ones being restored (below) — are held from the moment the state is read (up to 10 min): a
  retry that arrives before its subscription has re-registered gets `503` (retry), never `410` (which
  the draft treats as "stop"). Before any state is read, a daemon with a callback URL answers every
  unknown token `503` from its start until each session it starts to restore callbacks (the events
  session, and every session holding runtime subscriptions) has read its state and held its tokens
  (`webhook::restore_pending` / `restored`, also bounded at 10 min); after that an unknown token is
  `410` at once. A runtime subscription the server ended is not restored, so its token is not held
  and its old callback answers `410`. No subscription makes a request — configured, restored after a
  restart or a panic, or resubscribing — until the session can take the server's questions (its
  elicitation and sampling gates are installed: `McpEventsHub::start`), since a server may ask during
  the very first `events/poll`.
  After a _graceful_ shutdown the subscription was unsubscribed, so an event type the server cannot
  replay from a cursor loses what it emitted while the daemon was down; one with replay resumes from
  the persisted cursor. Refresh runs at ¾ of the way to `refreshBefore` (an unparseable one refreshes after
  30 s, with a warning — never silently in an hour) and **rotates the secret on every refresh**; the
  receiver accepts the current and the previous secret (one generation), and a rotation the server
  has not confirmed is resent unchanged on retry. **Push** holds one `events/stream` per subscription
  with no request timeout; silence past `2 × 30 s + slack` reconnects from the last cursor. **Poll**
  floors `nextPollMs` at 1 s, and a `hasMore: true` page with nothing new in it (no events, or only
  duplicates — counted after dedup) waits the floor too.
- **Durable delivery to the model.** An occurrence the server is told we received — webhook `2xx`,
  poll cursor advanced — is first appended to the session's pending log and `fdatasync`'d. The
  webhook `200` waits for that write (the draft: SHOULD NOT `2xx` before durably persisted); a full
  queue, a write that fails, or one that does not finish within 10 s answers `503` instead
  (retryable — the retry is accepted once the write succeeds, as a duplicate in memory). Poll
  advances its cursor only when every event of the page was accepted _and_ the write succeeded;
  otherwise it re-polls from the same cursor. Push reconnects from its last cursor. Nothing about a
  refused event (dedup, cursor) is recorded, and a persisted cursor never runs ahead of the events it
  passed (the log is written before the snapshot, and the snapshot not at all if the log failed).
  The coalescer commits before it injects. A batch leaves the pending queue only when the **model has
  received it** and the transcript holding it has been persisted (`McpEventsHub::finish_run`, from the
  `prompt` arm): the run's own prompt counts once the run did not fail (an abort still leaves the
  prompt in the transcript the next run reads); a batch steered in mid-run counts exactly when the
  model receives it: the steer is queued with its batch as the message's tag
  (`SteeringMessage::tag`), and the run's `AgentEvent::Steered` reports the tags it injected _after_
  checkpointing the transcript holding them — `mcp_events::Receipts::received` records the batch as
  delivered (durably) right then. Nothing is re-derived from the transcript later, so a compaction
  that summarizes the steered turn away does not make it look undelivered; an abort clears the steer
  lane (`Steering::clear_run_scoped`) before the model sees what is queued there, so no `Steered`
  reports it. A batch whose run failed, whose transcript did not persist, or whose
  steer was dropped goes back to pending and is injected again; after 3 such attempts an event is
  dropped and reported (`mcp_event_status` `kind: "dropped"`), so a poison event cannot re-run the
  model forever. A restart re-injects whatever is still pending. **Guarantee:** every acknowledged
  event reaches the model at least once (or is reported dropped after 3 attempts that never reached
  it). It reaches it exactly once except in three cases, each of which re-injects the batch: a run
  fails or is aborted before the model saw a steered batch (by design); the process dies, or the
  `done` record fails to be written, between a turn's checkpoint and that record. A graceful exit writes the record first, so
  SIGTERM, stdin EOF and the reaper never duplicate (`tests/mcp_events_durability.rs`).
- **Into the session.** Each subscription dedups by `eventId` (newest 1024, persisted), then every
  accepted occurrence is broadcast as `mcp_event`. Unless `action: "notify"`, it is queued for the
  model; one coalescer per session injects at most one synthetic `prompt` per
  `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_EVENTS_COALESCE_MS` (default 2 s), at most 50 events each (the rest waits —
  never dropped). At most `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_EVENTS_MAX_PENDING` (1000) events and
  `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_EVENTS_MAX_PENDING_BYTES` (16 MiB, as stored) wait; past either, new events are
  refused as above (backpressure, not loss). `follow_up` (default) events are **held while a run
  is in flight**; `steer` events go in immediately. The injected text labels payloads as untrusted
  data, escapes `<` inside them so a payload cannot close its own fence, carries the operator's
  `instructions`, and — when a server reports `truncated` or a `gap` — tells the model that events
  may have been missed so it can re-check authoritative state.
- **Never refused as busy.** Injected prompts carry `"mcp_events": <batch>`. One that lands while
  the loop runs something that cannot take a prompt — a host `bash`, a branch summary, a whole-run
  retry backoff — goes to `deferred_events` and is replayed the moment the loop is idle. A mid-run
  follow-up injection runs right after the run; a steer the lane refuses is deferred too. Inline
  commands that never read the channel wait an injection behind them; a manual `compact` reads it,
  and defers an injection like a host `bash` does.
- **Commands never block.** `mcp_events_*` commands are spawned tasks (`McpEventsCommands`), from
  the idle loop and every busy loop alike. Subscribe/unsubscribe take a lock **per subscription
  key**, so a slow server's discovery or verification challenge holds neither the session nor
  subscriptions on other servers.
- **Push never silently loses.** The per-connection `NotificationRouter` queues at most
  `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_EVENTS_STREAM_BUFFER` (256) notifications per stream. On overflow it marks the
  stream and forwards nothing more for it; the stream drains what is queued (all of it earlier than
  the drop), then reconnects at once from that cursor and the server replays the rest. A cursor never
  moves past a dropped event. Over HTTP the SSE reader awaits channel space instead (TCP
  backpressure).
- **Configured subscriptions are kept up.** Each one in `mcp_servers[].events` is subscribed in the
  background and, on failure, retried with backoff capped at 60 s — forever, for as long as the
  session runs; so is one the server later ends (any termination, after a 1 s pause, with
  `events/list` re-fetched). While one is not up it counts as live for the keep-alive: a daemon whose
  servers are all briefly down keeps its events session. An explicit `mcp_events_unsubscribe` stops
  keeping it up, including while a retry is waiting (membership is re-checked before every attempt).
  A **permanent refusal** — the server is unknown (gone from settings), does not offer the event,
  does not speak the extension (`-32601`), rejects the request as invalid (`-32602`, `-32011`,
  `-32014` other than `schema_changed`), or no delivery mode fits — is different: it is reported as
  `refused` (an `mcp_event_status` frame, and `mcp_events_list`'s `unestablished` list, which also
  shows what is `starting` or `retrying`), retried only every
  `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_EVENTS_REFUSED_RETRY_MS` (1 h), and does **not** count as live for the
  keep-alive. **Forbidden** (`-32012`) is not permanent at first — an expired credential looks like
  this: it is retried on a short backoff (1 s doubling to 5 s), each attempt dialing afresh so
  credentials are re-resolved, and becomes a refusal only after 5 in a row.
- **Runtime subscriptions survive a restart.** A successful `mcp_events_subscribe` stores its whole
  spec in the session's events state (`PersistedSub::runtime`). When the session starts again it
  subscribes each one again (retried like a configured one until it is back, or until it is
  explicitly unsubscribed); a daemon starts every session holding such a subscription at boot
  (`mcp_events::sessions_with_runtime_subscriptions`, pinned and unpinned like the events session),
  so its triggers resume with no client attached. An explicit unsubscribe forgets the spec, and so
  does the server ending the subscription (unless re-discovery brings it back), and so does a restore
  the server refuses for good (its server renamed or removed, say) — so a dead subscription cannot
  pin its session or bring it back at every boot. Forgetting one forgets all of it — spec, cursor,
  and webhook callback (token and secret) — so no credential outlives the subscription in the
  snapshot. Runtime subscriptions also **expire**: a session's last client command is recorded
  (coarsely, in the events state; creating a runtime subscription counts as one, so a subscription
  made by a single command still has a start to its time to live), and once it is older than
  `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_EVENTS_RUNTIME_TTL_MS` (7 days) its runtime subscriptions are forgotten
  instead of restored, and a daemon no longer starts it at boot. A state with runtime subscriptions
  and no record at all is not trusted: it is not restored. Boot restoration is bounded too: at most
  `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_EVENTS_MAX_RESTORED_SESSIONS` (32) sessions are started — the ones a client
  used most recently — and the rest come back when their clients do.
- **Schema changes.** For a runtime subscription, a termination saying the event type was removed
  (`-32011`, `kind: event`) or changed in place (`-32014`, `reason: schema_changed`) re-fetches
  `events/list` and resubscribes — the draft's SHOULD — up to 5 times, with backoff; the budget is
  restored once the subscription has stayed up for `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_EVENTS_HEALTHY_MS` (10 min).
  Whenever a subscription comes back after the server ended it, the model is told (a `gap` notice
  in its next injection) that events may have been missed in between.
- **Server identity (`v1a`), fail closed.** The draft lets a server add an Ed25519 `v1a,` signature,
  with the key discovered from an origin the client already authenticates; this client fetches
  `<MCP server origin>/.well-known/mcp-webhook-jwks.json` (the standalone-JWKS alternative the draft
  names; SEP-2127 server cards are not published yet) before every subscribe and refresh, under one
  deadline for the whole exchange, headers and body (`BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_EVENTS_JWKS_TIMEOUT_MS`,
  5 s), and with cancellation observed; a subscription task that overstays its cancellation is
  aborted, which also removes its webhook route. Every key
  ever published at an origin is remembered — in the session's state file and process-wide — and the
  set only grows: while it is non-empty, every delivery (the challenge included) must carry a valid
  `v1a,` or gets `401`. A later `404`, an empty document or a failed fetch never removes a key (the
  draft has no signal that could prove a server meant to stop signing). On a first subscribe with
  no key known, a failed fetch (timeout, `5xx`, oversized or unparseable body) is retried and then
  refuses the subscription; only a clear `404`/`410` means "this server does not sign", and then
  `v1a,` is ignored.
- **The receiver** (`webhook::receive_webhook`; routed by `serve_ws::handle_connection` ahead of the
  grant check, and **not at all in service mode**). Cheap answers come before a byte of the body is
  read: unknown token → `410`, non-POST → `405`, no length → `411`, a body over 1 MiB → `413`. The
  body is then read into a buffer that grows as bytes arrive (never sized from `Content-Length`),
  all of it within `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_EVENTS_BODY_TIMEOUT_MS` (10 s) or `408`.
  Missing Standard Webhooks headers or a `webhook-timestamp` more than 5 minutes off in either
  direction → `400` (computed with `abs_diff`, so no timestamp can overflow); no `v1,` signature
  verifying (constant time) under the current or previous secret, a missing/invalid `v1a,` where
  identity is enforced, or — once `events/subscribe` has returned the subscription id — a missing or
  contradicting `X-MCP-Subscription-Id` → `401`. Only the first 8 entries of `webhook-signature` are
  looked at, so a hostile header cannot buy unbounded HMAC/Ed25519 work. `verification` →
  `200 {"challenge"}`. The listener also serves the draft's receiver document at
  `/.well-known/mcp-webhook-receiver.json` (`{"receivers": ["<callback base path>/_beyond/mcp-events/"]}`).
- **Lifetime.** Subscriptions belong to the `serve_session` task (the slot, not the transcript).
  While a session has a live subscription, configured ones not yet (or no longer) up, or undelivered
  events, its `keep_alive` flag exempts it from the daemon's idle reaper; a session with none —
  including one whose only (runtime) subscription has terminated — is reaped as usual.
  `--mcp-events-reapable` opts back into ordinary reaping. Teardown unsubscribes webhooks and cancels
  streams (bounded, 5 s; then aborted), stops the coalescer (which watches shutdown even while its
  send is blocked on a full channel; bounded too), and commits the state.
- **The state files** (`state.rs`), beside the transcript. `<session>.mcp-events.json` is the
  _snapshot_ — cursors, dedup windows, webhook callbacks, server keys — small and bounded, rewritten
  whole when it changes (private temp file, `fsync`, `rename`, directory `fsync`).
  `<session>.mcp-events.log` is the _pending log_ — `{"add": event}` / `{"done": [seq…]}` lines —
  appended and `fdatasync`'d, so a commit costs the size of the change, not of the queue; it is
  rewritten with only the live events once it is over 1 MiB and more than twice its live content (a
  rewrite that fails puts back the records it displaced, so they still reach the disk by the next
  write). A torn tail (a crash mid-append) is cut off on disk when the log is read — truncated back
  to the last complete record and synced — before anything is appended, so the next record is never
  glued onto the fragment. One writer task owns both: writes happen
  one after another so the newest state always wins; ordinary changes are coalesced for up to 100 ms
  but a commit is never made to wait that window out; a failed write is reported to whoever is
  waiting and retried by the next one; files are read on the blocking pool; the writer writes once
  more and ends when its last handle drops. **Nothing is written while there is nothing to persist**,
  so a session that never subscribes leaves no files. On `new_session`/`switch_session` the state
  **moves** before the next command is read: what the target transcript already had (its own
  undelivered events, cursors, keys) is merged in — never overwritten — the merged state is written
  there and the old files removed. Both files are trashed and restored with their session
  (`session_store::move_sibling_memory`).
- **Idempotency.** Subscribe is an upsert keyed by `(server, name, canonical arguments)`. The same
  spec again is a no-op; a changed one replaces the old subscription only after the new one is
  confirmed, sharing its cursor and dedup window. Unsubscribing nothing is success (`removed: false`).
- **The stdio transport — all stdio MCP servers.** rmcp 3.x decodes every response into an untagged
  union of typed results, and `CallToolResult` matches any object carrying `_meta` — which every
  `2026-07-28` server attaches to every result — so a custom result like `events/list` came back as
  an empty tool result (found by the interop check below). To fix that, **every stdio MCP server**
  (not only ones with events) is now spawned by `mcp_stdio::stdio_transport` instead of rmcp's
  `TokioChildProcess`. It keeps that transport's behaviour: the caller's command and process group,
  inherited stderr, a non-UTF-8 stdout line skipped rather than fatal. **Shutdown** is
  `mcp_stdio::retire`, run when the transport is dropped, when the connection is (`McpConnection`'s
  `Drop`, the idle reap), and for every server still running on the way out of the process
  (`mcp_stdio::retire_all`). It closes the server's stdin at once — synchronously; the child and its
  stdin are shared, not owned by a task, so no runtime has to run anything — gives it
  `mcp_stdio::SHUTDOWN_GRACE` (3 s) to exit on its own (so a reap no longer SIGKILLs a server
  mid-cleanup), measured by a non-blocking wait on the child itself (portable, and never answered by
  a recycled pid), kills it if it has not exited, then kills **every process it started**: the
  server is spawned with a `bash_proc::TAG_ENV` tracking tag as its own group leader and tracked as
  a `bash_proc::ProcGroup` (tag, group while the server holds its number, or descent from either;
  each kill verified by start time through a pidfd, no kill-by-pid on a bare number). A group alone
  missed a grandchild that called `setsid`/`setpgid` (a browser's crash handler does), so restarting
  `serve` left it behind; the tag survives that, a double fork and the server exiting first. The
  tree is read **before** stdin closes, while every parent link is intact, so a descendant that also
  cleared its environment is still known after a server that exits in its grace has re-parented it
  (`mcp_stdio::tests::retire_kills_a_grandchild_that_left_the_process_group`,
  `retire_kills_an_untagged_grandchild_of_a_server_that_exits_on_its_own`). The waiting and killing
  run on a tracked OS thread (`exec::spawn_tracked_cleanup`). Every exit of `run` and `serve` after their tools exist
  runs `mcp_stdio::sweep_before_exit` — `retire_all`, then `exec::wait_for_pending_group_kills`,
  bounded by the grace plus 2 s: each `process::exit` goes through `exit_process` (stdin EOF,
  SIGTERM, a cancelled `run`, a refused one, and every configuration error found after the servers
  are up), and `main` returning — or a panic unwinding out of it — passes the `mcp_stdio::ExitSweep`
  guard's `Drop` (`tests/mcp_stdio_transport.rs`: `serve` on EOF and SIGTERM, `run` finishing,
  cancelled mid-turn and refused for bad configuration; the panic path by
  `mcp_stdio::tests::a_panic_unwinding_past_the_exit_guard_still_sweeps`). A panic out of the main
  future does not reach that guard by dropping the runtime — that would wait for every blocking
  task, and `serve`'s stdin reader is one, parked on a read that may never return, so the process
  hung. `main` catches the unwind instead, abandons the runtime's threads
  (`Runtime::shutdown_background`), runs the same `finish_process_cleanup` as every other exit
  (`kill_live_jobs`, then the sweep — not the sweep alone: the unwind drops only what the main future
  owned, and whatever else still holds a `bash` job is reached only through the live-job registry),
  and exits `101` (`a_panic_inside_serve_exits_promptly_and_still_sweeps`, through a
  debug-build-only `__test_panic` command; `tests/bash_jobs_panic_exit.rs` for `bash` jobs, in
  `serve` and in a multi-threaded daemon whose main future panics through the debug-build-only
  `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_TEST_PANIC_MAIN_ON` seam). In a daemon a session is a task, not the main future, so its panic is **contained**:
  `serve_ws` catches the session future's unwind (in-flight runs and MCP calls are dropped, its
  events hub cancelled and its state written by their `Drop`s), sends its clients an `error` frame,
  ends the session, and keeps serving every other one — sound because sessions share only state
  behind plain replace-the-value locks, and MCP server processes belong to the process, swept on its
  exit (`a_panic_in_a_daemon_session_ends_that_session_only`). The one session the daemon depends on
  — the MCP Events session, which runs the configured subscriptions — is started again after a
  panic, with backoff (1 s doubling to a minute, reset after ten minutes up, per session), so
  configured triggers do not stop until the next restart
  (`the_events_session_is_restarted_after_a_panic`); so is any session holding runtime
  subscriptions, which also run with no client attached
  (`a_session_with_runtime_subscriptions_is_restarted_after_a_panic`). The only exits that skip it
  are argument-parsing failures, before anything is spawned. **The cost, by design:** a process that
  ran a stdio server exits a little later — measured at about 166 ms instead of 44 ms for a server
  that exits on EOF — because each server is given the chance to exit cleanly and is then swept,
  and up to about 3.15 s when a server ignores its stdin closing and has to wait out its grace. **A
  hard-killed agent** (SIGKILL, the OOM killer) runs none of this, and a server that ignores stdin
  EOF used to outlive it. Under the agent binary (`subreaper.rs`) every server is started with a
  parent-death signal: `server_command` starts
  `<agent> __exec-with-parent-death-signal <agent pid> <program> <argv0> args…`, which arms
  `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG(SIGKILL)`, exits if the agent already died (`getppid` is no longer it), and execs
  the server in place: same pid, group, fds and environment. A trampoline because the workspace
  forbids `unsafe` (no `pre_exec`), the same move as the `web` parser's isolation; `program` is
  resolved on the server's `PATH` first, so a missing command still fails as a spawn error. The
  signal fires when the **thread** that forked the child exits, not the process, so every server is
  forked from one `mcp-spawner` thread that lives as long as the process (`spawn_lasting`, which
  enters the caller's runtime so the tokio child registers as before), never from a tokio blocking
  thread, which exits after 10 s idle and would take its servers with it
  (`tests/mcp_stdio_orphans.rs`: `a_sigkilled_agent_takes_its_stdio_server_down`). The agent is also
  a child subreaper, so a server's orphans re-parent to it instead of init and are reaped by it (see
  "The agent as its descendants' subreaper" above). What still escapes a SIGKILL: a grandchild that
  left the server's tree and ignores its parent dying. That is beyond in-process reach; a cgroup or
  the sandbox VM is that boundary. (The group kill now passes `--` before the
  group id. Without it procps-ng `kill` still killed a live group but exited 1 doing so — and 0 for
  a group already gone — so `kill_process_group`'s by-pid fallback ran after every successful group
  kill, which is the pid-reuse hazard.) Its stdout
  pump rewrites exactly the lossy responses (`mcp_stdio::rescue`); a cheap byte test means an
  ordinary tool result is never even parsed. `rescue`/`unwrap_rescued` are the whole workaround, one
  boundary shared with MCP skills (whose streamable-HTTP `skills/*` responses `mcp_wire::HttpClient`
  passes through the same `rescue`). Stateless
  (`2026-07-28`) streamable-HTTP servers get `events/*` directly over HTTP (`MCP-Protocol-Version`,
  `Mcp-Method`, per-request `_meta`, the server's resolved headers and OAuth bearer), with bodies
  bounded by the same per-message cap as every MCP transport (`mcp_stdio::max_message_bytes`, `BEYOND_AI_AGENT_MCP_MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES`: a unary JSON body, a unary SSE answer's event, an `events/stream` event — an over-cap answer fails its request, never read whole). An over-cap **event notification** (on a push stream, or from a stdio server) is skipped, not reconnected into: its bounded head is read structurally (`mcp_stdio::oversized_stand_in`, the same top-level member walk as `scan_head`) for its routing, cursor and id — **in any key order**: `method`, `id` and `params` are found wherever they fall within the window, and inside `params` every scalar and `_meta` that appears whole is kept — the rest is skipped unread, and a small `$oversized` stand-in takes its place. When the head does not reach the method (a payload-first `params` fills it), the message is still taken for an event unless the head proves it is a request (an `id`) or a response — and its gap says it was _possibly not an event_ (to the client, `possibly_not_an_event`, and to the model), since a request whose id and method both lay past the window looks the same. Over stdio, a stand-in whose routing lay past the head is delivered to every push stream on that connection (each records the gap in its own state, since which one it belonged to is unknowable), stamped with one id for the one dropped message (a per-process sequence from a secret start), so a session holding several of those streams tells its model **once**; the host-reserved `$`-keys (`$oversized`, `$ambiguous`, `$dropped_id`) are stripped from every server notification at ingress (`mcp_stdio::host_params`, at the router and on direct-HTTP streams) unless it carries the per-process secret the host stamps into its own stand-ins (`$host`), so a server cannot forge a gap or pre-empt a real drop's notice; with no push stream open it is logged, not reported. On a direct-HTTP stream it is that stream's. In either case the subscription keeps whatever cursor the head showed (or else the next event's or heartbeat's — never reconnecting into the same event), records an `oversized` gap (a `gap` frame, and a notice to the model that an event was dropped unread) and carries on (`tests/mcp_message_cap.rs`, both key orders over both transports) — JWKS documents at 64 KiB — and an SSE reader whose scan and drain
  are both linear (events are parsed in place; the consumed prefix is dropped once per read, not once
  per event); an older,
  session-bound HTTP server goes through rmcp's own connection, which carries its `Mcp-Session-Id`.
  A server→client request (an elicitation, a sampling request) raised during an `events/*` request
  is attributed to the session that owns it over rmcp — the same rule as during a `tools/call`
  (`track_call`); a session starts its hub only after its elicitation and sampling gates are installed, so one raised during the very first `events/*` request reaches its client rather than the default gate's decline — and, over direct HTTP, where nothing could route it to a session, answered at once
  with an error rather than left unanswered (`tests/mcp_events_nested.rs`). That answer is POSTed
  with the same `Accept` (`application/json, text/event-stream`) as every events request — a
  streamable-HTTP server refuses an answer without it `406` and keeps waiting (the fixture enforces
  it) — and through the same `Conn::send`, so with an OAuth login it carries the server's current
  token and a 401 refreshes and resends once (no `Mcp-Method`: an answer has no method) — and on an `events/stream` it is answered inline, one at a time, so a server flooding
  requests onto the stream cannot make the client spawn without limit
  (`a_flood_of_server_requests_on_an_events_stream_is_answered_one_at_a_time`).
- **`run` and service mode.** One-shot `run` does not subscribe: it ends when the model stops, and an
  event is a trigger for a _future_ run. Service mode refuses the `mcp_events_*` commands outright
  (`service::refused_command`), grant connectors carry no `events`, and the webhook and
  receiver-document routes do not exist there.

**Deployment: TLS in front of the listener.** The draft requires `https` callback URLs (servers
reject `http://` with `-32602`), and `serve --listen` speaks plain HTTP by design — it binds loopback
or an internal interface and trusts the front door, like the rest of the daemon. So
`--mcp-events-callback-url` must be the public `https://` base of whatever terminates TLS and routes
to the listener: an ingress, a load balancer, or a reverse proxy forwarding `/_beyond/mcp-events/*`
(and `/.well-known/mcp-webhook-receiver.json`) unchanged. Nothing in verification depends on
end-to-end TLS — the HMAC covers the raw body and timestamp — so terminating at the edge is safe.
Tests use plain `http://` against a fixture that allows it (`MCP_FIXTURE_ALLOW_HTTP_CALLBACK`).

Frames: `{type:"mcp_event", server, name, arguments, delivery, action, event:{eventId, name,
timestamp, data, cursor?}}` and `{type:"mcp_event_status", kind:"subscribed"|"resubscribed"|"error"|
"gap"|"terminated"|"delivery_status"|"dropped", …}`; `mcp_events_list` also reports `owns_configured`, the
pending count, and each webhook's last `deliveryStatus`. Proof:
`tests/mcp_events_{poll,push,webhook,receiver,busy,lifecycle,v1a,routing,durability}.rs` and
`tests/mcp_stdio_transport.rs` drive the real `serve` against `src/bin/mcp_fixture_events_server.rs`
(hand-rolled; stdio and streamable HTTP, stateless or legacy session-bound; it attaches
`_meta`/`resultType` to every result like real `2026-07-28` servers, signs `v1a`, replays from a
cursor inclusively, bursts, changes schemas, and verifies via the receiver document). Interop (not
in CI): `eval/mcp_events_interop/check.py` against the independent `mcp-webhook-events` 0.2.0 server
on the official Python SDK, over both transports.

## CLI flags: rationale

`--help` says what each flag does in a line or two: the doc comments on
`main.rs`'s `Command`. A test, `help_is_short_user_facing_text`, holds the
top-level page to 60 lines, `run`/`serve` to 350 and every other page to 120,
and refuses development history and internal paths in help text. Why a flag
behaves the way it does belongs here, next to the flag, when no other section of
this document already says it.

The parser binds one-character short flags only (`-a`, `-c`, `-n`, `-t`). The
two-character ones (`-nt`, `-xt`, `-ns`, `-np`, `-nc`, `-na`) and lowercase
`-v` are rewritten to their long forms by `expand_short_aliases` before parsing,
as exact whole tokens and never after `--`.

Most `run`/`serve` flags also read an `AI_AGENT_*` environment variable (shown
in `--help`). Where a stored default exists (`beyond-ai-agent settings`), the
order is: flag, then environment variable, then stored setting, then the
built-in default.

### Steer and follow-up queues

- **`--steering-mode` / `--follow-up-mode`** (run, serve): `run` honours both, not only `serve`. A
  one-shot `run` has no client to queue messages, but the agent queues its own steers: the `/session`
  pressure nudge and compaction reminder (`memory::SessionSteers`, the observer `run` and `serve`
  share). Unset, both fall back to the stored `steering_mode`/`follow_up_mode`, which `serve`'s
  `set_steering_mode`/`set_follow_up_mode` commands write.

### Compaction

- **`--no-compaction`** (run, serve): turns off only proactive, threshold-triggered compaction. A
  prompt that has already reached the model's input budget is still compacted before the next
  request, because sending it would only fail (`compaction::is_hard_overflow`).
  `serve` falls back to the stored `compaction_enabled`, which its `set_auto_compaction` command
  writes; `run` reads only the flag and `AI_AGENT_NO_COMPACTION`. Under `--service` the store is never
  opened, so a session starts with compaction on.

### Retries

- **`--retry-max-retries` / `--retry-base-delay-ms`** (run, serve) set both retry layers: the
  client's retry before the first byte, and the whole-run retry that re-runs a task which still ended
  in a transient-looking error (`retry::RunRetryPolicy`). So `--retry-max-retries 0` turns off both.
- **`--no-retry`** (run): turns off only the whole-run retry; the client's retry before the first byte
  keeps its `--retry-max-retries` count. `serve` has no such flag: its `set_auto_retry` command turns off the mid-stream and whole-run retries together, at runtime.

### Skills, templates and prompts

- **`--skill`, `--prompt-template`** (run, serve): an extra root fills gaps; it never overrides. On a
  name collision a standard root (`~/.claude/skills`, `<cwd>/.claude/skills`, and the rest) always
  wins over an extra one, so `--skill` cannot silently replace a project's own skill of the same name.
  Between two extra roots, the later one wins. A path that is neither a directory nor a `.md` file is
  refused at startup (see "Selection flags are checked at startup").
- **`--prompt-guideline`** (run, serve): each value is trimmed and deduplicated against the built-in
  guideline bullets. The bullets belong to the built-in base prompt, so they have no effect when
  `--system-prompt` or an on-disk `SYSTEM.md` replaces that base. A `run` subagent inherits them; a
  `serve` subagent does not, because `serve` renders its base prompt once and keeps no raw list.

### Sessions

- **`--name`** (run, serve): names only a fresh session (no messages and no title yet). A script that
  resumes the same session on a schedule would otherwise rewrite its title on every start, and the
  agent cannot tell "rename this" from "start it the way I always do". `set_session_name` renames an
  existing session. A whitespace-only value is refused, unlike `set_session_name`, where an empty title
  clears it: a startup argument is meant to be meaningful.
- **`--no-session-persistence`** (run, serve): in `run`, an explicit `--session`, `--fork` or
  `--continue` still persists, since asking to continue a session contradicts not persisting and the
  explicit verb wins; `--session-id` only names the in-memory session. In `serve`, an explicit `--session-dir`
  or `--session-file` takes precedence over it, but a stored `settings --session-dir` default does
  not: in both binaries `--no-session-persistence` beats the stored default and nothing is written.

### Output

- **`--export`** (run): the transcript is written however the run ends, failed or cancelled included,
  because a failed run's transcript (up to and including its closing error record) is the one most
  worth reading.

### Approval

- **`--approval-timeout`** (serve): `0` means no timeout at all, so a question nobody answers holds
  the call, and with it the session, until an `abort`. Use it only with a client that is reliably
  attached.

### Logins

- **`login`**: the stored credential is replaced only once the new login has succeeded. A failed or
  cancelled login leaves the old one in place.
- **`auth-status`**: reads only the local store and never calls the provider. `needs_reauth` means
  the last refresh attempt failed; the token stays on disk until a new `login` replaces it. A token
  that has expired without a refresh being tried still shows `logged_in`.
